Under a CLI backend the members travel to the job as a directory that the runtime reads back into a dict, and the code does not see that directory. A deepcell or deepfolder pin is a dict of checksum objects. Python code can resolve a member in memory ( Checksum.resolve() ), and in a CLI job under remote: daskserver only: no Seamless configuration is exported to a job on another backend. R and Julia code cannot resolve one, because their checksum class carries a checksum and no access to a buffer. These pins serve to select members and pass them on.
docs.title: Outside bash

docs.text: A folder pin is a new directory in the job directory , with the pin's name. It is never a link to a directory in a read-buffer directory. Seamless makes one entry in it for each key of the index: The member folder pin is on disk a symlink to that file is not the buffer is resolved, from any buffer source, and written The directory lives as long as the job directory , which is removed when the job ends. A folder entry has the form that the pin's name asks for. The pin mydata gets each member's bytes, and the pin mydata.zst gets them compressed, with .zst on each entry. An entry is a symlink where the stored form fits, and a file that is written in the asked form where it does not ( Compression ). In a container , a written entry is a file in the job directory, and a symlink points into a read-buffer directory that the wrapper binds, so it resolves there. A buffer file that the container cannot read counts as not on disk: a folder member is read through the link and copied into the job directory, in the form that the pin's name asks for. A deepcell or deepfolder pin is refused. The message names the pin and says to declare it folder or plain . It is refused when the pin's celltype is set, and again before launch for a transformation that arrives by another road.
docs.title: In bash

docs.text: A pin gets another form when it is declared with another celltype than its source. The cast is an Expression that is constructed when the Transformation is built, and a backend cannot tell what a pin was cast from. The legal pairs are those of Zero-path conversions : From To Legal The pin is then deepcell deepfolder yes, free a deepfolder pin deepfolder folder yes, free a folder pin folder deepfolder yes, free a deepfolder pin deepcell folder no. Go through deepfolder deepcell , deepfolder plain yes, free an ordinary plain pin that holds the index: a JSON file in bash, a dict of 64-hex strings elsewhere folder plain no. Go through deepfolder folder mixed yes, and it fetches every member an ordinary mixed pin: a dict of byte arrays deepcell , deepfolder mixed no. Go through folder deepfolder deepcell no A plain pin holds strings, not objects. Plain data holds no checksum objects in any language. A rule for a pin never depends on what it was cast from. The way to get another form is a cast. A transformer that wants 64-hex strings declares the pin plain . One that wants contents declares it folder . deepcell and deepfolder both give checksum objects.
docs.title: The casts

docs.text: The table above is the input side. The output side is not a second contract: a deep result is an index, exactly like a deep input. A result may be declared deepcell or folder , not deepfolder and not module ( transformer_class ). A result names what the transformer produced, and producing an index of buffers the transformer never wrote is not a claim it can make. How the dict is produced follows the same two columns. Bash writes a RESULT directory, for folder and for deepcell . Each file in it is a member that holds the file's bytes. For a deepcell result, each file is also verified to deserialize as mixed . One that does not fails the transformation, and the message names the file. A text file, an empty file and JSON with a trailing comma do not. A RESULT that is one file is never split into members. It fails, for deepcell as for folder . So does an empty RESULT directory. A member keeps its file's bytes, so it can be a buffer that Seamless would not write: the files 3 and {"a":[1,2]} are members as they are. Two scripts that write the same value with different whitespace get different member checksums. Every other backend returns a dict, as an in-memory Python transformer does. Under a CLI backend the dict travels from the job to the process that runs the transformation, and the code does not see how. pack_deep_structure turns the produced dict into an index. The produced dict must be flat at the key level — a dict with string keys — and each member is either a checksum object , inserted as is, or a value , serialized and replaced by its checksum. A deepcell member may be any mixed value, including a dict or a list : it is serialized as mixed , and the index stays flat because it holds only that member's checksum. A member is a value unless it is a checksum object. This holds in every language and under every backend: Member deepcell result folder result a checksum object a checksum a checksum a string of 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters a value, serialized as mixed , like any other string fails with a TypeError , like any other string any other string a value, serialized as mixed fails with a TypeError bytes a value a value: the member's bytes, also when they are 64 hexadecimal characters Code that returns 64-hex strings as checksums wraps them , in Checksum or in the class of its language. That includes code that takes the strings from a plain pin. Unwrapped, a deepcell result holds the strings as values, and nothing fails. A checksum inserted as a member is not checked. Nothing verifies that such a buffer exists. A checksum object is a member, or a checksum result, and nothing else. Returned under any other result celltype it fails the transformation. A checksum result accepts a checksum object and a 64-hex string: there the celltype says what the string is. No pickle is used to carry a member or a checksum. A job's result is read as data only. The transformation's result checksum is that index's checksum, so a Transformation handle, a Cell fed by it, a pin fed by it and a direct call all end up with that index. A transformation returns a checksum, as it always does; for a deep celltype the corresponding value is the index, {key: Checksum} — the general rule of What a deep buffer is , with nothing added for results. This includes the direct compiled transformer ( Transformer(..., compiled=True, direct=True) ): a deepcell result is returned as the validated index of Checksum objects, with no child resolved. A compiled result holds no checksum objects, so each of its members is a value. Two consequences follow, and both are contract: No fan-out on the way out. Reading a deep result never resolves its children. folder is not a special case here: a caller that wants the bytes asks for them, through the one conversion that materializes children ( folder → mixed , above), and pays that cost explicitly. Sugar that resolves all children behind a property read would hide an all children cost inside a shape that looks free, which is what The organising principle exists to prevent. No claim on the leaves. A transformation that produces a deep result holds a reference on the index checksum only , never on the members — the general no-recursive-deep-ownership rule, of which this is one instance ( contracts/internal/checksum-reference-lifecycle.md , §8). Members rely on ordinary deep-buffer resolution and remote durability.
docs.title: The output side: a deep result is an index

docs.text: Deep .buffer reads now validate both the mapped plain celltype and index flatness, in standalone and bound Cells and Pins. They return the index buffer without resolving its children; failures are raised on each read and leave the owner complete. Focused plain tests cover these routes in the deep-celltype and Pin contract test files. Current limitations (not contract violations): folder → mixed fetches its children one at a time. _evaluate_expression_async awaits each child's resolution() in index order, the synchronous path calls resolve() per child, and the folder pin ( unpack_deep_structure ) does the same. Resolution order and concurrency are unspecified ( folder → mixed ), so this is not a gap. The parallel multi-checksum waiter is deferred.
docs.title: Implementation status

docs.text: Treat a deep checksum as an index you may pass around freely. Holding it costs nothing and materializes nothing; reading its value gives {key: Checksum} , which is still nothing materialized. Use deepfolder when you want to refer to a directory, folder only when the consumer needs the bytes. The conversion between them is free, so declare the cheap one and widen late. Reach a single child with the one-step path, cell["key"] (bracket form): it yields the child's checksum at the member celltype, or at checksum for the reference form. Do not chain a second step or a second conversion into it; apply further conversions as separate Expressions, keyed at the child. Never write a nested deep index. Flat, string keys, 64-hex values. A deepcell member may be any mixed value, dicts and lists included. To change one member, write at k ( d["k"].set(v) , .checksum = , .buffer = ); never write below k . Do not expect null to rescue an illegal deep conversion: an illegal pair fails for null too. Do not expect a decoded-text view of a folder . Decode per file with bytes → text , or decode the whole folder inside a transformer. Do not depend on the order in which folder → mixed resolves children, nor on it being parallel. A deep result is an index, like a deep input: reading it resolves no children, and nothing holds a claim on the leaves. Outside bash, a folder pin is a dict of contents, and deepcell and deepfolder pins are dicts of checksum objects. Declare the pin plain to get 64-hex strings. Bash refuses deepcell and deepfolder pins. Wrap a checksum that you return as a member of a deep result: a naked 64-hex string is a value.
docs.title: Agent guidance

docs.text: direct / delayed / Transformation (Contract) This page defines the direct / delayed call modes and the immutable Transformation handle. The mutable Transformer builder, its standalone and bound modes, and the snapshot boundary are specified in contracts/transformers.md . One page of “how it behaves” (practical) This is the smallest reliable example shape: from seamless.transformer import direct, delayed @direct def f(a, b): return 10 * a + 2 * b @delayed def g(a, b): return 10 * a + 2 * b v = f(30, 12) # returns a value now tf = g(30, 12) # returns a Transformation handle cs = tf.compute() # computes and returns a checksum identifier v2 = tf.run() # resolves checksum into the value If you call the same transformer again with the same explicit inputs, Seamless may reuse cached results (when available) rather than recomputing. What the decorators return The direct and delayed decorators both return a Transformer. They do not return a Transformation and do not execute the decorated function at decoration time. Builder state, pins, binding and the mode-independent build() / transformation() operation are contracts/transformers.md . Calling the returned Transformer applies the call mode below. Callable versus signature-less pin declaration is contracts/pins.md , and compiled builders are contracts/compiled-transformers.md . Both functions are Python-only and accept exactly one argument: a Python function or an existing ordinary Transformer to clone into the requested call mode. They have no language argument. Bash, handler-language (R, Julia) and compiled builders are constructed with the Transformer(...) factory described in contracts/transformers.md . direct Treat direct(f) as “ __call__ builds a Transformation and returns its value now”. Directness affects __call__ only. f.build(...) and f.transformation(...) always return an unexecuted Transformation ( contracts/transformers.md ). direct is for ergonomic call-sites and small steps where immediate evaluation is desirable. If called from an environment that forbids blocking (common in notebooks/event loops), prefer the async APIs of Transformation instead. delayed Treat delayed(f) as “calling the returned Transformer is shorthand for f.build(...) and returns a Transformation handle”. delayed is the default for pipelines: you can build a graph of handles and decide when/how to run them. Constructing a delayed Transformation snapshots its concrete (non-dependency) inputs to checksums at construction time. A malformed concrete input can therefore raise when the handle is built , not only when it is run — building a handle you never intend to run is not guaranteed to be error-free. Transformation-valued inputs remain unresolved dependency edges and are not snapshotted. Transformation handle Assume these meanings (confirm with docs/docstrings for exact behavior): - .compute() : execute and return an identifier (checksum) for the result. On failure it returns None and sets .exception ; it does not raise (one rule with Cells and Pins: contracts/cells.md , Failures , How a failure is delivered ). - .run() : execute and return the resolved/materialized value. This is the call that raises: a failure raises TransformationError , whose message carries the recorded exception. - .start() : schedule computation (useful when starting many tasks before collecting results). - .task() / await : async execution; preferred in Jupyter/async contexts. - .cancel(*, recursive=False) / await .cancel_async(*, recursive=False) : move this handle to a terminal canceled state, and softcancel its participation in the underlying run — which is shared, so it continues for every other member and stops only when the last member leaves ( contracts/cancellation.md ). Returns True if it transitioned active work (or a local promise) to canceled or requested backend cancellation, False if nothing was active. After cancellation, status reports "Status: canceled" , result_checksum raises TransformationError , and clear_exception() does not revive it — a retry requires a new object. Cancellation never invalidates the tf_checksum ; a later submission of the same checksum is a new submission. With recursive=True , known upstream dependency handles are softcancelled with the same semantics. - .logs : a passive read that returns a str or None . On a failed handle it is the same string as .exception . After a successful execution in this process, or on a remote backend submitted from it, it is the captured stdout and stderr followed by the execution time. It is None on a canceled handle, and whenever this process holds no log for the tf_checksum : nothing has run yet, the run is in flight, or the result came from a cache. It never constructs or executes. See contracts/transformation-logs.md . Immutability A returned Transformation is a frozen computation definition plus a mutable execution promise. The definition (checksum payload, orthogonal dunder envelope, dependency edges, scratch policy) is immutable: tf.meta is a recursively read-only view and assigning tf.meta , tf.meta[...] , or tf.scratch raises. Mutating the objects you passed in (the original meta /dunder dict, inputs) after the handle is built does not affect its checksum or execution. Only execution-promise state (computed checksums, futures, result, status, exception) changes over the handle's lifetime. - process_lock and driver : both are in tf.meta on every built handle, and both are read-only there. They are set on the Transformer before the build ( contracts/transformers.md , process_lock and driver ). What they do when the handle runs is contracts/execution-backends.md , The process lock . - .streaming : when true, opt into live stdout/stderr streaming for fresh remote: daskserver executions without changing transformation identity. See Streaming . Optional Dask backend If Seamless’s Dask integration is available/configured: - a Transformation may delegate execution/scheduling to Dask (distributed task graph execution) - this improves HPC/distributed throughput without changing the “step identity” mental model An agent should check docs for how Dask is configured/enabled and what requirements exist for worker environments. Composition Passing one Transformation as an input to another wires an explicit dependency. Avoid implicit dependencies via globals/closures unless explicitly injected and content-bound. Minimal examples Prefer examples that don’t touch time/RNG/threads so caching and referential transparency are obvious.
docs.title: direct/delayed/Transformation

Mutating the objects you passed in (the original meta /dunder dict, inputs) after the handle is built does not affect its checksum or execution. Only execution-promise state (computed checksums, futures, result, status, exception) changes over the handle's lifetime. - process_lock and driver : both are in tf.meta on every built handle, and both are read-only there. They are set on the Transformer before the build ( contracts/transformers.md , process_lock and driver ). What they do when the handle runs is contracts/execution-backends.md , The process lock . - .streaming : when true, opt into live stdout/stderr streaming for fresh remote: daskserver executions without changing transformation identity. See Streaming .
docs.title: Immutability

docs.text: If Seamless’s Dask integration is available/configured: - a Transformation may delegate execution/scheduling to Dask (distributed task graph execution) - this improves HPC/distributed throughput without changing the “step identity” mental model An agent should check docs for how Dask is configured/enabled and what requirements exist for worker environments.

docs.text: Environments (Contract) An environment says where the script of a CLI job runs: in a named conda environment, or in a container made from a Docker image. The script, its inputs and its result stay the same. Only the place changes. A CLI job is the way a bash transformation always runs, and the way a transformation in R, Julia or Python runs under its CLI backend ( Language backends ). In this page "the script" is the script of a bash transformation, or the launcher of an interpreter for another language. The wrapper is the same for all of them. An in-memory backend cannot enter an environment, and has a rule of its own ( Language backends , Environments ). The implementation plan describes the launch mechanics and the phases, and the language backends plan their generalization to every language. The surface Python face. Every Transformer has an environment object: tf = Transformer("bash", direct=True) tf.code = "samtools --version > RESULT" tf.environment.set_conda_env("bio") # a named conda environment tf.environment.set_docker({"name": "ubuntu:22.04"}) # or a Docker image get_conda_env() and get_docker() read the values back. Passing None clears one. Unix face. seamless-run --conda ENV … and seamless-run --docker IMAGE … . --conda-env and --conda-environment are aliases of the first, --docker-image of the second. Workflow Context. A node that is bound from a Transformer carries that Transformer's environment, and the graph file saves it. On the bound node, environment is a read-only copy. Transformation dict. The environment travels as __env__ . In it, the conda environment is the string conda_environment and the image is the mapping docker ( The image spec ). These rules hold on every face: Every language can carry an environment, and what it does with it follows from its language backend. A CLI backend enters the environment: bash, and the CLI backends of R, Julia and Python. An in-memory backend cannot. It runs only when its process is already in exactly the conda environment that is asked for, and it fails for a Docker image. This is the rule for compiled transformers, for Python in memory, and for the in-memory backends of R and Julia. Language backends , Environments , has the rules. Building a Transformation with an environment never fails for this reason. The check happens when the transformation runs. - A record probe is exempt. The probe that captures a job's surroundings for a full execution record is a Python transformation that carries the job's __env__ ( Execution records , Probing is manual ). It runs on the host and it does not fail for the conda environment or the image that it carries. A full record can therefore be made for a bash job that has an environment. - A conda environment and a Docker image together are an error. A Transformer that has both builds, and the transformation fails when it is dispatched, before anything is launched. The check is repeated before launch on the executing host. seamless-run refuses the two flags together at dispatch as well. The message says to pick one. A script that needs a conda environment inside an image activates it itself. - Neither is ever ignored. A transformation with an environment runs in that environment, or in an in-memory backend satisfies it as a requirement on its process, or fails. It does not fall back to the plain host. What an environment changes, and what it does not Unchanged, with or without an environment, for a bash transformation ( seamless-run and argtyping , Pins ): the job directory: one file, link or directory per pin, and the script's working directory; the pin variables that the script sees; the header set -u -e ; the result: the file or directory RESULT ; stdout and stderr: two separate streams, relayed while the script runs ( Transformation logs , Streaming ). A conda environment The script runs as under conda run -n NAME . A name that contains / is the path of an environment , as for conda run -p . Activation happens before the script and outside its set -u -e . An activation script that reads an unset variable does not abort the job. The script inherits the environment variables of the process that runs it , as a plain bash transformation does, plus what activation adds. The environment must exist on the executing host , and so must a conda launcher ( The runtime is chosen where the job runs ). Seamless does not create environments. Entering the environment takes time on every job. With conda as the launcher that is in the order of a second. mamba and micromamba are much faster. A site that runs many short jobs sets SEAMLESS_CONDA_EXE . A Docker image The script runs inside a container made from the image. The image must contain bash . A bash transformation requires nothing else of it. A CLI backend of another language also needs its interpreter and its packages ( Language backends , The CLI rule ). Seamless does not need to be installed in it, except where the code itself uses Seamless, or a Python CLI job carries a value that needs seamless-core. The image's ENTRYPOINT is not used. The job directory is the working directory, at /seamless-job . That path is the same on every run, so $PWD is too. The container sees the job directory and nothing else of the host , with one exception: the read-buffer directories of the executing process are visible at their own paths, read-only. An input that Seamless provides as a link into such a directory therefore resolves. Every other buffer in those directories is readable by the image as well. A link that the container cannot follow is not used. A buffer file in a read-buffer directory can itself be a symlink to a file elsewhere, and that target is not bound. Where the transformation will run in a container, Seamless follows each buffer file before it links it, and treats one that ends outside what the wrapper binds as a buffer that is not on disk. An ordinary input and a folder member are then copied into the job directory. Bash refuses deepfolder pins before launch; handler backends carry their checksum objects without needing member files in the container ( Deep celltypes , How deep values reach a transformer ). What the wrapper binds is the job directory and the read-buffer directories. A bind that an operator adds with SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_ARGS is not seen, so such a bind makes a copy that was not needed. The host's environment variables are not inherited. The pin variables are set. HOME is /seamless-job , the working directory. It is a writable directory owned by the user running the job, including when the image has no passwd entry for that user. Apptainer maps the job directory there with --home ; its --env option cannot override HOME . The script runs as the user that runs the job on the host. Files it writes belong to that user. An image that only works as root or as a named user of its own may fail. Background processes of the script end with the container. The container is removed when the script ends , however it ends. Nothing is kept from one job to the next, and what the script writes outside the job directory is lost. Identity and caching The environment is not part of the transformation's identity. It is carried in __env__ , an orthogonal key ( Identity and caching , Load-bearing vs orthogonal keys ). Two transformations that differ only in their conda environment or their image have the same checksum. A result that is cached is returned whatever the environment says. Nothing is launched, and none of the checks on this page run. A tag that moves still gets a cache hit. ubuntu:22.04 rebuilt upstream changes nothing for a transformation that already has a result. Seamless does not police mutable tags. For work that must be reproducible, name the image by digest: name@sha256:… . The container runtimes share one cache. A result computed under docker is a cache hit for the same transformation on an apptainer host. Fingertipping runs the environment where the buffer is wanted. A fingertip is never dispatched ( Scratch, witness, audit , Fingertipping ). The machine that asks needs the conda environment, or a container runtime and the image. What the tag points to there decides what is recomputed. Two submissions of one transformation with different environments latch on to each other , unless strict_dunder is used ( Identity and caching , Concurrent submissions of the same checksum ). The image spec set_docker takes a mapping. seamless-run --docker sets name only. Key Type Meaning name str, required A Docker image reference. A digest reference is allowed gpus bool, default false Give the container access to the host's NVIDIA GPUs shm_size str, such as "1g" Size of /dev/shm . Ignored under apptainer Every other key is an error. It is checked when the transformation is dispatched, and again before launch on the executing host. Setting the spec, and building a Transformation, check nothing. For three legacy keys the message names the replacement: options : use gpus and shm_size ; version , checksum : use name@sha256:<digest> . gpus gives access to GPUs on the machine where the job runs, and it needs the runtime's NVIDIA support there. It does not send the job to a machine that has a GPU. That is done by choosing the stage ( Execution backends ). The runtime is chosen where the job runs A Docker image can be run by three container runtimes: docker , podman and apptainer . Which one runs a job is a property of the executing host, never of the transformation. Setting on the executing host Values Default SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_RUNTIME docker , podman , apptainer , none the first that works, in that order SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_PULL never , missing never SEAMLESS_APPTAINER_DIR a directory of SIF files none SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_ARGS extra arguments for the runtime's run command none SEAMLESS_CONDA_EXE the conda launcher: conda , mamba or micromamba , or a path to one $CONDA_EXE , else $CONDA_ROOT/bin/conda , else conda on PATH Without the setting, the runtime is detected. docker is taken when its daemon answers, else podman, else apptainer. A process detects once and keeps the answer. none refuses container jobs. An operator uses it on a host that has a runtime installed but must not run containers. The failure says that the host does not allow them. With no working runtime the job fails. The failure names the image, the host and the runtimes that were tried. The runtime is chosen before the job directory is written. A host that cannot run a container job refuses it in the same way on every backend. By default nothing is pulled. An image that is not present on the executing host is a failure. With missing , the runtime fetches it. apptainer looks for <SEAMLESS_APPTAINER_DIR>/<name>.sif , with the image name used literally: ubuntu:22.04 is the file ubuntu:22.04.sif , and biocontainers/samtools:1.19 is samtools:1.19.sif in the subdirectory biocontainers . When the file is missing, the failure prints the apptainer pull command that creates it. With missing , apptainer runs docker://<name> from its own cache instead. SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_ARGS is the only way to pass further options to the runtime , and it is per host. It is split into words as a shell does. A site puts its SELinux label option, a network flag or an extra bind there. A submitter chooses the image and nothing else. A transformation cannot choose mounts, privileges, networks or limits. With no conda launcher the job fails , and the failure says so. The product that is still called Singularity is not supported. A singularity command is not looked for, and the legacy variables SEAMLESS_SINGULARITY_DIR and SEAMLESS_DOCKER_DISABLED and the legacy .simg files are not read. Where the settings are read, per backend: Backend Executing host Settings come from process , spawn the submitting machine the environment of the submitting process remote: jobserver the jobserver host the environment the jobserver was started in remote: daskserver the Dask worker nodes the queue's job_script_prologue What a shared executing host exposes. Whoever can submit a bash transformation, or a CLI job of another language, to it can run any image that is present there, with GPUs if the spec asks for them, and that image can read the read-buffer directories. This adds little to a plain bash transformation, which already runs arbitrary code as the user of that host. With the pull policy never , the operator decides which images are present. SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_RUNTIME=none switches containers off. Required binaries tf.environment.set_which([...]) lists binaries that must exist. For a CLI backend, of every language, they are looked up where the script runs : after conda activation, or inside the image. A binary that exists only in the environment satisfies the check, and one that exists only on the host does not. For an in-memory backend they are looked up on the PATH of the process that runs the code. There is no environment to enter, so the host is where the code runs ( Language backends , Required binaries ). A record probe that carries a conda environment or an image does not check them. The probe runs on the host, where a binary of the environment need not exist. Failures Each of the following is a failure of the transformation, and failures are not cached. Before anything is launched , a job is refused when: its spec is invalid: an unknown key in the image spec, or a conda environment together with an image. Both are found at dispatch, and checked again here; the executing host cannot run it: SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_RUNTIME=none , no working runtime, no conda launcher, or a Docker daemon that is not local ( Current limitations ). After the launched process has exited , the outcome is classified in this order: The environment was not entered. The script did not start: the conda environment does not exist, the image is absent, or the image has no bash . The failure names the environment (the conda environment, or the runtime and the image), the exit code and the command that was run. What the launcher printed is in the stdout and stderr trailers. Docker reported 125 for a runtime error, such as an absent image under the pull policy never , and 127 when its init process could not find bash in the image. Podman 4.9.3 reported 125 for a runtime error and 1 when catatonit could not exec bash ; its stderr identifies that case. The start marker distinguishes it from a script that itself exits 1. Preserve the runtime's exit code rather than treating 1 alone as proof that the environment was not entered. apptainer exits 255 in both cases. Only its stderr tells them apart. This class is what separates a missing conda environment, for which conda run exits 1, from a script that exits 1. Without an environment, this class means that the script itself could not be started. A required binary is missing where the script runs. The text is Required environment binaries are unavailable: … , followed by where they were looked for. The script exits with a non-zero code. This is the Bash transformer exception report ( Transformation logs , The failure text ), with one more line that names the environment. For a container, exit code 137 adds a hint that the job was killed, possibly for exceeding a memory limit. RESULT is missing or empty , as for a plain bash transformation. After a failing script, conda run adds a line of its own to stderr. It is part of the captured stderr. The job directory on disk Seamless materializes a job directory for every CLI job and runs bash transform.sh in it. seamless-run --dry --write-remote-job DIR writes that directory without running it ( seamless-run and argtyping ). Only a bash transformation can be written instead of run. The other CLI backends run their job and never write a directory for the user. bash transform.sh is the way to run it, with or without an environment. What is written is what Seamless itself would have run. Without an environment, transform.sh is the script. With an environment, transform.sh is a launcher of one command, and the script is transform-inner.sh next to it. The launcher enters the conda environment or starts the container, and runs the script there. The script sets every pin variable itself. It does not rely on the environment variables of the process that wrote it. The script is run as a file. Its length is not limited by the size of a command-line argument, $0 is its file name, and bash's own error messages start with transform.sh: line N: or transform-inner.sh: line N: . The directory can be moved. The launcher refers to the directory it is run from. A container launcher names the runtime of the host that wrote the directory. It is plain text and can be edited for another site. File names that start with .seamless- are reserved in a job directory. Seamless's part of the script writes two of them: .seamless-started when the script starts, and .seamless-missing when a required binary is absent. User code does not create or remove such files. The first word of a seamless-run command Without an environment, seamless-run looks the first word of a command up on the submitting machine's PATH , and uploads the program when it is found outside the standard tool directories ( seamless-run and argtyping , The first word of a command ). With --conda or --docker : seamless-run does not look. The first word is the name of a tool in the environment, even when the submitting machine has a tool of that name. A local file is still uploaded. seamless-run --docker IMAGE ./analyze.sh data.txt uploads analyze.sh , as it uploads data.txt , and runs it inside the image. A personal tool that is on the submitting machine's PATH must be given by its path to be uploaded. The process lock, nesting and cancellation A job with an environment is a bash body , and so is every CLI job. It takes the process lock of the process that runs it, like any other body, and holds it until the script ends ( Execution backends , The process lock ). A long container job occupies its process for that time. process_lock false, or seamless-run --no-process-lock , lets it run next to others. Under a conda environment, nested work is signalled as for plain bash. A seamless-run that the script starts tells the body, and the body gives the lock up ( Execution backends , Bash bodies ). Inside a container it is not. The signal does not cross the container boundary. A containerized script that submits nested work must be declared a driver, or have process_lock false. A cancel that stops the run ends the environment too ( Cancellation , A bash run that is cancelled ). The script is killed, with the processes it started. Under a conda environment that includes conda run . A container is removed. It does not keep running after its job was cancelled. There is no grace period. The script is not given time to clean up. Hard cancellation tears down the environment in process , spawn and remote: jobserver . It also did so in remote: daskserver in the measured local harness; see Cancellation , A bash run that is cancelled . A softcancel never stops a Dask run. A docker or podman container that Seamless starts carries the label seamless.tf=<tf_checksum> for as long as it exists. docker ps --filter label=seamless.tf=<tf_checksum> lists the container of a running job, and nothing once the job has ended or was cancelled. Current limitations A bound node's environment cannot be changed. It is set on the Transformer before binding. The execution record does not say which image ran. It identifies the spec text, and a probe looks the image name up when the probe runs ( Execution records ). A moved tag is not visible in it afterwards. The record's environment bucket describes the process that ran the job, not the conda environment or the image of the script. A remote Docker daemon is not supported. A job fails before launch when DOCKER_HOST or CONTAINER_HOST names anything but a local unix:// socket. The daemon must see the job directory at the path Seamless sees it. A Seamless process that itself runs in a container and uses the host's daemon works only when those paths are shared. Otherwise the environment is not entered, and the failure says what to suspect. Under docker and podman, a path that contains a comma cannot be mounted. A job whose job directory or read-buffer directory has such a path is refused with a message. docker and podman need their init helper on the executing host. Without it the container does not start. apptainer must be able to create mount points inside the image , which is its default. A site that has disabled this cannot run container jobs under apptainer. Nested Seamless commands inside a container need Seamless in the image and a route to the services. Neither is provided. Non-goals Running compiled transformers in a container or in another conda environment. A compiled call runs inside the worker process, which cannot be wrapped. Creating a conda environment from a specification. set_conda stores one, and execution does not act on it. Building images, or converting them to SIF files. Per-transformation container options beyond the image spec, and a per-transformation choice of runtime. An allowlist of images.
