When the file is missing, the failure prints the apptainer pull command that creates it. With missing , apptainer runs docker://<name> from its own cache instead. SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_ARGS is the only way to pass further options to the runtime , and it is per host. It is split into words as a shell does. A site puts its SELinux label option, a network flag or an extra bind there. A submitter chooses the image and nothing else. A transformation cannot choose mounts, privileges, networks or limits. With no conda launcher the job fails , and the failure says so. The product that is still called Singularity is not supported. A singularity command is not looked for, and the legacy variables SEAMLESS_SINGULARITY_DIR and SEAMLESS_DOCKER_DISABLED and the legacy .simg files are not read. Where the settings are read, per backend: Backend Executing host Settings come from process , spawn the submitting machine the environment of the submitting process remote: jobserver the jobserver host the environment the jobserver was started in remote: daskserver the Dask worker nodes the queue's job_script_prologue What a shared executing host exposes. Whoever can submit a bash transformation, or a CLI job of another language, to it can run any image that is present there, with GPUs if the spec asks for them, and that image can read the read-buffer directories. This adds little to a plain bash transformation, which already runs arbitrary code as the user of that host. With the pull policy never , the operator decides which images are present. SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_RUNTIME=none switches containers off.
docs.title: The runtime is chosen where the job runs

docs.text: tf.environment.set_which([...]) lists binaries that must exist. For a CLI backend, of every language, they are looked up where the script runs : after conda activation, or inside the image. A binary that exists only in the environment satisfies the check, and one that exists only on the host does not. For an in-memory backend they are looked up on the PATH of the process that runs the code. There is no environment to enter, so the host is where the code runs ( Language backends , Required binaries ). A record probe that carries a conda environment or an image does not check them. The probe runs on the host, where a binary of the environment need not exist.
docs.title: Required binaries

docs.text: Each of the following is a failure of the transformation, and failures are not cached. Before anything is launched , a job is refused when: its spec is invalid: an unknown key in the image spec, or a conda environment together with an image. Both are found at dispatch, and checked again here; the executing host cannot run it: SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_RUNTIME=none , no working runtime, no conda launcher, or a Docker daemon that is not local ( Current limitations ). After the launched process has exited , the outcome is classified in this order: The environment was not entered. The script did not start: the conda environment does not exist, the image is absent, or the image has no bash . The failure names the environment (the conda environment, or the runtime and the image), the exit code and the command that was run. What the launcher printed is in the stdout and stderr trailers. Docker reported 125 for a runtime error, such as an absent image under the pull policy never , and 127 when its init process could not find bash in the image. Podman 4.9.3 reported 125 for a runtime error and 1 when catatonit could not exec bash ; its stderr identifies that case. The start marker distinguishes it from a script that itself exits 1. Preserve the runtime's exit code rather than treating 1 alone as proof that the environment was not entered. apptainer exits 255 in both cases. Only its stderr tells them apart. This class is what separates a missing conda environment, for which conda run exits 1, from a script that exits 1. Without an environment, this class means that the script itself could not be started. A required binary is missing where the script runs. The text is Required environment binaries are unavailable: … , followed by where they were looked for. The script exits with a non-zero code. This is the Bash transformer exception report ( Transformation logs , The failure text ), with one more line that names the environment. For a container, exit code 137 adds a hint that the job was killed, possibly for exceeding a memory limit. RESULT is missing or empty , as for a plain bash transformation. After a failing script, conda run adds a line of its own to stderr. It is part of the captured stderr.
docs.title: Failures

docs.text: Seamless materializes a job directory for every CLI job and runs bash transform.sh in it. seamless-run --dry --write-remote-job DIR writes that directory without running it ( seamless-run and argtyping ). Only a bash transformation can be written instead of run. The other CLI backends run their job and never write a directory for the user. bash transform.sh is the way to run it, with or without an environment. What is written is what Seamless itself would have run. Without an environment, transform.sh is the script. With an environment, transform.sh is a launcher of one command, and the script is transform-inner.sh next to it. The launcher enters the conda environment or starts the container, and runs the script there. The script sets every pin variable itself. It does not rely on the environment variables of the process that wrote it. The script is run as a file. Its length is not limited by the size of a command-line argument, $0 is its file name, and bash's own error messages start with transform.sh: line N: or transform-inner.sh: line N: . The directory can be moved. The launcher refers to the directory it is run from. A container launcher names the runtime of the host that wrote the directory. It is plain text and can be edited for another site. File names that start with .seamless- are reserved in a job directory. Seamless's part of the script writes two of them: .seamless-started when the script starts, and .seamless-missing when a required binary is absent. User code does not create or remove such files.
docs.title: The job directory on disk

docs.text: Without an environment, seamless-run looks the first word of a command up on the submitting machine's PATH , and uploads the program when it is found outside the standard tool directories ( seamless-run and argtyping , The first word of a command ). With --conda or --docker : seamless-run does not look. The first word is the name of a tool in the environment, even when the submitting machine has a tool of that name. A local file is still uploaded. seamless-run --docker IMAGE ./analyze.sh data.txt uploads analyze.sh , as it uploads data.txt , and runs it inside the image. A personal tool that is on the submitting machine's PATH must be given by its path to be uploaded.
docs.title: The first word of a seamless-run command

docs.text: A job with an environment is a bash body , and so is every CLI job. It takes the process lock of the process that runs it, like any other body, and holds it until the script ends ( Execution backends , The process lock ). A long container job occupies its process for that time. process_lock false, or seamless-run --no-process-lock , lets it run next to others. Under a conda environment, nested work is signalled as for plain bash. A seamless-run that the script starts tells the body, and the body gives the lock up ( Execution backends , Bash bodies ). Inside a container it is not. The signal does not cross the container boundary. A containerized script that submits nested work must be declared a driver, or have process_lock false. A cancel that stops the run ends the environment too ( Cancellation , A bash run that is cancelled ). The script is killed, with the processes it started. Under a conda environment that includes conda run . A container is removed. It does not keep running after its job was cancelled. There is no grace period. The script is not given time to clean up. Hard cancellation tears down the environment in process , spawn and remote: jobserver . It also did so in remote: daskserver in the measured local harness; see Cancellation , A bash run that is cancelled . A softcancel never stops a Dask run. A docker or podman container that Seamless starts carries the label seamless.tf=<tf_checksum> for as long as it exists. docker ps --filter label=seamless.tf=<tf_checksum> lists the container of a running job, and nothing once the job has ended or was cancelled.
docs.title: The process lock, nesting and cancellation

docs.text: A bound node's environment cannot be changed. It is set on the Transformer before binding. The execution record does not say which image ran. It identifies the spec text, and a probe looks the image name up when the probe runs ( Execution records ). A moved tag is not visible in it afterwards. The record's environment bucket describes the process that ran the job, not the conda environment or the image of the script. A remote Docker daemon is not supported. A job fails before launch when DOCKER_HOST or CONTAINER_HOST names anything but a local unix:// socket. The daemon must see the job directory at the path Seamless sees it. A Seamless process that itself runs in a container and uses the host's daemon works only when those paths are shared. Otherwise the environment is not entered, and the failure says what to suspect. Under docker and podman, a path that contains a comma cannot be mounted. A job whose job directory or read-buffer directory has such a path is refused with a message. docker and podman need their init helper on the executing host. Without it the container does not start. apptainer must be able to create mount points inside the image , which is its default. A site that has disabled this cannot run container jobs under apptainer. Nested Seamless commands inside a container need Seamless in the image and a route to the services. Neither is provided.
docs.title: Current limitations

docs.text: Running compiled transformers in a container or in another conda environment. A compiled call runs inside the worker process, which cannot be wrapped. Creating a conda environment from a specification. set_conda stores one, and execution does not act on it. Building images, or converting them to SIF files. Per-transformation container options beyond the image spec, and a per-transformation choice of runtime. An allowlist of images.
docs.title: Non-goals

docs.text: Execution Backends (Contract) This page defines the minimum operational model an agent may rely on when discussing “remote execution” or HPC with Seamless. Terms Execution mode : how transformations execute: process , spawn , or remote . Remote target (only relevant when execution: remote ): jobserver or daskserver . Mutual exclusivity : a single configured cluster/frontend should not expose both jobserver and daskserver without explicitly selecting one. This page is about Transformations. Expressions also run on a jobserver or daskserver, but they are placed by a different rule and on a different axis — see Expressions are placed, not configured below. Do not read the execution: configuration key and an Expression's execution= argument as the same setting. Backend semantics (agent assumptions) 1) process - Runs in the caller’s Python process. - No infrastructure required. - By default, one transformation runs its code at a time ( The process lock ). 2) spawn - Runs in local spawned worker processes. - Still “single machine”, but parallel: by default, one transformation runs its code at a time in each worker process. 3) remote: jobserver - Uses a jobserver process plus a worker pool, reached over HTTP. - Intended as a low-ops remote mode (development/testing/single-node remote execution). 4) remote: daskserver - Uses Dask as the execution/scheduling substrate. - Intended for HPC/distributed throughput; can integrate with schedulers (commonly via dask-jobqueue on SLURM/OAR). - Operationally: typically long-lived/bundled workers execute many tasks (not one scheduler submission per Seamless step). - Supports opt-in live stdout/stderr streaming per transformation; see Streaming . Output and logs per backend A transformation's stdout and stderr are captured on every backend. After a successful run they are in Transformation.logs , followed by the execution time. After a failure they are in the trailers of .exception . Backends differ in where the capture happens and in whether the output is also visible while the run is in flight: Backend Streams in the success log Live output while the run is in flight process captured by a tee in the caller's process on the caller's stdout and stderr spawn captured in the worker child none remote: jobserver captured in the worker child, returned in the jobserver's response none remote: daskserver captured in the worker child, returned to the client with the result only with streaming Streaming is Dask-only. process , spawn and remote: jobserver ignore the flag ( contracts/streaming.md ). A log exists only for a run that executed. A result that comes from a cache or from the database has no log, on any backend. The execution time in the log is the dispatcher's measurement , the same number as wall_time_seconds in the execution record. It includes queueing, inter-process transfer and input resolution. The log's layout, its per-process store, what is and is not captured, and the rules for bash and compiled transformers are contracts/transformation-logs.md . Environments are entered on the executing host A transformation can name a conda environment or a Docker image. A CLI backend, which is the bash transformer and the CLI backends of Python, R and Julia ( contracts/language-backends.md ), runs its script there ( contracts/environments.md ). The executing host is the machine on which the script runs. It enters the environment, so it must provide it. Backend Executing host Its settings are read from process , spawn the submitting machine the environment of the submitting process remote: jobserver the jobserver host the environment the jobserver was started in remote: daskserver the Dask worker nodes the queue's job_script_prologue For a conda environment, the executing host needs that environment and a conda launcher. For a Docker image, the executing host needs a container runtime and the image. The runtime is docker, podman or apptainer. The host chooses it, by the setting SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_RUNTIME or else by detection. A transformation never names a runtime. By default no image is pulled. Every backend behaves the same. The job is wrapped where it executes, and no backend does anything of its own for an environment. A host that cannot enter the environment fails the job. No backend falls back to running the script on the plain host. A fingertip needs the environment where the buffer is wanted. A fingertip is never dispatched, so the process that asks for the buffer enters the environment itself ( contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md , Fingertipping ). An in-memory backend is never wrapped. Its code runs inside the process that executes it: Python in memory, compiled transformations, and the in-memory backends of R, Julia and other handler languages. A Docker image on one is an error, on every backend. A conda environment is a requirement on that process, which must already be in exactly that environment ( contracts/language-backends.md , The in-memory rule ). The process is the one that the execution backend runs bodies in: the calling process in process , a worker process otherwise. Required binaries are looked up where the code runs. For a CLI backend that is the executing host's environment or image, after it is entered, and for an in-memory backend the PATH of the executing process ( contracts/language-backends.md , Required binaries ). A specification that could never work is refused when the transformation is dispatched on the submitting side: a conda environment together with a Docker image, and an unknown key of the image spec. It is checked again on the executing host before launch ( contracts/language-backends.md , The check happens at dispatch ). The image spec's gpus does not place a job. It gives the container access to the GPUs of the host on which the job runs. Which host that is follows from the backend and the queue, as for any transformation. contracts/environments.md has the settings, the failures and the limitations. Current limitation: fingertipping in a worker needs Dask In spawn and remote: jobserver , a transformation runs in a worker process that cannot see its parent's fingertip candidates: neither the parent's reverse caches nor its database. A fingertip in such a worker tries only the producers that the worker itself launched (nested transformations). If those do not recover the buffer, it raises NotImplementedError , and the job fails with that error in its traceback. It does not report a CacheMissError , because the search was incomplete. In spawn , the parent recovers a transformation's direct inputs before dispatch. When input fingertipping is enabled and Dask is not in use, the parent fingertips every input pin whose buffer is absent, before it hands the transformation to a worker. The worker then downloads the bytes from the parent over the local worker channel, as it does for any input. Pins that the worker reads from the file system are left alone. If the parent's fingertip fails, the transformation fails with that CacheMissError and its fingertip category; the worker never runs. What this still blocks. In remote: jobserver : a transformation with allow_input_fingertip whose input buffer is absent (a scratch result, or an evicted one) fails, unless the worker launched the input's producer itself. In spawn : a buffer that is not a direct input but that the worker needs, such as a member of a folder or deep input whose index is present. The worker fingertips it itself, which raises NotImplementedError as above. What works. process (the fingertip runs in the caller's process, which holds the candidates), the direct inputs in spawn (above), and remote: daskserver (the workers of a Dask worker can query the database). This is a limitation, not the contract. The contract is that an input fingertip inside a job works on every backend ( contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md , Case 1 ). The process lock Two terms are used below. The body of a transformation is its user code: the Python function, the bash script or the compiled call. For a handler language such as R or Julia, the body is the call of the handler that runs the code ( contracts/handler-languages.md ). For Python under its CLI backend, the body is the run of the job. Nested work is a transformation whose execution is requested from inside a body. Every process that runs bodies has one process lock, and by default a body runs while holding it. A transformation whose process_lock is true waits for the lock of the process it was placed in, runs its body while holding the lock, and releases the lock when the body ends. process_lock is true by default ( contracts/transformers.md , process_lock and driver ). Among such transformations, at most one body runs at a time in any one process. This holds on every backend, and for Python, bash, handler-language and compiled transformers alike. The lock is held around the body only. Input resolution, module building and result serialization happen outside it. Several transformations in one process therefore download and upload at the same time. The lock keeps holders apart, and nothing else. A body that does not hold the lock can run next to a holder in the same process. Three kinds of body do not hold it: a body with process_lock false, a driver ( Drivers ), and a body that gave the lock up ( Nested work gives the lock up ). Code outside any transformation, such as the script that submits work in process mode, never waits for the lock. What the lock is for. It protects state that the bodies of one process share, such as the working directory, environment variables or a library that is not thread-safe, as long as every body there keeps the default. It also fixes how many bodies run at once: one per process ( Concurrency per backend ). The lock is controlled by metadata only. There is no lock object for user code to take. The name global_lock is retired without an alias. Neither seamless_transformer nor seamless.transformer exports it, and reading it as an attribute of either module raises AttributeError with a message that points to process_lock . Code that took it inside a body declares process_lock on the transformer instead. Nested work gives the lock up A body that submits nested work gives up the lock at that moment, if it holds it, and never takes it again. It happens at submission , before it is known whether the nested result is cached. Whether a body keeps its lock therefore does not depend on the state of any cache. The reason is that nested work can land in the submitter's own process. In process mode it always does. In a worker pool it does when the nested transformation is dispatched to the worker that submitted it, and when the pool is full, in which case the worker runs it itself. A parent that kept the lock would wait for a child that waits for the parent's lock. Afterwards the body runs without the lock until it ends. That includes the code that follows the return of the nested results. A body has its process to itself only up to its first nested submission. No declaration is needed. A transformation that keeps every default may submit nested work. These calls, made by a body, are nested submissions: Call Kind tr.start() scheduling tr.compute() , tr.run() , a call of a direct Transformer synchronous execution await tr.computation() , tr.task() asynchronous execution parallel() , parallel_async() batches a fingertip that recomputes a transformation recovery of an absent buffer by running its producer again ( contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md , Fingertipping ) Building a Transformation without running it is not a submission. Neither is reading a handle: status , exception , result_checksum , value , buffer , logs . The rule covers the body's own thread and the coroutines of its event loop. A submission from a thread that the body started itself is not attributed to the body, and the lock stays held. A workflow Context created inside a body is such a case, because a Context submits its nodes from its own controller thread. A body that submits in this way must have process_lock false, or be a driver. If it keeps the default, a nested transformation that lands in its process waits for the lock while the body waits for the transformation. The two then hang, and no error is raised. Drivers A driver is a transformation declared with driver true: its body mainly launches other transformations and waits for them. A driver never takes the lock. Its body starts even while the lock of its process is held, and it runs next to whatever else runs there. Its submissions are marked as coming from a driver. On remote: daskserver , a nested submission normally asks for permission before it goes to Dask. It can be made to wait, and it can be handed back to the submitter to run itself. This is the anti-deadlock routine described in seamless-dask/anti-deadlock.txt . A submission made by a driver's body skips the routine. So does the submission of a driver itself. The mark is not inherited. A transformation launched by a driver is an ordinary transformation. It takes or leaves the lock according to its own settings, it is deduplicated as usual, and the nested work that it submits in turn asks for permission again. Nested work from a CLI job gets what its configuration gives it: A nested seamless-run finds its configuration from SEAMLESS_CACHE , or from SEAMLESS_REMOTE_CLIENTS together with the Dask scheduler, or else from a configuration file in its working directory. For a job, the working directory is the job directory, which holds none. Only the Dask worker exports these variables. Under remote: daskserver a nested seamless-run from a bash job, and a nested transformation from a Python CLI job ( contracts/language-backends.md , Drivers and nested work ), therefore go to the same cluster and share its caches. On process , spawn and remote: jobserver nothing is exported. A nested seamless-run there fails for lack of a configuration, unless one of the variables is in the environment that the job inherits, and a nested call in a Python CLI job runs inside the job's own process, with no cache and no dispatch. A submission from the job's own process skips the permission routine , because the process is neither a worker nor one that has spawned workers. The mark of a driver is not what decides it. Inside a container nothing is exported and the nesting signal does not cross. Nested work from a containerized job is not supported. Declaring a driver is never needed for correctness, because an undeclared body gives the lock up at its first nested submission. The declaration matters in two cases: when the body should not wait for the lock at all, and on Dask, where it lifts the permission routine from the body's launches. Bash bodies What this section says of a bash body holds for the body of every CLI backend : the bash transformer, and the CLI backends of Python, R and Julia ( contracts/language-backends.md ). A job in any of them is a process of its own, started by the process that runs the transformation, and is signalled and torn down in the same way. A bash transformation never changes the working directory of the process that runs it. The script runs in a job directory of its own, which is its working directory. The process keeps the working directory it had, so a relative path used by other code in that process keeps its meaning. A bash body takes the lock like any other body , unless process_lock is false or the transformation is a driver. For seamless-run these are --no-process-lock and --driver ( contracts/seamless-run-and-argtyping.md ). A bash body that holds the lock is told when its script submits nested work. The script's environment contains the variable SEAMLESS_PROCESS_LOCK_NOTIFY . A Seamless program that the script starts, such as seamless-run , uses the variable to signal the body when it first submits a transformation. The body then gives the lock up, as any body does. seamless-run --qsubmit signals as well. The script itself has nothing to do. The nested command keeps its own defaults. It does not become a driver, and neither does the bash transformation whose script started it. The variable is set only when the body holds the lock as its script starts. Otherwise the body removes it from the script's environment, so that a nested command never signals a process further up. The signal works for as long as the script's process runs , also after the script has closed its stdout and stderr. The signal is a named pipe on the local filesystem. The nested command must see the same filesystem as the body, and the signal does not cross ssh or a container boundary. A bash body that submits nested work through one of those must be declared a driver, or have process_lock false. A bash body with an environment is a bash body like any other ( contracts/environments.md ). It takes the lock and holds it until its script ends, so a long container job occupies its process for that time. A script under a conda environment has the variable and is signalled as a plain script is. A script in a container made from the transformation's Docker image is behind a container boundary: the variable is not passed in, and the previous rule applies. Handler languages and embedded interpreters A handler-language transformation runs R, Julia or another registered language through a handler. The R and the Julia handler each have two ways to run the code, which this section calls a CLI backend and an in-memory backend. Python has both as well: in memory by default, and as a CLI job with BACKEND="cli" . These are language backends , selected per Transformer, and they are independent of the execution backends of this page. contracts/language-backends.md specifies the two kinds and the Python CLI backend, and contracts/handler-languages.md the handler ones. A CLI backend starts one interpreter process for each run , on the machinery of bash transformations. Bash bodies holds for it: the process keeps its working directory, and the body is told when the code starts a nested seamless-run . By default one such run is in flight per process. With process_lock false they run side by side, each in its own interpreter process. An in-memory backend embeds the interpreter in the process that runs the body. That is the caller's process in process mode, and each worker process otherwise. A process has one embedded interpreter per language. It starts at its first use and lives until the process ends. An in-memory backend of a handler language refuses to run without the lock. A transformation that has process_lock false fails when its body starts, and so does a driver. The message names the CLI backend as the alternative. A result that is already recorded is still returned, because nothing runs. Python and compiled bodies in memory have no such rule: they run without the lock when process_lock is false, as always. The process lock is the only lock around an embedded interpreter. Among transformations that hold it, one body runs at a time in a process, so one transformation at a time uses the interpreter. An in-memory body holds the lock from its start to its end. It cannot give the lock up: there is no nesting signal as for a bash body. Code that submits nested work, for example by running seamless-run , belongs under the CLI backend. Two facts about where bodies run matter to whoever writes a handler: The lock gives exclusion, not a fixed thread. A body never runs on the main thread of its process, and successive bodies in one process run on different threads. In process mode the thread that ran one body may no longer exist when the next body runs. An interpreter that must always be called from the same thread gets that thread from run_in_interpreter_thread ( contracts/handler-languages.md , Threads, and run_in_interpreter_thread ), not from the lock. A body may hold Python's GIL for a long time. A worker pool checks each of its worker processes about once a second. A body that keeps the GIL, as a call into an embedded interpreter can, makes its worker miss the check, but a worker that is running a transformation is not restarted for that. It is restarted only when its process exits or its connection closes. This holds in spawn and in both remote modes. Concurrency per backend The lock is per process, so the number of bodies that run at once follows from the number of processes in which a backend runs bodies. A worker process accepts up to three transformations at once. That number is the transformation throttle. The lock then decides how many of their bodies run. Backend Processes that run bodies Bodies at once when every transformation keeps the default Bodies at once with process_lock false process the caller's process 1 not limited by the lock spawn with N workers N worker processes N, one per worker up to 3 per worker, 3N in total remote: jobserver with N workers N worker processes N, one per worker up to 3 per worker, 3N in total remote: daskserver the Seamless worker processes inside each Dask worker one per Seamless worker process up to the throttle per Seamless worker process A transformation that waits for the lock occupies one of the slots of its worker while it waits. Bodies that do not hold the lock are not counted in the third column. A parent that gave the lock up keeps its slot in its worker while it waits for its nested work, and so does a driver, but neither holds the lock. On remote: daskserver , the lock does not decide how many transformations a Dask worker accepts. Dask resources and the permission routine decide that ( seamless-dask/anti-deadlock.txt ). The second column is also the number of embedded interpreters. A handler language under an in-memory backend keeps one R or Julia interpreter in each process that has run such a body ( Handler languages and embedded interpreters ). Current limitations of the process lock Dispatch does not look at the lock. In a worker pool, a transformation can be given to a worker whose lock is held. It then waits for that lock, and it does not move when another worker becomes free. A body that hangs blocks its process, not one slot. Every transformation that is placed in that process afterwards and takes the lock waits behind it. In a worker pool, cancelling the hung transformation terminates its worker process and frees the lock. In process mode a cancel does not interrupt a body that runs inside the process, such as Python code, a compiled call or an embedded interpreter, so the lock stays held until the body returns ( contracts/cancellation.md , A transformation that waits for the process lock ). A bash body is different: a cancel kills its script, and the body then returns and frees the lock ( contracts/cancellation.md , A bash run that is cancelled ). Expressions are placed, not configured A jobserver or daskserver also evaluates Expressions (the jobserver endpoint is GET /run-expression ). Three differences from the transformation backends above matter: It is not a backend choice but a placement rule. An Expression is evaluated where the data is : local when no buffer is needed or the input buffer is already in this process's memory, otherwise dispatched. Selecting a backend does not turn this on or off. execution="auto" | "local" | "remote" is a per-Expression argument, not the execution: config key. Here "local" means in this process's memory and "remote" means not in this process's memory — independently of which transformation backend is configured. One deliberate deviation: for placement, a buffer available from a local buffer source — a configured read-buffer directory, or a leaf file of an active directory write mount, both read from this process's file system — also counts as local ( contracts/expressions.md , Placement ). A Context fixes the policy for its own Expression jobs with Context(expression_execution=…) . A daskserver is a jobserver mode for Expressions , not a competing backend: both expose the same checksum, error, caching and HashType contracts. The full rule, the resolution order, the no-silent-fallback rules and the two open placement questions are contracts/expressions.md , Placement . Storage prerequisite (by-checksum submission, shared hashserver) Remote execution — jobserver and daskserver alike — submits work by checksum, not by value . A remote target receives input checksums ; it materializes the input buffers server-side from a shared hashserver , writes produced (non- scratch ) results back to that hashserver, and records tf_checksum → result_checksum in the shared database. So a shared hashserver and database, reachable by the remote workers, are a hard prerequisite for any remote backend — they are what make server-side input materialization and result persistence possible. (A minimal local cluster that defines a hashserver/database but no jobserver/daskserver therefore cannot run execution: remote ; it must use execution: process — see ../main/cluster.md .) Consequences an agent may rely on: Inputs are not necessarily uploaded at submission. They may be pre-present — staged by a prior upload, or by design , when the client already holds the checksum of a large server-side dataset. Only buffers actually missing on the server are staged (e.g. --upload , or --write-remote-job which implies it). Results are durable out-of-process. A remote run's non- scratch results live in the shared hashserver/database independently of the submitting client, so tearing the client down does not lose them. (A scratch result is the exception: a scratch transformation may be dispatched, but its result is not stored. It is recomputed at a consumer via input fingertipping, or on the client by Transformation.run() , which then runs the transformation a second time — see contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md . Input fingertipping does not yet work on every backend: see Current limitation: fingertipping in a worker needs Dask above.) Materialization is content-addressed, not a side effect. A worker resolving an input checksum is performing materialization, not "reading whatever is on disk" (see contracts/identity-and-caching.md ). Testing surface Agents should not assume HPC or scheduler-backed testing lives only in seamless-dask . HPC/Dask-oriented tests also exist in seamless-transformer/tests/dask . The seamless-transformer/tests/cmd suite is backend-agnostic: it tests the seamless-run CLI contract rather than a specific backend. Those tests/cmd cases can be, and have been, exercised against a SLURM-backed remote: daskserver cluster. Minimal configuration shape (command language) Agents should expect configuration to be expressed as a YAML list of commands (project defaults + local overrides). A minimal shape for selecting a backend: - cluster: mycluster - execution: remote - remote: daskserver # or: jobserver - queue: main # queue is typically relevant for scheduler-backed daskserver clusters Porting implication (important) Backend selection is an operational choice: an agent should assume pipeline/step logic does not need to be rewritten to move between these backends, but the environment and deployment details must still be made deterministic enough for the workflow’s goals.
docs.title: Execution Backends

docs.text: This page defines the minimum operational model an agent may rely on when discussing “remote execution” or HPC with Seamless.
docs.title: Execution Backends (Contract)

docs.text: Execution mode : how transformations execute: process , spawn , or remote . Remote target (only relevant when execution: remote ): jobserver or daskserver . Mutual exclusivity : a single configured cluster/frontend should not expose both jobserver and daskserver without explicitly selecting one. This page is about Transformations. Expressions also run on a jobserver or daskserver, but they are placed by a different rule and on a different axis — see Expressions are placed, not configured below. Do not read the execution: configuration key and an Expression's execution= argument as the same setting.
docs.title: Terms

docs.text: 1) process - Runs in the caller’s Python process. - No infrastructure required. - By default, one transformation runs its code at a time ( The process lock ). 2) spawn - Runs in local spawned worker processes. - Still “single machine”, but parallel: by default, one transformation runs its code at a time in each worker process. 3) remote: jobserver - Uses a jobserver process plus a worker pool, reached over HTTP. - Intended as a low-ops remote mode (development/testing/single-node remote execution). 4) remote: daskserver - Uses Dask as the execution/scheduling substrate. - Intended for HPC/distributed throughput; can integrate with schedulers (commonly via dask-jobqueue on SLURM/OAR). - Operationally: typically long-lived/bundled workers execute many tasks (not one scheduler submission per Seamless step). - Supports opt-in live stdout/stderr streaming per transformation; see Streaming .
docs.title: Backend semantics (agent assumptions)

docs.text: A transformation's stdout and stderr are captured on every backend. After a successful run they are in Transformation.logs , followed by the execution time. After a failure they are in the trailers of .exception . Backends differ in where the capture happens and in whether the output is also visible while the run is in flight: Backend Streams in the success log Live output while the run is in flight process captured by a tee in the caller's process on the caller's stdout and stderr spawn captured in the worker child none remote: jobserver captured in the worker child, returned in the jobserver's response none remote: daskserver captured in the worker child, returned to the client with the result only with streaming Streaming is Dask-only. process , spawn and remote: jobserver ignore the flag ( contracts/streaming.md ). A log exists only for a run that executed. A result that comes from a cache or from the database has no log, on any backend. The execution time in the log is the dispatcher's measurement , the same number as wall_time_seconds in the execution record. It includes queueing, inter-process transfer and input resolution. The log's layout, its per-process store, what is and is not captured, and the rules for bash and compiled transformers are contracts/transformation-logs.md .
docs.title: Output and logs per backend

docs.text: A transformation can name a conda environment or a Docker image. A CLI backend, which is the bash transformer and the CLI backends of Python, R and Julia ( contracts/language-backends.md ), runs its script there ( contracts/environments.md ). The executing host is the machine on which the script runs. It enters the environment, so it must provide it. Backend Executing host Its settings are read from process , spawn the submitting machine the environment of the submitting process remote: jobserver the jobserver host the environment the jobserver was started in remote: daskserver the Dask worker nodes the queue's job_script_prologue For a conda environment, the executing host needs that environment and a conda launcher. For a Docker image, the executing host needs a container runtime and the image. The runtime is docker, podman or apptainer. The host chooses it, by the setting SEAMLESS_CONTAINER_RUNTIME or else by detection. A transformation never names a runtime. By default no image is pulled. Every backend behaves the same. The job is wrapped where it executes, and no backend does anything of its own for an environment. A host that cannot enter the environment fails the job. No backend falls back to running the script on the plain host. A fingertip needs the environment where the buffer is wanted. A fingertip is never dispatched, so the process that asks for the buffer enters the environment itself ( contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md , Fingertipping ). An in-memory backend is never wrapped. Its code runs inside the process that executes it: Python in memory, compiled transformations, and the in-memory backends of R, Julia and other handler languages. A Docker image on one is an error, on every backend. A conda environment is a requirement on that process, which must already be in exactly that environment ( contracts/language-backends.md , The in-memory rule ). The process is the one that the execution backend runs bodies in: the calling process in process , a worker process otherwise. Required binaries are looked up where the code runs. For a CLI backend that is the executing host's environment or image, after it is entered, and for an in-memory backend the PATH of the executing process ( contracts/language-backends.md , Required binaries ). A specification that could never work is refused when the transformation is dispatched on the submitting side: a conda environment together with a Docker image, and an unknown key of the image spec. It is checked again on the executing host before launch ( contracts/language-backends.md , The check happens at dispatch ). The image spec's gpus does not place a job. It gives the container access to the GPUs of the host on which the job runs. Which host that is follows from the backend and the queue, as for any transformation. contracts/environments.md has the settings, the failures and the limitations.
docs.title: Environments are entered on the executing host

docs.text: In spawn and remote: jobserver , a transformation runs in a worker process that cannot see its parent's fingertip candidates: neither the parent's reverse caches nor its database. A fingertip in such a worker tries only the producers that the worker itself launched (nested transformations). If those do not recover the buffer, it raises NotImplementedError , and the job fails with that error in its traceback. It does not report a CacheMissError , because the search was incomplete. In spawn , the parent recovers a transformation's direct inputs before dispatch. When input fingertipping is enabled and Dask is not in use, the parent fingertips every input pin whose buffer is absent, before it hands the transformation to a worker. The worker then downloads the bytes from the parent over the local worker channel, as it does for any input. Pins that the worker reads from the file system are left alone. If the parent's fingertip fails, the transformation fails with that CacheMissError and its fingertip category; the worker never runs. What this still blocks. In remote: jobserver : a transformation with allow_input_fingertip whose input buffer is absent (a scratch result, or an evicted one) fails, unless the worker launched the input's producer itself. In spawn : a buffer that is not a direct input but that the worker needs, such as a member of a folder or deep input whose index is present. The worker fingertips it itself, which raises NotImplementedError as above. What works. process (the fingertip runs in the caller's process, which holds the candidates), the direct inputs in spawn (above), and remote: daskserver (the workers of a Dask worker can query the database). This is a limitation, not the contract. The contract is that an input fingertip inside a job works on every backend ( contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md , Case 1 ).
docs.title: Current limitation: fingertipping in a worker needs Dask

docs.text: Two terms are used below. The body of a transformation is its user code: the Python function, the bash script or the compiled call. For a handler language such as R or Julia, the body is the call of the handler that runs the code ( contracts/handler-languages.md ). For Python under its CLI backend, the body is the run of the job. Nested work is a transformation whose execution is requested from inside a body. Every process that runs bodies has one process lock, and by default a body runs while holding it. A transformation whose process_lock is true waits for the lock of the process it was placed in, runs its body while holding the lock, and releases the lock when the body ends. process_lock is true by default ( contracts/transformers.md , process_lock and driver ). Among such transformations, at most one body runs at a time in any one process. This holds on every backend, and for Python, bash, handler-language and compiled transformers alike. The lock is held around the body only. Input resolution, module building and result serialization happen outside it. Several transformations in one process therefore download and upload at the same time. The lock keeps holders apart, and nothing else. A body that does not hold the lock can run next to a holder in the same process. Three kinds of body do not hold it: a body with process_lock false, a driver ( Drivers ), and a body that gave the lock up ( Nested work gives the lock up ). Code outside any transformation, such as the script that submits work in process mode, never waits for the lock. What the lock is for. It protects state that the bodies of one process share, such as the working directory, environment variables or a library that is not thread-safe, as long as every body there keeps the default. It also fixes how many bodies run at once: one per process ( Concurrency per backend ). The lock is controlled by metadata only. There is no lock object for user code to take. The name global_lock is retired without an alias. Neither seamless_transformer nor seamless.transformer exports it, and reading it as an attribute of either module raises AttributeError with a message that points to process_lock . Code that took it inside a body declares process_lock on the transformer instead.
docs.title: The process lock

docs.text: A body that submits nested work gives up the lock at that moment, if it holds it, and never takes it again. It happens at submission , before it is known whether the nested result is cached. Whether a body keeps its lock therefore does not depend on the state of any cache. The reason is that nested work can land in the submitter's own process. In process mode it always does. In a worker pool it does when the nested transformation is dispatched to the worker that submitted it, and when the pool is full, in which case the worker runs it itself. A parent that kept the lock would wait for a child that waits for the parent's lock. Afterwards the body runs without the lock until it ends. That includes the code that follows the return of the nested results. A body has its process to itself only up to its first nested submission. No declaration is needed. A transformation that keeps every default may submit nested work. These calls, made by a body, are nested submissions: Call Kind tr.start() scheduling tr.compute() , tr.run() , a call of a direct Transformer synchronous execution await tr.computation() , tr.task() asynchronous execution parallel() , parallel_async() batches a fingertip that recomputes a transformation recovery of an absent buffer by running its producer again ( contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md , Fingertipping ) Building a Transformation without running it is not a submission. Neither is reading a handle: status , exception , result_checksum , value , buffer , logs . The rule covers the body's own thread and the coroutines of its event loop. A submission from a thread that the body started itself is not attributed to the body, and the lock stays held. A workflow Context created inside a body is such a case, because a Context submits its nodes from its own controller thread. A body that submits in this way must have process_lock false, or be a driver. If it keeps the default, a nested transformation that lands in its process waits for the lock while the body waits for the transformation. The two then hang, and no error is raised.
docs.title: Nested work gives the lock up

docs.text: A driver is a transformation declared with driver true: its body mainly launches other transformations and waits for them. A driver never takes the lock. Its body starts even while the lock of its process is held, and it runs next to whatever else runs there. Its submissions are marked as coming from a driver. On remote: daskserver , a nested submission normally asks for permission before it goes to Dask. It can be made to wait, and it can be handed back to the submitter to run itself. This is the anti-deadlock routine described in seamless-dask/anti-deadlock.txt . A submission made by a driver's body skips the routine. So does the submission of a driver itself. The mark is not inherited. A transformation launched by a driver is an ordinary transformation. It takes or leaves the lock according to its own settings, it is deduplicated as usual, and the nested work that it submits in turn asks for permission again. Nested work from a CLI job gets what its configuration gives it: A nested seamless-run finds its configuration from SEAMLESS_CACHE , or from SEAMLESS_REMOTE_CLIENTS together with the Dask scheduler, or else from a configuration file in its working directory. For a job, the working directory is the job directory, which holds none. Only the Dask worker exports these variables. Under remote: daskserver a nested seamless-run from a bash job, and a nested transformation from a Python CLI job ( contracts/language-backends.md , Drivers and nested work ), therefore go to the same cluster and share its caches. On process , spawn and remote: jobserver nothing is exported. A nested seamless-run there fails for lack of a configuration, unless one of the variables is in the environment that the job inherits, and a nested call in a Python CLI job runs inside the job's own process, with no cache and no dispatch. A submission from the job's own process skips the permission routine , because the process is neither a worker nor one that has spawned workers. The mark of a driver is not what decides it. Inside a container nothing is exported and the nesting signal does not cross. Nested work from a containerized job is not supported. Declaring a driver is never needed for correctness, because an undeclared body gives the lock up at its first nested submission. The declaration matters in two cases: when the body should not wait for the lock at all, and on Dask, where it lifts the permission routine from the body's launches.
docs.title: Drivers

docs.text: What this section says of a bash body holds for the body of every CLI backend : the bash transformer, and the CLI backends of Python, R and Julia ( contracts/language-backends.md ). A job in any of them is a process of its own, started by the process that runs the transformation, and is signalled and torn down in the same way. A bash transformation never changes the working directory of the process that runs it. The script runs in a job directory of its own, which is its working directory. The process keeps the working directory it had, so a relative path used by other code in that process keeps its meaning. A bash body takes the lock like any other body , unless process_lock is false or the transformation is a driver. For seamless-run these are --no-process-lock and --driver ( contracts/seamless-run-and-argtyping.md ). A bash body that holds the lock is told when its script submits nested work. The script's environment contains the variable SEAMLESS_PROCESS_LOCK_NOTIFY . A Seamless program that the script starts, such as seamless-run , uses the variable to signal the body when it first submits a transformation. The body then gives the lock up, as any body does. seamless-run --qsubmit signals as well. The script itself has nothing to do. The nested command keeps its own defaults. It does not become a driver, and neither does the bash transformation whose script started it. The variable is set only when the body holds the lock as its script starts. Otherwise the body removes it from the script's environment, so that a nested command never signals a process further up. The signal works for as long as the script's process runs , also after the script has closed its stdout and stderr. The signal is a named pipe on the local filesystem. The nested command must see the same filesystem as the body, and the signal does not cross ssh or a container boundary. A bash body that submits nested work through one of those must be declared a driver, or have process_lock false. A bash body with an environment is a bash body like any other ( contracts/environments.md ). It takes the lock and holds it until its script ends, so a long container job occupies its process for that time. A script under a conda environment has the variable and is signalled as a plain script is. A script in a container made from the transformation's Docker image is behind a container boundary: the variable is not passed in, and the previous rule applies.
docs.title: Bash bodies

docs.text: A handler-language transformation runs R, Julia or another registered language through a handler. The R and the Julia handler each have two ways to run the code, which this section calls a CLI backend and an in-memory backend. Python has both as well: in memory by default, and as a CLI job with BACKEND="cli" . These are language backends , selected per Transformer, and they are independent of the execution backends of this page. contracts/language-backends.md specifies the two kinds and the Python CLI backend, and contracts/handler-languages.md the handler ones. A CLI backend starts one interpreter process for each run , on the machinery of bash transformations. Bash bodies holds for it: the process keeps its working directory, and the body is told when the code starts a nested seamless-run . By default one such run is in flight per process. With process_lock false they run side by side, each in its own interpreter process. An in-memory backend embeds the interpreter in the process that runs the body. That is the caller's process in process mode, and each worker process otherwise. A process has one embedded interpreter per language. It starts at its first use and lives until the process ends. An in-memory backend of a handler language refuses to run without the lock. A transformation that has process_lock false fails when its body starts, and so does a driver. The message names the CLI backend as the alternative. A result that is already recorded is still returned, because nothing runs. Python and compiled bodies in memory have no such rule: they run without the lock when process_lock is false, as always. The process lock is the only lock around an embedded interpreter. Among transformations that hold it, one body runs at a time in a process, so one transformation at a time uses the interpreter. An in-memory body holds the lock from its start to its end. It cannot give the lock up: there is no nesting signal as for a bash body. Code that submits nested work, for example by running seamless-run , belongs under the CLI backend. Two facts about where bodies run matter to whoever writes a handler: The lock gives exclusion, not a fixed thread. A body never runs on the main thread of its process, and successive bodies in one process run on different threads. In process mode the thread that ran one body may no longer exist when the next body runs. An interpreter that must always be called from the same thread gets that thread from run_in_interpreter_thread ( contracts/handler-languages.md , Threads, and run_in_interpreter_thread ), not from the lock. A body may hold Python's GIL for a long time. A worker pool checks each of its worker processes about once a second. A body that keeps the GIL, as a call into an embedded interpreter can, makes its worker miss the check, but a worker that is running a transformation is not restarted for that. It is restarted only when its process exits or its connection closes. This holds in spawn and in both remote modes.
docs.title: Handler languages and embedded interpreters

docs.text: The lock is per process, so the number of bodies that run at once follows from the number of processes in which a backend runs bodies. A worker process accepts up to three transformations at once. That number is the transformation throttle. The lock then decides how many of their bodies run. Backend Processes that run bodies Bodies at once when every transformation keeps the default Bodies at once with process_lock false process the caller's process 1 not limited by the lock spawn with N workers N worker processes N, one per worker up to 3 per worker, 3N in total remote: jobserver with N workers N worker processes N, one per worker up to 3 per worker, 3N in total remote: daskserver the Seamless worker processes inside each Dask worker one per Seamless worker process up to the throttle per Seamless worker process A transformation that waits for the lock occupies one of the slots of its worker while it waits. Bodies that do not hold the lock are not counted in the third column. A parent that gave the lock up keeps its slot in its worker while it waits for its nested work, and so does a driver, but neither holds the lock. On remote: daskserver , the lock does not decide how many transformations a Dask worker accepts. Dask resources and the permission routine decide that ( seamless-dask/anti-deadlock.txt ). The second column is also the number of embedded interpreters. A handler language under an in-memory backend keeps one R or Julia interpreter in each process that has run such a body ( Handler languages and embedded interpreters ).
docs.title: Concurrency per backend

docs.text: Dispatch does not look at the lock. In a worker pool, a transformation can be given to a worker whose lock is held. It then waits for that lock, and it does not move when another worker becomes free. A body that hangs blocks its process, not one slot. Every transformation that is placed in that process afterwards and takes the lock waits behind it. In a worker pool, cancelling the hung transformation terminates its worker process and frees the lock. In process mode a cancel does not interrupt a body that runs inside the process, such as Python code, a compiled call or an embedded interpreter, so the lock stays held until the body returns ( contracts/cancellation.md , A transformation that waits for the process lock ). A bash body is different: a cancel kills its script, and the body then returns and frees the lock ( contracts/cancellation.md , A bash run that is cancelled ).
docs.title: Current limitations of the process lock

docs.text: A jobserver or daskserver also evaluates Expressions (the jobserver endpoint is GET /run-expression ). Three differences from the transformation backends above matter: It is not a backend choice but a placement rule. An Expression is evaluated where the data is : local when no buffer is needed or the input buffer is already in this process's memory, otherwise dispatched. Selecting a backend does not turn this on or off. execution="auto" | "local" | "remote" is a per-Expression argument, not the execution: config key. Here "local" means in this process's memory and "remote" means not in this process's memory — independently of which transformation backend is configured. One deliberate deviation: for placement, a buffer available from a local buffer source — a configured read-buffer directory, or a leaf file of an active directory write mount, both read from this process's file system — also counts as local ( contracts/expressions.md , Placement ). A Context fixes the policy for its own Expression jobs with Context(expression_execution=…) . A daskserver is a jobserver mode for Expressions , not a competing backend: both expose the same checksum, error, caching and HashType contracts. The full rule, the resolution order, the no-silent-fallback rules and the two open placement questions are contracts/expressions.md , Placement .
docs.title: Expressions are placed, not configured

docs.text: Remote execution — jobserver and daskserver alike — submits work by checksum, not by value . A remote target receives input checksums ; it materializes the input buffers server-side from a shared hashserver , writes produced (non- scratch ) results back to that hashserver, and records tf_checksum → result_checksum in the shared database. So a shared hashserver and database, reachable by the remote workers, are a hard prerequisite for any remote backend — they are what make server-side input materialization and result persistence possible. (A minimal local cluster that defines a hashserver/database but no jobserver/daskserver therefore cannot run execution: remote ; it must use execution: process — see ../main/cluster.md .) Consequences an agent may rely on: Inputs are not necessarily uploaded at submission. They may be pre-present — staged by a prior upload, or by design , when the client already holds the checksum of a large server-side dataset. Only buffers actually missing on the server are staged (e.g. --upload , or --write-remote-job which implies it). Results are durable out-of-process. A remote run's non- scratch results live in the shared hashserver/database independently of the submitting client, so tearing the client down does not lose them. (A scratch result is the exception: a scratch transformation may be dispatched, but its result is not stored. It is recomputed at a consumer via input fingertipping, or on the client by Transformation.run() , which then runs the transformation a second time — see contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md . Input fingertipping does not yet work on every backend: see Current limitation: fingertipping in a worker needs Dask above.) Materialization is content-addressed, not a side effect. A worker resolving an input checksum is performing materialization, not "reading whatever is on disk" (see contracts/identity-and-caching.md ).
docs.title: Storage prerequisite (by-checksum submission, shared hashserver)

The seamless-transformer/tests/cmd suite is backend-agnostic: it tests the seamless-run CLI contract rather than a specific backend. Those tests/cmd cases can be, and have been, exercised against a SLURM-backed remote: daskserver cluster.

A minimal shape for selecting a backend: - cluster: mycluster - execution: remote - remote: daskserver # or: jobserver - queue: main # queue is typically relevant for scheduler-backed daskserver clusters

docs.title: Porting implication (important)

docs.text: Execution Records (Contract) This page defines the agent-facing behavior of execution records: structured metadata that seamless-database stores for every successful, non-probe transformation. What execution records are An execution record is a JSON body stored in the MetaData table of seamless.db , keyed by tf_checksum . It captures what ran, where, and how it performed — not the result itself, which lives in the normal Transformation cache. Records are write-once per tf_checksum : once a successful execution writes a row, subsequent calls hit the normal cache and never re-enter the record path. Records exist for three concrete reasons: Cache lifecycle decisions. Resource cost (CPU time, memory peak) feeds eviction policy. Fingertipping diagnosis. When fingertipping fails, or an automatic observation or manual quarantine records a divergent result, the original execution record is the breadcrumb back to the original execution context. Trust under sharing. When seamless.db is shared, the record lets a recipient inspect in what context was this result produced without trusting the publisher unconditionally. Records are not consulted for cache hits in normal operation. They are evidence preserved across the moment of execution. Mental model: evidence, not identity Seamless is a referential-transparency system, not a database-integrity system . The cache contract is "same tf_checksum ⇒ same result"; the cache key is the tf_checksum , and the determinant of identity for a transformation is its declared inputs and code, not its execution context. Execution records are evidence about the envelope , not part of the identity. They exist to make the optimistic null hypothesis (that scientifically meaningful results are invariant under environment variation) falsifiable later. Concretely: A metadata conflict is not automatically a cache-identity conflict. If two parties have the same tf_checksum and same result_checksum but different metadata bodies, that is evidence disagreement about the execution envelope — informative for audit, but it does not invalidate the cached result. A result_checksum mismatch for the same tf_checksum is a referential-transparency violation. An automatic IrreproducibleTransformation observation records the divergent result without replacing the forward result or moving metadata. A manual quarantine moves the normal result and its metadata into the irreproducible table and removes the forward row. During fingertipping, the goal is to rematerialize a checksum, not to author a new canonical execution record. Fingertip retries do not displace the original record. Treat records as a forensic substrate for human or agent investigators when something has gone wrong; do not treat them as a query target or a synchronization point in the normal cache path. When records are written Trigger Record? Mode Successful, non-probe execution Yes (always) record: false → minimal; record: true → full Probe execution No — Failed execution No — Canceled execution No — Cache hit on Transformation No — Already-recorded tf_checksum No (idempotent) identical body → success; differing body → reject The record boolean is a seamless-config command ( - record: true in seamless.profile.yaml , or seamless.config.select_record(True) ). It defaults to false , meaning the minimal record is persisted by default. The record: true opt-in adds the full payload. A successful execution writes exactly one record — never minimal first then full. The runtime honors the active record mode at the moment the call completes. Capture is worker-side : the record describes the environment in which the transformation actually ran (jobserver worker, Dask worker, spawn child, or local process), not where it was submitted. This is enforced across all backends — process , spawn , remote: jobserver , remote: daskserver . Minimal record body (default) The minimal record contains exactly: { "schema_version": 1, "tf_checksum": "<hex>", "result_checksum": "<hex>", "seamless_version": "<string>", "execution_mode": "process | spawn | remote", "remote_target": null | "jobserver" | "daskserver", "wall_time_seconds": <float>, "cpu_time_user_seconds": <float>, "cpu_time_system_seconds": <float>, "memory_peak_bytes": <int|null>, "gpu_memory_peak_bytes": <int|null> } No environment fingerprint, no compilation context, no validation snapshot, no per-job freshness. The hot path pays only timing/memory capture and one database write. Full record body ( record: true ) The full record extends the minimal body with: Environment signature (content-addressed checksums to sub-buffers): node — stable physical properties (CPU, RAM, GPU, OS, kernel, container) environment — Python packages + conda env dump + numerics runtime config (BLAS, thread pools, relevant env vars) node_env — per-node environment binding queue / queue_node — scheduler/queue context Compilation context ( compilation_context ) — checksum to a buffer recording compiler versions, flags, headers, and linked objects. Only for compiled transformers; cached by compiled-module digest. Validation snapshot ( validation_snapshot ) — checksum to a buffer recording pre-execution validation state. Execution summary/envelope — load-bearing execution summary such as language kind, plus requested cluster/queue/node, scratch/fingertip flags, resolved __env__ checksum, and active orthogonal dunder-key set. Freshness — required bucket labels/checksums, live tokens, bucket tokens. Contract violations — bucket_contract_violations , job_contract_violations , contract_violations (e.g., native_link_outside_conda_prefix for compiled transformers linking outside the conda prefix). Per-run diagnostics — started_at , finished_at , hostname , pid , process_started_at , process_create_time_epoch , worker_execution_index , compilation_time_seconds , retry counts. The checksum_fields list at the top of the record names which fields hold checksum pointers to content-addressed sub-buffers (currently node , environment , node_env , queue , queue_node , compilation_context , validation_snapshot ). If you change a numerical library, upgrade a driver, or reprovision a node and do not re-probe, Seamless keeps reusing the prior bucket checksum — by design. Auto-recapturing on suspicion of drift would couple records to ambient state and defeat the content-addressed deduplication that makes buckets cheap; staleness is therefore an operator responsibility, not an automatic guarantee. This exception is narrow by construction and does not loosen the rule elsewhere: It fires on a definite miss, not a suspicion of staleness. The environment is simply not present and the job cannot run at all; a present-but-possibly-outdated cache is never auto-recaptured. It is bounded : exactly one re-probe, then a hard failure whose message names the target and states that rhl-cache-conda has already been run. It is observable : the refresh is dispatched as the ordinary rhl-cache-conda helper (not an inline shell probe), so it appears in the launcher's debug logs like any manually triggered probe. The five record-mode environment buckets themselves have no equivalent auto-refresh; they remain manual-only. (Note: this exception lives in the launcher's own conda-discovery cache, which is reusable outside Seamless — so "record mode" is never named there; the principle and the exception are described here, on the Seamless side.) Database protocol Protocol version: 2.3 PUT metadata (request type): atomically creates Transformation , RevTransformation , and MetaData when missing. Validates identity ( tf_checksum matches request, result_checksum matches request, schema_version integer, checksum_fields format if present). Identical duplicate is idempotent success; differing duplicate or result mismatch is rejected. PUT transformation : inserts the forward result and ensures one reverse row. Repeating the same result is idempotent; a different result answers HTTP 409 and leaves both stored rows unchanged. GET metadata : returns the canonical record body for a tf_checksum . GET irreproducible : returns all rows for a tf_checksum (optionally filtered by result ), each carrying checksum , result , and metadata . PUT irreproducible , manual mode ( mode omitted or "manual" ): moves the normal entry into IrreproducibleTransformation , preserving its metadata body and removing the forward and reverse rows. This is the explicit quarantine operation. PUT irreproducible , automatic mode ( mode: "automatic" ): requires a forward row with a different result, else answers 404 for no forward row or 409 for the same result. It adds one row for the divergent (tf_checksum, result_checksum) pair, with empty metadata, and skips duplicate reports. The forward, reverse, metadata, and original execution record remain unchanged. Automatic rows carry no execution record of their own; an investigator runs the candidate separately. PUT metadata still refuses a checksum once any irreproducible row exists, including an automatic observation. Runtime recording writes metadata only for a newly inserted forward result, before any automatic observation; an identical result writes nothing. The refusal therefore remains observable to an external caller but is not reached by the normal automatic-report path. Schema upgrade: a fresh database creates the upgraded meta_data table directly. An empty legacy two-column table is dropped and recreated. A non-empty legacy table fails loudly (it must be migrated explicitly). Remote client API seamless-remote/seamless_remote/database_client.py and database_remote.py expose: set_execution_record(tf_checksum, result_checksum, record) — write a record. get_execution_record(tf_checksum) — read a record. get_irreproducible_records(tf_checksum, result_checksum=None) — read irreproducible rows. report_irreproducible_result(tf_checksum, result_checksum) — report a divergent result in automatic mode; a 404 or 409 returns False . Worker-side payloads carrying the record back from jobserver/daskserver are structured (typed dicts); the remote client tolerates legacy string responses for backwards compatibility but new code should expect structured payloads. What records do not do They are not a query target . Records are not indexed for reverse lookups ( find all rows with environment = X ); the database stores them as JSON blobs. Audit tooling consumes whole records, not selective columns. They are not a sharing redaction layer . Hostnames and timestamps stay in the record body; whether to redact on export is a per-share operator decision, not a schema column. They are not produced for failed or canceled executions . Failed or canceled jobs do not create durable reusable identities; a canceled submission also writes no result_checksum , even if its dropped work later completes. They may be tracked elsewhere but not in MetaData . They are not the sole source of "how to run" . The orthogonal execution-only dunder values ( __env__ , __compilation__ , __meta__ , __record_probe__ , …) needed to rerun or audit a transformation are stored by the transformation/replay substrate, not solely in the record. (Load-bearing keys such as __schema__ live in the checksum-defining payload itself; __header__ is derived from __schema__ .) Agent guidance Default to minimal records. Do not enable record: true unless the user is explicitly debugging reproducibility, auditing, or measuring environment drift. The full record adds significant per-execution overhead. Records describe the worker environment. When a record's hostname differs from the submitter's host, that is correct, not a bug. Records are write-once per tf_checksum . Re-running a transformation that already has a record is a cache hit; the record is not refreshed. To force a fresh record, the underlying inputs must change (different tf_checksum ). Don't conflate metadata conflicts with cache-identity conflicts. A metadata difference for the same (tf_checksum, result_checksum) pair is evidence disagreement about the envelope — interesting for audit, but not a referential-transparency violation. Only a differing result_checksum for the same tf_checksum indicates a real reproducibility problem (and that path goes through IrreproducibleTransformation , not metadata rejection). Fingertipping retries do not author new records. Fingertipping rematerializes a checksum; it does not displace the original record or trigger a new write. Probing is manual; do not script auto-recapture. Full-record environment buckets are captured by manually triggered probes and reused by checksum until the operator re-probes. Seamless deliberately does not detect staleness or recapture on its own (see "Probing is manual" above). The sole exception is a missing conda environment, which triggers one bounded launcher-side refresh — do not generalize that into auto-refreshing buckets whenever you suspect environment drift. For compiled transformers , the full record's compilation_context is cached by compiled-module digest — repeated builds of the same source produce the same context checksum without re-invoking compiler-version subprocesses. Strict-mode failures : under record: true , record-write failures propagate. Under record: false , minimal-record write failures are best-effort for narrow transport/storage errors and emit a warning; programmer errors and RecordBucketError always propagate.
