Reading one gives the value that was set, or else the handler's default. Any other name raises, on read and on write. The exception class is not specified. BACKEND accepts "cli" and "mem" , and nothing else. Any other value is refused when it is assigned, and nothing is stored. The names of the tools, such as "Rscript" or "juliacall" , are not values. A value that arrives in a transformation dict fails when the transformation runs. A build writes every metavar into the Transformation , defaults included, under meta["metavars"] . The backend is not part of the transformation's identity ( Identity and caching ). Bound Transformers. ctx.tf.metavars behaves the same. The values belong to the workflow Context node: every view of ctx.tf reads and writes the one mapping, the node keeps it in its meta , and ctx.get_graph() saves it. A node whose result is recorded does not run its code again after a change of BACKEND , because its tf_checksum is the same. What a backend needs on the machine that runs the transformation: Language "cli" needs "mem" needs r Rscript on the PATH ; the R packages RcppCNPy and jsonlite the Python package ryp , with R and the R package arrow ; the R package jsonlite julia julia on the PATH ; the Julia packages NPZ and JSON in the active project the Python package juliacall ; the Julia package JSON in the project that juliacall uses Seamless installs none of these. A tool or a package that is missing is a failure of the transformation. The machine that runs the transformation needs them, not the one that builds it , unless they are the same. Which machine runs it follows from the execution backend ( Execution backends ). Under a CLI backend with a Docker image, the image needs them. A conda environment needs them too, where the transformer has one ( Environments ). CLI backends Every run starts a new interpreter process , in a job directory of its own, on the machinery of bash transformations. What Execution backends , Bash bodies , says of a bash body holds for it: the process that runs the transformation keeps its working directory, and a nested seamless-run that the code starts is signalled. The interpreter does not read the user's startup files. The commands are Rscript --vanilla and julia --startup-file=no . The transformer's environment is entered first , when it has one: its conda environment is activated, or the interpreter is started in a container made from its Docker image ( Environments ). One run at a time per process, by default , because the run takes the process lock. With tf.process_lock = False , several run side by side in one process. Each has its own interpreter process, so they share no interpreter state. In-memory backends The interpreter is embedded in the process that runs the transformation. That is the calling process in process mode, and a worker process otherwise. It starts at its first use and lives until the process ends. There is one embedded interpreter per process , and one transformation uses it at a time ( The process lock ). transform() isolations are reused from one run to the next ( Isolation and persistent state ). That is what an in-memory backend is for: the interpreter starts once, and definitions are evaluated once. It cannot enter an environment. A conda environment must already be the one of the process, and a Docker image is refused ( Environments ). The process lock A handler-language transformation takes the process lock like any other ( Execution backends , The process lock ). The handler receives whether it did ( Writing a handler , The arguments ). An in-memory backend refuses to run without the process lock. A transformation that has process_lock false and an in-memory backend fails when it runs. The message names the CLI backend as the alternative. A driver is refused too , because driver true means process_lock false ( Transformers , process_lock and driver ). The process lock is the only lock around an embedded interpreter. Among transformations that hold it, one runs at a time in a process, and that is what keeps two transformations out of one interpreter. The refusal happens when the transformation runs. Building succeeds. A result that is already recorded is returned without the check. An in-memory body holds the lock from its start to its end. The code has no way to give it up: the nesting signal of a bash body does not exist here. Code that submits nested work, for example by running seamless-run , belongs under the CLI backend. A transformation that arrives without its __meta__ takes the lock and runs under the default backend , which is the CLI ( Transformers , Absent keys in a transformation dict ). Backend parity Both backends of a language give the same result, bit for bit, when both succeed. A backend may fail where the other succeeds. It may not succeed with a different result. This is what lets the backend stay outside identity. A result that was computed under one backend is served, from the cache, to a transformation that names the other. How it holds. Each language has one runtime, written in that language, and both backends use it. The runtime recognizes the code style, builds the isolation, turns each pin into a native value, runs the code, and classifies and encodes the result. The backends differ only in how bytes travel. JSON values cross as JSON text under both backends , and are parsed and written by the same call. That is why jsonlite and JSON are needed by the in-memory backends too. There is no fallback encoding. A backend that cannot carry a value fails. It never substitutes another representation. A deep pin has the same form under both backends , and a deep result has the same member rule ( Deep celltypes and checksum objects ). Code that filters the keys of a deepcell pin and returns the rest gives the same result under both. A deepfolder pin is a dict of checksum objects under both backends. Its form does not depend on where the member buffers are stored. The R CLI backend also refuses float32 arrays and arrays with more than two dimensions ( Array rules ). Isolations are never dropped. An embedded interpreter keeps every transform() isolation it has built, and Julia cannot unload a module. A worker process that lives long and sees many different transform() codes grows. A failure under a CLI backend is titled Bash transformer exception , although the code is R or Julia. The execution record reports the language kind of a handler-language transformation as python ( Execution records ). A user-registered language cannot be built where it is not registered ( The handler travels with the transformation ). A process that loads a workflow graph with a node of that language must register the handler first. Writing a job directory instead of running it is for bash transformations only. Non-goals R or Julia through seamless-run , direct or delayed ( Faces ). Reading pin declarations from an R or a Julia signature, and optional pins. Installing R, Julia, their packages, ryp or juliacall . Compiled code. A language that compiles to a C-ABI transform() is a compiled language ( Compiled transformers ). Code locations Concern Module / symbol The handler API and the registry seamless_transformer.languages ( register_language_handler , get_language_handler , is_handler_language , available_languages , run_in_interpreter_thread ) The two functions that honour an environment seamless_transformer.languages ( check_in_memory_environment , execute_cli ) The R and the Julia handler seamless_transformer.languages.handlers ( r , julia ) Builders seamless_transformer.transformer_class ( HandlerTransformer , DirectHandlerTransformer ); they are not public constructors __handler__ and the __format__ entries seamless_transformer.pretransformation.direct_transformer_to_pretransformation Dispatch to the handler seamless_transformer.run.run_transformation_dict Bound builders seamless_workflow.context.Context._transformer_handle
docs.title: Handler Languages

docs.text: A handler language is a transformation language whose code is run by a handler : a Python function that receives the code and the pins, runs the code in the other language, and returns the result. R ( language="r" ) and Julia ( language="julia" ) are the two built-in handler languages. The set is open: register_language_handler adds a language, and Seamless itself does not change for it. This page is about the Python face and the workflow Context. A handler language is used through the Transformer factory. direct and delayed decorate Python functions only, and seamless-run wraps commands, as before ( Faces ). This page owns the handler API, what a handler receives, what R and Julia code sees and returns, what each backend of each language runs and needs and their parity, the checksum classes of R and Julia, and where the handler and the backend sit in transformation identity. Other pages own the rest: the two kinds of language backend, BACKEND , the environment rule and the two public functions that carry it: Language backends ; deep pins and deep results: Deep celltypes ; builder modes, building, binding and the named work methods: Transformers ; pin declarations, pin celltypes and the null rules: Pins ; the identity model: Identity and caching ; the process lock: Execution backends , The process lock . The implementation plan describes the mechanics and the phases.
docs.title: Handler languages (Contract)

docs.text: Kind Languages Constructed with The code is run by native python , bash Transformer(language) . For Python also direct , delayed and ctx.tf = function Seamless itself compiled the languages registered with define_compiled_language , such as c , cpp , fortran and rust Transformer(language, compiled=True) a native call of the compiled transform() ( Compiled transformers ) handler r , julia , and what register_language_handler adds Transformer(language) the handler of the language from seamless_transformer.languages import available_languages available_languages() # {"python": "native", "bash": "native", "c": "compiled", ..., # "r": "handler", "julia": "handler"} available_languages() maps every accepted language value to its kind : "native" , "compiled" or "handler" . It lists the languages that the factory can construct, and nothing else. A name that the factory does not accept, such as ipython , is not in it. A language name belongs to one kind. Registering a handler under a native or compiled name raises. is_handler_language(name) says whether a name has a handler. get_language_handler(name) returns the registration of a handler language, and raises for any other name. The two built-in handlers are always registered. seamless_transformer.languages registers them when it is imported. That import loads neither R nor Julia, and neither ryp nor juliacall .
docs.title: The three kinds of language

docs.text: Face Handler languages Python: the Transformer factory Transformer("r") , Transformer("julia") , with direct=True for an immediate call Python: direct , delayed none. Both decorate Python functions only Workflow Context a handler-language builder is bound like any other: ctx.tf = Transformer("julia") Unix: seamless-run none seamless-run Rscript analysis.R data.csv remains what it was: a bash transformation of a command that happens to start R. The script is an input file, the identity is that of the command and its files, and the result is a file or the command's output. Nothing on this page applies to it: there are no pins as variables, no BACKEND and no parity guarantee.
docs.title: Faces

docs.text: The code is ordinary R or Julia. It loads no input files, writes no result file and does not mention Seamless. from seamless.transformer import Transformer tf = Transformer("r", direct=True) tf.code = "result <- a + b" tf.pins.a = 2 tf.pins.b = 3 tf() # -> 5 tf = Transformer("julia", direct=True) tf.code = """ function transform(a, b) return a + b end """ tf.pins.a = 2 tf.pins.b = 3 tf() # -> 5 The code is source text. tf.code takes a string. A new builder has no code. The pins are declared by the user , by writing through tf.pins or tf.celltypes , as for Bash ( Pins , Which pins exist ). Seamless does not read a signature from R or Julia code, not even from a transform function. A declared pin has celltype mixed until it is given another. There are no optional pins. They exist for Python only. The output name is result , and its celltype is tf.celltypes.result , which is mixed by default. Everything else is the common builder contract ( Transformers ): standalone and bound modes, build() , the named work methods, scratch , process_lock and driver . A builder's language is fixed at construction and read-only. A handler-language builder also has tf.metavars , which holds the settings of its handler ( Backends ).
docs.title: R and Julia transformers

docs.text: The R and the Julia handler accept code in two styles. Block transform() The code is statements that run from top to bottom a definition of a function named transform , with whatever else it needs Recognized by no top-level definition of transform a top-level definition of a function named transform Pins each pin is a variable of its name each pin is passed as the argument of its name Result the value of the variable result when the code ends the return value of transform Isolation a new one for every run built once, and reused ( Isolation and persistent state ) The style is recognized by parsing the code in its own language , when the transformation runs. R: a top-level assignment, with <- or = , of a function to the name transform . Julia: a top-level definition of a function named transform , in the long form or the short form ( transform(a, b) = … ), also with a where clause, a return type or a docstring. Only the top level counts. A definition inside a block, or one that the code produces by source , include or eval , does not make the code transform() style. Block code cannot have a top-level function named transform . It would be read as the other style. In the block style, the code must assign result . A run whose code ends without it fails. A variable of that name outside the code's own isolation does not count. In the transform() style, the top-level code runs with no pins bound. It defines things. Only transform receives the pins. What happens when the pins and the parameters of transform do not match is not specified. Declare one pin for each parameter.
docs.title: The two code styles

docs.text: An isolation is the scope in which the code runs: an environment in R, a module in Julia. Block code gets a new isolation for every run. transform() code gets one isolation per interpreter , for each combination of code, output name and pin names. It is built at first use and kept inside the interpreter. Later runs in that interpreter call the function that is already defined. Seamless keeps no cache of isolations. A worker process that is restarted starts with none. Under a CLI backend every run starts a new interpreter, so nothing is reused there. An isolation separates names, not the process. Under an in-memory backend ( Backends ), these outlive a transformation and are seen by the next one in the same process: loaded packages and their state; options; explicit assignments to the global scope; in the transform() style, the top-level variables of the isolation; compiled Julia code. The result must not depend on any of that. The constraint is the one that holds for compiled transformers ( Compiled transformers , Referential transparency constraint ): code whose return value depends on state from an earlier call cannot be wrapped. Seamless does not detect a violation. The consequence is a cached result that is silently wrong, and a result that differs between the two backends. Inputs are never writable through to Seamless. Code may modify a pin's value in place. The change stays inside that run, and the pin's checksum is unchanged.
docs.title: Isolation and persistent state

docs.text: Each of the two languages has two backends : a CLI backend and an in-memory backend ( Language backends ). The metavariable BACKEND selects one, with the values "cli" and "mem" . Language "cli" , the default "mem" r an Rscript process per run R embedded in the Python process, through ryp julia a julia process per run Julia embedded in the Python process, through juliacall tf = Transformer("r") tf.metavars.BACKEND # "cli" tf.metavars.BACKEND = "mem" tf.metavars has the names that the handler declared. Reading one gives the value that was set, or else the handler's default. Any other name raises, on read and on write. The exception class is not specified. BACKEND accepts "cli" and "mem" , and nothing else. Any other value is refused when it is assigned, and nothing is stored. The names of the tools, such as "Rscript" or "juliacall" , are not values. A value that arrives in a transformation dict fails when the transformation runs. A build writes every metavar into the Transformation , defaults included, under meta["metavars"] . The backend is not part of the transformation's identity ( Identity and caching ). Bound Transformers. ctx.tf.metavars behaves the same. The values belong to the workflow Context node: every view of ctx.tf reads and writes the one mapping, the node keeps it in its meta , and ctx.get_graph() saves it. A node whose result is recorded does not run its code again after a change of BACKEND , because its tf_checksum is the same. What a backend needs on the machine that runs the transformation: Language "cli" needs "mem" needs r Rscript on the PATH ; the R packages RcppCNPy and jsonlite the Python package ryp , with R and the R package arrow ; the R package jsonlite julia julia on the PATH ; the Julia packages NPZ and JSON in the active project the Python package juliacall ; the Julia package JSON in the project that juliacall uses Seamless installs none of these. A tool or a package that is missing is a failure of the transformation. The machine that runs the transformation needs them, not the one that builds it , unless they are the same. Which machine runs it follows from the execution backend ( Execution backends ). Under a CLI backend with a Docker image, the image needs them. A conda environment needs them too, where the transformer has one ( Environments ).
docs.title: Backends

docs.text: Every run starts a new interpreter process , in a job directory of its own, on the machinery of bash transformations. What Execution backends , Bash bodies , says of a bash body holds for it: the process that runs the transformation keeps its working directory, and a nested seamless-run that the code starts is signalled. The interpreter does not read the user's startup files. The commands are Rscript --vanilla and julia --startup-file=no . The transformer's environment is entered first , when it has one: its conda environment is activated, or the interpreter is started in a container made from its Docker image ( Environments ). One run at a time per process, by default , because the run takes the process lock. With tf.process_lock = False , several run side by side in one process. Each has its own interpreter process, so they share no interpreter state.
docs.title: CLI backends

docs.text: The interpreter is embedded in the process that runs the transformation. That is the calling process in process mode, and a worker process otherwise. It starts at its first use and lives until the process ends. There is one embedded interpreter per process , and one transformation uses it at a time ( The process lock ). transform() isolations are reused from one run to the next ( Isolation and persistent state ). That is what an in-memory backend is for: the interpreter starts once, and definitions are evaluated once. It cannot enter an environment. A conda environment must already be the one of the process, and a Docker image is refused ( Environments ).
docs.title: In-memory backends

docs.text: A handler-language transformation takes the process lock like any other ( Execution backends , The process lock ). The handler receives whether it did ( Writing a handler , The arguments ). An in-memory backend refuses to run without the process lock. A transformation that has process_lock false and an in-memory backend fails when it runs. The message names the CLI backend as the alternative. A driver is refused too , because driver true means process_lock false ( Transformers , process_lock and driver ). The process lock is the only lock around an embedded interpreter. Among transformations that hold it, one runs at a time in a process, and that is what keeps two transformations out of one interpreter. The refusal happens when the transformation runs. Building succeeds. A result that is already recorded is returned without the check. An in-memory body holds the lock from its start to its end. The code has no way to give it up: the nesting signal of a bash body does not exist here. Code that submits nested work, for example by running seamless-run , belongs under the CLI backend. A transformation that arrives without its __meta__ takes the lock and runs under the default backend , which is the CLI ( Transformers , Absent keys in a transformation dict ).
docs.title: The process lock

docs.text: Both backends of a language give the same result, bit for bit, when both succeed. A backend may fail where the other succeeds. It may not succeed with a different result. This is what lets the backend stay outside identity. A result that was computed under one backend is served, from the cache, to a transformation that names the other. How it holds. Each language has one runtime, written in that language, and both backends use it. The runtime recognizes the code style, builds the isolation, turns each pin into a native value, runs the code, and classifies and encodes the result. The backends differ only in how bytes travel. JSON values cross as JSON text under both backends , and are parsed and written by the same call. That is why jsonlite and JSON are needed by the in-memory backends too. There is no fallback encoding. A backend that cannot carry a value fails. It never substitutes another representation. A deep pin has the same form under both backends , and a deep result has the same member rule ( Deep celltypes and checksum objects ). Code that filters the keys of a deepcell pin and returns the rest gives the same result under both. A deepfolder pin is a dict of checksum objects under both backends. Its form does not depend on where the member buffers are stored. Cases where one backend fails and the other succeeds: Case CLI backend In-memory backend A mixed pin whose value combines arrays and plain data: a buffer in the Seamless-mixed format ( Celltypes and conversion ) fails accepted R: a float32 array, or an array with more than two dimensions ( Array rules ) fails accepts supported element types A conda environment that is not the one of the process that runs the transformation ( Environments ) runs, in that environment fails A Docker image ( Environments ) runs, in a container fails The guarantee is about the handler, not about the code. Code that is not a pure function of its pins is not made reproducible by it ( Isolation and persistent state ). The text of a failure is not covered either: the two backends report the same failure in different words.
docs.title: Backend parity

docs.text: Pin celltype Native value in R Native value in Julia text a character string, without the final newline a String , without the final newline plain , and mixed whose buffer is JSON what jsonlite::fromJSON returns what JSON.parse returns bytes a raw vector a Vector{UInt8} binary , and mixed whose buffer is an array a double or logical vector or array ( Array rules ) an Array ( Array rules ) int , float , bool , str , and every other celltype that is neither deep nor checksum as plain as plain folder a named list of raw vectors, one for each member's bytes a Dict{String, Vector{UInt8}} deepfolder a named list of checksum objects a Dict{String, Checksum} deepcell a named list of checksum objects a Dict{String, Checksum} checksum a checksum object a Checksum A mixed pin is read by what its buffer is : an array, JSON, or a Seamless-mixed buffer that holds both. The handler looks at the first bytes of the buffer. A Seamless-mixed buffer is accepted by the in-memory backends only. Its plain parts follow the JSON rule, and its arrays the array rule. text and str differ. A text pin is the text itself. A str pin is a JSON string, and reaches the code through the JSON parser. A deep pin has the same form under both backends ( Deep celltypes and checksum objects ). The code never sees a directory or a file for a folder pin. The value is the same whether the pin arrived as a value or as a file ( Pins on file ).
docs.title: What the code receives

docs.text: Result Returned to Seamless as anything, when the result celltype is bytes raw bytes a numeric array, when the result celltype is binary or mixed a C-contiguous NumPy array a named list or a Dict with string keys, when the result celltype is deepcell or folder that dict, each member a value or a checksum object ( Deep celltypes and checksum objects ) a checksum object or a string of 64 hexadecimal characters, when the result celltype is checksum that checksum anything else the value that Python parses from the runtime's JSON encoding of it Seamless serializes the returned value under the result celltype , as it does for the return value of a Python transformer. The null rules for results apply ( Pins , Null, required pins, optional pins ). In R, a vector of length one without dimensions is a scalar. It is not an array of one element. Arrays inside a list or a dictionary become nested JSON lists. Only a result that is itself an array is returned as an array. The R and the Julia handler never return a value that combines arrays and plain data. A value that the runtime cannot encode fails the transformation. A checksum object is returned only as a member of a deepcell or folder result, or as a checksum result. Returned under any other result celltype it fails the transformation. A deepfolder result is refused , as for every transformer ( Deep celltypes , The output side ).
docs.title: What the code returns

docs.text: Deep pins and deep results are accepted under both backends. Their forms are those that every non-bash backend gives ( Deep celltypes , How deep values reach a transformer ), in the forms of R and Julia: Pin R Julia folder a named list of raw vectors a Dict{String, Vector{UInt8}} deepfolder a named list of checksum objects a Dict{String, Checksum} deepcell a named list of checksum objects a Dict{String, Checksum} a deepfolder or deepcell source, declared plain a named list of 64-hex strings a Dict{String, String} of 64-hex strings The keys are the keys of the index , which may contain / . An empty index is an empty named list or Dict . A folder pin holds every member's bytes in memory. The process that runs the transformation resolves the members, from any buffer source, before the code runs. A deepfolder or deepcell pin resolves no member. Each is a dict of checksum objects. The class of R and of Julia carries a checksum and has no access to a buffer. These pins serve to select members and pass them on, for example in a deepcell result. Declaring the pin plain hands the code the index as data: strings, not objects. A string that is returned from it is a value ( Results , below). Results. The code returns the dict itself, and Seamless packs it into an index ( Deep celltypes , The output side ). A member is a value unless it is a checksum object. A string of 64 hexadecimal characters is a value, like any other string. Code that wants to return a checksum wraps the string in the checksum class. A member that is a value is classified as an ordinary result is in that language: by the rule of a mixed result for a deepcell , and by the rule of a bytes result for a folder . A member that is a checksum object is inserted into the index as it is. Nothing checks that the buffer exists.
docs.title: Deep celltypes and checksum objects

docs.text: Each language has a class that holds a checksum. It exists under both backends, and the runtime puts its functions in the scope of the code. R Julia Make one from a string seamless_checksum("…") Checksum("…") Test for one is_seamless_checksum(x) x isa Checksum It is made from a string of 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters. Any other value is an error. It can be tested for, converted to its string, compared and printed. Two objects with the same string are equal. It can be told from a plain string. It cannot resolve. The class carries the checksum and no access to a buffer. Python code has Checksum.resolve() , and R and Julia code has nothing like it. A checksum pin is one such object , and a checksum result accepts one, or a string of 64 hexadecimal characters. Plain data holds no objects. A plain pin that is a dict of checksums holds strings.
docs.title: Checksum classes

docs.text: Array element types are normalized before the user code runs , including arrays inside an embedded Seamless-mixed pin: NumPy input dtype Native R element type Native Julia element type boolean logical Bool signed integer double Int64 unsigned integer double UInt64 floating point double Float64 Other input array dtypes are refused. Integer values in R are subject to the precision of double: integers beyond the exact range of a double may be rounded. Both R backends apply the same conversion. R dimensions: a one-dimensional input becomes a vector; an input with two or more dimensions retains those dimensions. A returned vector of length one without dimensions is a scalar. R CLI backend restrictions: float32 inputs and arrays with more than two dimensions are refused. The R in-memory backend accepts them under the normalization above. Returned arrays: R numeric and integer arrays become NumPy float64 , and logical arrays become NumPy bool . Julia boolean, signed integer, unsigned integer and floating arrays become NumPy bool , int64 , uint64 and float64 , respectively. Other array element types are refused when an array result is required. Shape and layout: returned arrays retain their shape and are C-contiguous NumPy arrays. Input memory layout does not change their values. Parity remains fixed: both backends of one language give the same result when they succeed; a backend that cannot transport a value refuses it.
docs.title: Array rules

docs.text: A handler-language pin of celltype mixed , plain , text , bytes or binary reaches the handler as a file when one exists, and as a value otherwise. This holds for every handler language, the registered ones included. As a file: when the pin's buffer is on file in a read-buffer directory that is configured for the process that runs the transformation. The handler receives the path, and nothing is read into memory for it. As a value: in every other case. The handler receives the value, parsed under the pin's celltype, as a Python transformer would. The file holds the buffer, byte for byte: Celltype Bytes of the buffer text the text and a final newline plain JSON bytes the bytes binary a NumPy .npy array mixed .npy for an array, JSON for a plain value, the Seamless-mixed format for a value that combines both The file can be compressed. Its path then ends in .zst or .gz , and the handler decompresses ( Compression ). Which form arrives is not part of identity. The transformation says that the pin may be a file. That statement is the same for every transformation of a handler language, and it does not depend on any machine ( Identity and caching ). The R and the Julia handler convert either form. The code sees the same native value, and cannot tell the forms apart. Other pins always arrive as values. deepcell , deepfolder and folder pins arrive in the forms of Deep celltypes and checksum objects ( Deep celltypes , How deep values reach a transformer ).
docs.title: Pins on file

docs.text: Part of the transformation Where it is carried In the checksum the language name __language__ yes the code text; each pin's checksum and celltype; the result celltype the pins, __output__ yes "this pin may be a file", for each pin of Pins on file __format__ yes, and the same for every transformation of a handler language the handler's source __handler__ no the metavars, BACKEND included __meta__ , under metavars no the conda environment __env__ no The split is the one of Identity and caching , Load-bearing vs orthogonal keys . The same code text under r and under julia is two transformations. A cached result is returned whatever the backend and whatever the handler. Nothing is launched, and neither R nor Julia needs to be installed for a cache hit. Two submissions of one transformation with different backends latch on to each other , unless strict_dunder is used ( Identity and caching , Concurrent submissions of the same checksum ). A fingertip runs the code where the buffer is wanted. A fingertip is never dispatched ( Scratch, witness, audit , Fingertipping ). The machine that asks needs the language's tools. When it recomputes from the checksum alone, it uses its own registered handler and the default backend. A handler defines what its language name means. Because the handler is outside the checksum, two handlers that are registered under one name must give the same result for the same code and pins. A new version of a handler is such a second handler. Seamless does not detect a violation, and the cache then serves results of the old meaning. A metavar must not change the result. It selects how the code is run. The rule is the one for the metavars of a compiled transformer ( Compiled transformers , Output-only wildcards ).
docs.title: Identity and caching

docs.text: from seamless.transformer import Transformer from seamless_transformer.languages import register_language_handler def template_handler(code, pins, filesystem): import json # imports go inside the function values = {} for name, value in pins.items(): if filesystem.get(name, {}).get("filesystem"): with open(value) as f: # a path: the file holds the buffer value = json.load(f) # (not handled here: .zst and .gz) values[name] = value # otherwise: the pin's value return code.strip().format(**values) register_language_handler("template", template_handler) tf = Transformer("template", direct=True) tf.code = "Hello, {who}!" tf.celltypes.who = "plain" tf.pins.who = "world" tf() # -> "Hello, world!" register_language_handler(name, handler, *, metavars=None) : handler is one self-contained Python function. It is defined with def . Its imports are inside its body. It has no closure and uses no global of the module that defines it. This is the discipline of Python transformer code, and for the same reason: the function travels as source text. Decorators are not part of that source. Its parameters choose what it receives. Each parameter name must be one of the names under The arguments , and the handler is called with exactly those, by keyword. A parameter of another name, a positional-only parameter, *args and **kwargs are refused at registration. metavars maps each metavar that the handler understands to its default. These names are the ones that tf.metavars accepts. A handler that has both a CLI and an in-memory backend declares BACKEND among them, with the default "cli" or "mem" . The builder refuses any other value of a metavar of that name when it is assigned ( Language backends , Selecting a backend ). name must not be a native or a compiled language. Registering a name again replaces its handler. Transformations that are built afterwards carry the new one. A registration that is refused raises. The exception class is not specified.
docs.title: Writing a handler

docs.text: Parameter Value code the source text of the transformation pins a dict: pin name to the pin's value, or to the path of a file ( Pins on file ) filesystem a dict: pin name to an entry, for the pins that may arrive as a file. entry["filesystem"] is true when pins[name] is a path. entry["celltype"] is the pin's celltype output_name the name of the result. For a Transformer it is result output_celltype the result celltype metavars a dict of every declared metavar: the transformer's value, or else the registered default environment the transformer's environment, as a dict, with keys such as conda_environment and docker . It is empty when none is set. A handler honours it through one of the two public functions ( Honouring the environment ) process_lock a bool: whether this run took the process lock pins holds the input pins only. The code is not in it. The handler runs in a namespace that holds its arguments and nothing else. The pins are not visible as global variables. The return value is the result. Seamless serializes it under the result celltype, as it does for a Python transformer. An exception that the handler raises is the failure of the transformation.
docs.title: The arguments

docs.text: A handler honours its environment argument, or the transformation does not honour it. Seamless offers two public functions, in seamless_transformer.languages ( Language backends , The two public functions ): The handler runs the code It calls in the Python process that runs the transformation, as an embedded interpreter check_in_memory_environment(environment, language) before it runs the code as a process of its own execute_cli(command, pins_, PINS, FILESYSTEM, OUTPUTPIN, environment) in place of starting the process itself check_in_memory_environment raises for a Docker image, and for a conda environment that is not the one of the process. It also looks the names of set_which up on the process's PATH . execute_cli wraps a conda environment and a Docker image, looks set_which up inside the environment, and is cancelled and torn down with the transformation. A handler that starts a process itself gets none of it. A handler returns a Python value. For a deep result that is a dict whose members are values or seamless.Checksum objects. Nothing else is asked of it. Both functions can be called outside a running transformation , for example when a test calls the handler directly. Nothing enforces it. A handler that calls neither function ignores the environment, and gets no which check.
docs.title: Honouring the environment

docs.text: A build puts the handler's source into the Transformation. It is carried in __handler__ , outside the checksum. The process that runs the transformation needs no registration. A handler that is registered only in the script that builds the transformation also runs in a worker process, on a jobserver and on a Dask worker. What the handler imports, and the tools it starts, must exist there. A transformation without __handler__ uses the registry of the process that runs it. This happens when a transformation is run from its checksum alone: by a fingertip, or by seamless-run-transformation without a dunder file. When that process has no handler for the language, the transformation fails. Building needs the registration. A builder for a registered language can be constructed, and a Transformation can be built from it, only in a process where that handler is registered. The two built-in handlers always are.
docs.title: The handler travels with the transformation

docs.text: The process lock gives exclusion, not a fixed thread. A handler never runs on the main thread of its process, and successive runs in one process may run on different threads. In process mode the thread that ran one handler may no longer exist when the next one runs. run_in_interpreter_thread(name, func, /, *args, **kwargs) gives a fixed thread. It runs func(*args, **kwargs) on one thread per process and per name , waits, and returns the result. An exception in func is raised in the caller. The thread is created at the first call and lives until the process ends. A call from that thread itself runs func at once, on that thread. It takes no lock. Exclusion comes from the process lock. The Julia in-memory backend runs Julia on its interpreter thread. Every call into Julia goes through run_in_interpreter_thread("juliacall", ...) , and so does Julia's exit hook when the process ends. Julia is never called from another thread. The R in-memory backend does not use it. Do not rely on which thread runs R code. Output that func prints on the interpreter thread is not in the transformation's log. Capture belongs to the thread that runs the handler ( Transformation logs , What is captured ). Return the text, and write it from the handler. A handler may hold Python's GIL for a long time. A worker pool checks each of its processes about once a second. A worker that is running a transformation is not restarted when it misses that check. It is restarted only when its process exits or its connection closes. The Julia in-memory backend ( juliacall ) runs the Julia code with the GIL released.
docs.title: Threads, and run_in_interpreter_thread

docs.text: Output that the code prints is in the transformation's log, under both backends ( Transformation logs ). CLI backend: stdout and stderr are two streams, relayed while the code runs, as for a bash transformation. On remote: daskserver they can be streamed ( Streaming ). In-memory backend: the output may arrive only when the code has finished. A failure of the code is a failure of the transformation , and failures are not cached. The common ones: the code raises an error; block code never assigns result ; a tool or a package is missing; a value cannot be carried by the backend; an in-memory backend runs without the process lock, or with an environment that it cannot honour. The failure text depends on the backend. CLI backend: the Bash transformer exception report ( Transformation logs , The failure text ). Its command is the one that starts the interpreter, not the user's code. The language's own error message is in the standard error trailer. In-memory backend: a Python traceback that carries the language's error message. Cancellation ( Cancellation ). A run under a CLI backend is cancelled as a bash transformation is. Under an in-memory backend, a cancel in a worker pool terminates the worker process, and its interpreter with it. In process mode a cancel does not interrupt code that is running in the embedded interpreter, as it does not interrupt Python code.
docs.title: Logs, failures and cancellation

docs.text: A transformer's environment ( Environments ) is honoured, or the transformation fails. It is never ignored. Language backends , Environments , has the rule. For R and Julia: The transformer has CLI backend In-memory backend a conda environment activates it, and starts the interpreter in it runs only when its process is already in exactly that environment. Otherwise the transformation fails a Docker image starts the interpreter in a container made from the image the transformation fails both refused at dispatch refused at dispatch A CLI backend runs in the transformer's conda environment , when tf.environment.set_conda_env(...) names one. The environment is activated before the interpreter starts, as for a bash transformation. This is how a transformer chooses its R or Julia installation. A CLI backend runs in a container , when tf.environment.set_docker(...) names an image. The image must hold the interpreter and the packages of the backend ( What a backend needs ). The host does not need R or Julia. The runtime, the image pull policy and the other settings are those of bash transformations ( Environments , The runtime is chosen where the job runs ). An in-memory backend cannot enter an environment. Its interpreter is the one embedded in the process that runs the transformation. A conda environment is therefore a requirement on that process: the process must already be running in exactly the environment that the transformer names. A specification that contains / is a path, compared with the process's CONDA_PREFIX . Any other specification is a name, compared with its CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV . The calling process must be in it in process mode, and the worker processes otherwise. When it is not, the transformation fails. An in-memory backend fails for a Docker image , always. The message names BACKEND="cli" as the alternative. The checks run when the transformation runs. A result that is already recorded is returned without them, and building never fails for an environment. The Julia project of a CLI job is the tracked Seamless Julia project. Seamless stages its Project.toml and Manifest.toml in the job directory and starts Julia with --project=. . JULIA_PROJECT does not select another project. The job uses a writable depot in its own directory first, followed by the depots named by JULIA_DEPOT_PATH , the conda installation's packaged depot when present, and the user's depot. In a container the image must name its packaged depot with JULIA_DEPOT_PATH , readable by the host user who runs the job. Its precompiled packages must be compatible with the executing CPU. For juliacall the project is the one that juliacall uses in the process. The environment is not part of identity , here as everywhere. tf.environment.set_which([...]) lists binaries that must exist. They are looked up where the code runs. For a CLI backend that is inside the environment, after it is entered: a binary that exists only in the environment satisfies the check, and one that exists only on the host does not. For an in-memory backend it is the PATH of the process that runs the transformation.
docs.title: Environments

docs.text: R and Julia code cannot resolve a checksum. A deepcell pin serves to select and pass on members. A folder pin holds every member in memory at once , under both backends. The CLI backends cannot take a Seamless-mixed pin. The R CLI backend also refuses float32 arrays and arrays with more than two dimensions ( Array rules ). Isolations are never dropped. An embedded interpreter keeps every transform() isolation it has built, and Julia cannot unload a module. A worker process that lives long and sees many different transform() codes grows. A failure under a CLI backend is titled Bash transformer exception , although the code is R or Julia. The execution record reports the language kind of a handler-language transformation as python ( Execution records ). A user-registered language cannot be built where it is not registered ( The handler travels with the transformation ). A process that loads a workflow graph with a node of that language must register the handler first. Writing a job directory instead of running it is for bash transformations only.

docs.text: R or Julia through seamless-run , direct or delayed ( Faces ). Reading pin declarations from an R or a Julia signature, and optional pins. Installing R, Julia, their packages, ryp or juliacall . Compiled code. A language that compiles to a C-ABI transform() is a compiled language ( Compiled transformers ).
