This split is the heart of the identity model: load-bearing keys capture the "what to run" identity, orthogonal keys capture the "how to run" envelope. An agent must not move load-bearing data into the orthogonal set to avoid cache misses — doing so corrupts the identity model by aliasing distinct computations to one key.
docs.title: Load-bearing vs orthogonal keys in a transformation dict

docs.text: A transformation in a handler language, such as R or Julia, is run by a handler : a Python function that receives the code and the pins ( contracts/handler-languages.md ). Such a transformation has two keys that the split above must place. __handler__ is orthogonal. It holds the checksum of the handler's source text. It travels with the transformation, so a process that never registered the handler can run it. It is outside the checksum. Identity sees the language name , in __language__ . Replacing a handler, or upgrading it, is not a cache miss. This puts an obligation on handlers: two handlers registered under one name must give the same result for the same code and inputs. Seamless does not check it. The handler's settings are orthogonal too. They are its metavars, in __meta__ , and the BACKEND that selects how the code is run is one of them. The handler contract guarantees that both backends of a language give the same result bit for bit whenever both succeed ( contracts/handler-languages.md , Backend parity ). That guarantee is what makes the backend orthogonal rather than load-bearing. __format__ gets a neutral entry. For every pin of celltype mixed , plain , text , bytes or binary of a handler language, the dict carries: {"filesystem": {"mode": "file", "optional": true}, "celltype": "<the pin's celltype>"} The entry says that the pin may be handed to the handler as a file. That happens when the pin's buffer is on file where the transformation runs. Otherwise the handler gets the value ( contracts/handler-languages.md , Pins on file ). __format__ is load-bearing, so the entry is in the checksum. It is neutral : every transformation of every handler language carries it for every such pin, whichever form is delivered and on whichever machine. It adds nothing to identity beyond the language and the pin celltypes, which are in the checksum already. Identity therefore does not depend on where a buffer is stored, and neither does the result: both forms hold the same bytes. Only folder pins carry a directory entry. seamless-run writes one for each directory argument. A deepfolder pin carries checksum objects outside bash and is refused by bash, so it has no directory entry. contracts/pins.md , Pins on file , has the entry, who writes it and what the executing process does with it. A language backend does not change the pin form.
docs.title: Handler languages: __handler__ and the neutral __format__ entry

docs.text: An agent should assume there is (or should be) a way to: bypass transformation-result caches for a specific computation recompute the step compare results bitwise (checksum equality), and if not equal, compare a user-provided witness output (see contracts/scratch-witness-audit.md ) If docs do not specify audit/recompute controls, ask the user; don’t guess.
docs.title: Forcing recomputation / auditing

docs.text: Language backends (Contract) The code of a transformation is run by a language backend . A language backend is either a CLI backend or an in-memory backend , and what it does with the transformer's environment follows from which of the two it is. A language backend is not an execution backend. process , spawn and remote decide where a transformation runs ( Execution backends ). A language backend decides how the code is run once the transformation is there. The two axes are independent. A CLI backend starts a process for each run, in a job directory of its own, on the machinery of bash transformations. Its command is a script (bash) or an interpreter with a runner file (R, Julia, Python). An in-memory backend runs the code inside the process that runs the transformation: the calling process in process mode, a worker process otherwise. This page owns the two kinds, their names, the setting that selects one, the environment rule of each kind, the rule that these rules apply when the transformation runs, the lookup of required binaries, the two public functions that carry the rules, and the Python CLI backend. Other pages own the rest: the wrapper that a CLI backend uses (conda, containers, the failure classes, the job directory): Environments ; R, Julia and the handler API: Handler languages ; deep pins and deep results: Deep celltypes ; compiled transformers: Compiled transformers ; the builder, process_lock and driver : Transformers ; the process lock and nested work: Execution backends . The implementation plan describes the mechanics and the phases. The languages and their backends Language CLI backend In-memory backend tf.metavars.BACKEND bash the only one none none python a Python process per run today's execution, in the process "mem" (default), "cli" compiled ( c , cpp , fortran , rust , …) none the only one none r an Rscript process per run R embedded in the Python process "cli" (default), "mem" julia a julia process per run Julia embedded in the Python process "cli" (default), "mem" a language added with register_language_handler what its handler does what its handler does what its handler declares ( Selecting a backend ) "In-memory backend" is the term for the kind whose BACKEND value is "mem" , and "CLI backend" for the kind whose value is "cli" . A language with one kind has no setting. A bash transformation always runs as a CLI job, and a compiled transformation always runs in memory. seamless-run makes bash transformations. It has no BACKEND , and it never runs a command in memory. Compiled transformers have no CLI backend. A compiled call cannot be wrapped. Selecting a backend BACKEND is a metavariable of the transformer, on the Python face and on a bound node. tf = Transformer("python", direct=True) tf.metavars.BACKEND # "mem" tf.metavars.BACKEND = "cli" The values are "mem" and "cli" , in every language. The names of the tools that a backend runs, such as "Rscript" or "juliacall" , are not values. Any other value is refused when it is assigned , on the Python face and on a bound node. The refusal happens before anything is stored, and the builder keeps the value it had. The exception class is not specified. A value that arrives in a transformation dict is not assigned by anyone. Such a transformation fails when it runs. Every Python builder has tf.metavars.BACKEND : Transformer("python") , a function decorated with direct or delayed , and a bound ctx.tf . The default is "mem" . tf.metavars of a Python builder has the one name BACKEND . Reading or writing any other name raises. Bound Transformers. ctx.tf.metavars.BACKEND behaves the same. The value belongs to the workflow Context node: every view of ctx.tf reads and writes it, the node keeps it in its meta , and ctx.get_graph() saves it. A node whose result is recorded does not run its code again after a change of BACKEND . Where the value is stored. A Python build writes BACKEND into the Transformation's meta["metavars"] only when it was set. A Python transformation without it runs in memory. A handler language writes every metavar, defaults included ( Handler languages , Backends ). A handler that has both kinds declares BACKEND among its metavars and uses the same two values. The builder checks the value of a metavar with that name for every handler language. A compiled builder has no BACKEND . Its tf.metavars holds its output maxima ( Compiled transformers ), and assigning BACKEND raises. Backend and identity BACKEND is not part of the transformation's identity. It is carried in __meta__ , under metavars , which is outside the checksum ( Identity and caching , Load-bearing vs orthogonal keys ). A result computed under one backend is served, from the cache, to a transformation that names the other. That is valid only because of parity ( Parity ). Two submissions of one transformation with different backends latch on to each other , unless strict_dunder is used. A transformation that arrives without its __meta__ runs under the default backend of its language. That is the in-memory backend for Python and the CLI backend for R and Julia. A fingertip recomputes under the default backend , in the process that wants the buffer. Every backend rule applies when the transformation runs A rule about a backend is checked when the transformation runs, and at no other moment. Building a Transformation checks none of them, and neither does setting an environment. A result that is already recorded is returned without any of them, so a recorded result is served on a machine that has neither the environment nor the interpreter. This holds for the rules about conda, Docker, required binaries, properly mixed pins and seamless-core in this page and in Environments . The reason is that a result does not know which backend produced it. The environment and the backend are outside identity, so a cache hit runs nothing and needs nothing. The check of BACKEND itself is not such a rule. It does not depend on where the transformation runs, and it happens at assignment ( Selecting a backend ). A specification that could never work is refused at dispatch , not when it is set and not when the Transformation is built ( Environments , below). Environments A transformer's environment ( Environments ) is honoured, or the transformation fails. It is never ignored. What a backend can honour depends on its kind: The environment has CLI backend In-memory backend nothing runs runs a conda environment enters it, as a bash transformation does ( conda run ) runs only when its process is already in exactly that environment. Otherwise it fails a Docker image runs in a container, as a bash transformation does fails both refused at dispatch refused at dispatch The in-memory rule The rule is one rule for every in-memory backend: compiled transformers, Python in memory, and the in-memory backends of R, Julia and any other handler language. An in-memory backend cannot enter an environment. The code runs in the process that runs the transformation. That process is the calling process in process mode, and a worker process of the pool, the jobserver or the Dask worker otherwise. A Docker image always fails. The message names the language and, where the language has a CLI backend, says to use BACKEND="cli" . A conda environment is a requirement on the process. The process must already be running in exactly that environment: a specification that contains / is a path. The real path of the process's CONDA_PREFIX must equal the real path of the specification, so a symlink to the environment matches; any other specification is a name. The process's CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV must equal it. When they do not match, the transformation fails , and the message names both: what the transformer asks for and what the process has. The requirement is on every process that can run the transformation. In a worker pool that means the pool's own processes, which have the environment that the pool was started in. Which process that is follows from the execution backend ( Execution backends ). The check happens before the body , so no code has run when it fails. The CLI rule A CLI backend wraps both specifications properly , for every language: conda as conda run , and a Docker image as a container run by docker, podman or apptainer, chosen by the executing host. The bash, R, Julia and Python CLI backends do the same thing, on the same machinery ( Environments ). What an environment needs from the executing host and from the image is in Environments , A conda environment , A Docker image and The runtime is chosen where the job runs . A CLI backend inherits the bash transformer's behaviour for everything else : the interpreter runs after the environment is entered, from the launcher transform.sh ; the executing host chooses the container runtime, and no image is pulled by default; in a container the job runs as the host user, in the job directory mounted at /seamless-job , which is also HOME ; read-buffer directories are bound read-only at their own paths; the failure classes, and the teardown of a cancelled job and its container; the nesting signal under conda, and none in a container. What the image or the conda environment must hold, besides bash in an image: CLI backend of Needs R Rscript ; the R packages RcppCNPy and jsonlite Julia julia ; the Julia packages NPZ and JSON Python python3 ; NumPy when an array crosses; seamless-core when a properly mixed value or a checksum crosses ( The Python CLI backend ) Seamless does not install any of these. Something that is missing is a failure of the transformation. In a container the host's environment variables are not inherited. The image supplies library and package depot paths. The Julia CLI backend uses the tracked Seamless Julia project staged in the job directory, regardless of JULIA_PROJECT ( Handler languages , Environments ). Docker together with conda A conda environment together with a Docker image is refused, for every language and both kinds of backend. A script that needs a conda environment inside an image activates it itself. The check happens at dispatch Two things are checked at dispatch: a conda environment together with a Docker image, and the keys of the image spec ( Environments , The image spec ). Dispatch is the moment at which a transformation that has no recorded result is handed to an execution backend. Setting an environment, and building a Transformation, check nothing. A Transformer that has both a conda environment and an image builds, and so does one whose image spec has an unknown key. A recorded result is returned without the check. A submission that latches on to a running one dispatches nothing, and is not checked either. The executing host validates again before launch. A transformation that is run from its checksum alone, or that arrives by another road, has no other check. seamless-run is covered : --docker together with --conda fails when the command is dispatched, not while its arguments are parsed. Dispatch happens on the submitting side for process , spawn , remote: jobserver and remote: daskserver alike. Required binaries tf.environment.set_which([...]) lists binaries that must exist. They are looked up where the code runs. Backend Looked up CLI backend, every language in the script, after the conda environment is entered or inside the image. A binary that exists only in the environment satisfies the check, and one that exists only on the host does not in-memory backend on the PATH of the process that runs the code A record probe checks nothing. The look-up is not done on the submitting machine for any language. A record probe is exempt A record probe is a Python in-memory transformation that carries the __env__ of the job whose surroundings it captures ( Execution records ). It runs on the host and is not checked against the environment that it carries: it does not fail for the conda environment or the image, and it does not check which . The two public functions The two rules are carried by two functions of seamless_transformer.languages . They are public: a handler of any language honours its environment through one of them, or fails. from seamless_transformer.languages import ( check_in_memory_environment, execute_cli, ) check_in_memory_environment(environment, language) # raises, or returns None execute_cli(command, pins_, PINS, FILESYSTEM, OUTPUTPIN, environment) check_in_memory_environment(environment, language) applies The in-memory rule and looks the names of which up on the PATH of the process. environment is the transformer's environment as a dict, as the handler receives it ( Handler languages , The arguments ). It may be empty. language is the language name. It is used in the message. It returns None , or raises. The exception class is not specified. It is a function of its arguments and of the process's environment. It needs no running transformation, so it can be called outside one. execute_cli(command, pins_, PINS, FILESYSTEM, OUTPUTPIN, environment) runs a command as a CLI job and applies The CLI rule . Parameter Meaning command the command that starts the interpreter, run by bash in the job directory pins_ the names of the files and directories to write into the job directory PINS a dict from each of those names to its content: a Buffer , bytes, a dict of checksums, or the path of a file that exists on the executing host FILESYSTEM a dict from each name to its entry, as for a pin on file ( Handler languages , The arguments ) OUTPUTPIN the celltype in which the content of RESULT is read environment the transformer's environment, as a dict It returns the content of RESULT . For bytes , folder and deepfolder as OUTPUTPIN the bytes. For any other celltype the file is parsed as an .npy array, then as JSON, then as text, and a content that is none of these is returned as a uint8 array. A RESULT that is a directory gives a dict from each file's path in it to its content, in the same form. It takes the transformation's checksum and its abort test from the running transformation. Inside one, a cancel finds the job and tears it down, and a docker or podman container carries the label seamless.tf=<tf_checksum> . Outside one, the launch works without them. It wraps conda and Docker from environment . A handler cannot wrap one and forget the other. It looks which up in the script. A handler passes environment as it received it. A handler that calls neither function gets no environment handling and no which check from Seamless. Nothing enforces it. The Python CLI backend BACKEND = "cli" makes a Python transformation run as a CLI job: the code runs in a python3 process of its own, in a job directory, on the machinery of bash transformations. Faces. The Python face ( Transformer("python") , direct , delayed ) and the workflow Context ( ctx.tf = function , a bound ctx.tf ). seamless-run has no such setting. What stays the same The code is the same code. The in-memory backend and the CLI backend give it the same names with the same values: The code modes are the same : a block, a function, a lambda and an expression, recognized in the same way. The pins are the same values. The process that runs the transformation parses each pin as the in-memory backend does, and the job gets it back unchanged. Plain data, text, arrays and bytes cross without Seamless in the job. A bytes pin is bytes under both backends ( Pins , A transformer's code receives ). A deep pin has the form of How deep values reach a transformer ( Deep celltypes ) under both backends. The result is what the code returns , or the variable of the output name for block code, serialized under the result celltype as the in-memory backend does it. print and the standard streams are relayed while the code runs, as two streams ( Transformation logs , Streaming ). The code is self-contained, as it always is ( Modules and closures ). What differs The code runs in another process , with its own interpreter. Imports, global state and open files are not shared with the process that runs the transformation. Every run starts an interpreter, plus conda run or a container start. The interpreter is python3 on the PATH where the job runs: in the conda environment or the image when there is one, otherwise the PATH of the executing process. It is not the interpreter of the submitting process. The job needs what the code imports. The submitting process's packages do not exist there. A transformation with modules or globals fails when it runs. The message says to use BACKEND="mem" . Packages the job needs When The job needs always python3 an array is a pin or a result NumPy a properly mixed value is a pin or a result seamless-core, installed where the code runs a deepcell pin or a checksum pin seamless-core the code itself uses Seamless, for example for nested work Seamless A properly mixed value is a mixed value whose buffer is in the Seamless-mixed format, which is a value that does not reduce to plain data or to an array ( Celltypes and conversion ). A pin or a result of that kind is carried to and from the job through seamless-core. A checksum crossing into the job also needs seamless-core, whether the code only passes its members on or resolves them. A job with none of these runs in an environment that has no Seamless. Nothing checks for seamless-core beforehand ( Every backend rule applies when the transformation runs ). When it is missing, the import fails inside the job, and the failure is the Python error in the standard error trailer. Results A returned value is carried as plain data, an array, bytes , a properly mixed value, or, as a member of a deep result, a checksum object. The process that runs the transformation then serializes it under the result celltype, with the calls that the in-memory backend uses. No serialization rule exists twice. There is no fallback encoding. A value that cannot be carried fails the transformation, and it never travels in a different representation. A folder or deepcell result is the dict that the code returns. Each member is a value or a checksum object ( Deep celltypes , The output side ). Nothing that a job wrote is loaded as a pickle. The process that runs the transformation reads a job's result as data only. The host rebuilds each CLI result and uses the in-memory serialization call. For a mixed result and for a value member of a deepcell result, the CLI accepts the same values as the in-memory backend: Returned value In-memory outcome Python CLI outcome None , booleans, integers, finite floats and strings Accepted as mixed values Accepted; carried as JSON, with the same result checksum Non-finite floats Accepted as mixed values using NumPy storage Accepted through .mixed , with the same result checksum Lists, tuples and dicts whose members are supported mixed values Accepted as mixed values Accepted as JSON where possible, otherwise .mixed , with the same result checksum bytes Accepted as a mixed value Accepted through .bytes ; the host serializes it as mixed and gets the same result checksum A NumPy scalar or array with a supported dtype, including an aligned structured array without padding Accepted as a mixed value Accepted through .mixed or .npy ; structured arrays use .mixed to preserve aligned-dtype metadata, with the same result checksum An aligned structured array with implicit padding and a supported structured dtype, directly or nested in a dict, list, or tuple result or deepcell value member Accepted as a mixed value Refused recursively because the NumPy mixed round trip can change padding bytes and the result checksum A structured subarray field whose base dtype has padding Fails; the in-memory mixed serializer does not support this dtype Refused by the recursive padding guard; both backends fail Another value accepted by Buffer(value, "mixed") Accepted as a mixed value Accepted through .mixed , using seamless-core in the job, with the same result checksum A Checksum object as an ordinary result Refused for mixed (and other non-checksum result celltypes) Refused with the same rule A Checksum object as a direct deepcell member A checksum, not a value A checksum entry in the index; the host rebuilds the same checksum object A Checksum nested inside a deepcell value member Part of the value; mixed serialization treats it as its checksum string Part of the .mixed value; host serialization gives the same member checksum A 64-character lowercase hexadecimal string as a deepcell member A value serialized under mixed A value, not a checksum; the same member checksum is produced A set or another value rejected by the in-memory serializer Fails Fails The same direct-member rule applies to a folder result: a Checksum object is a checksum, and any other member is a value. In particular, a checksum-looking string is never promoted to a checksum. A checksum nested inside a deepcell member follows the mixed-value serializer's recursive handling; only a direct Checksum member gets a checksum entry. Parity Both Python backends give the same result, bit for bit, when both succeed. A backend may fail where the other succeeds. It may not succeed with a different result. This is what lets the backend stay outside identity. A result type is accepted by the CLI backend only when both backends give it the same result checksum. Every other type fails under the CLI backend. One-sided failures : Case CLI backend In-memory backend modules or globals fails accepted a properly mixed or checksum value, with no seamless-core in the job fails accepted a conda environment other than the process's, or a Docker image runs, in that environment fails a Decimal result with output celltype str fails because the runner cannot encode it accepted; the str celltype serializes str(value) an aligned structured array with implicit padding and a supported structured dtype, directly or nested in a dict, list, or tuple mixed result or deepcell value member refused recursively because the NumPy mixed round trip cannot preserve the padding bytes and checksum accepted as a mixed value Checksum.resolve() in the code, for a member of a deepcell pin works under remote: daskserver only works The guarantee is about the backend, not about the code. Code that depends on the interpreter's state, the working directory, an environment variable or a file outside its pins is not covered, as for any transformation. The text of a failure is not covered : the two backends report the same failure in different words. The process lock, cancellation and failures The run takes the process lock like a bash body , and may run without it ( process_lock false, or a driver) ( Execution backends , The process lock ). A cancel tears the job down as it does for bash , and a container is removed ( Cancellation , A bash run that is cancelled ). A failure is the Bash transformer exception report ( Transformation logs , The failure text ). Its command is the interpreter's, and the Python traceback is in the standard error trailer. An in-memory Python body may run without the process lock , as it always has. The rule that an in-memory body must hold the lock is that of embedded interpreters ( Handler languages , The process lock ), and it does not extend to Python or compiled bodies. Drivers and nested work A Python CLI job is in the position of a bash job. A driver never takes the lock , under either backend. That is decided before the body starts. Code that is not a driver signals its parent at its first nested submission , as a bash body's seamless-run does, and the parent then gives the lock up ( Execution backends , Bash bodies ). The signal exists without an environment and under conda. It does not cross a container boundary. The job's process is configured from SEAMLESS_REMOTE_CLIENTS , before the code runs, when that variable is set in the job's environment and Seamless can be imported there. Nested work then goes to the same cluster and shares its caches, as a nested seamless-run does. Only the Dask worker exports the variable. Under remote: daskserver nested work therefore goes to the cluster. On the other execution backends nothing is exported, and a nested transformation runs inside the job's own process, with no cache and no dispatch. A nested seamless-run in a bash job fails there, for lack of a configuration, unless SEAMLESS_CACHE or SEAMLESS_REMOTE_CLIENTS is in the environment that the job inherits. Submissions from the job's process skip the permission routine of Dask , driver or not. The mark of a driver is not what decides it ( Execution backends , Drivers ). The code needs Seamless where it runs , and inside a container nested work is not supported. Deep pins and results Deep celltypes follow the matrix of Deep celltypes , How deep values reach a transformer . Bash has a column of its own, and every other backend, CLI and in-memory alike, follows the other. A folder pin is a dict of contents under every backend but bash , and deepcell and deepfolder pins are dicts of checksum objects. Under a CLI backend a folder travels to the job as a directory that the runtime reads back into a dict. The code does not see that directory. A deepcell or deepfolder pin uses the checksum class of its language : seamless.Checksum in Python, and the checksum class of the language in R and Julia ( Handler languages , Checksum classes ). A deep result is a dict under every backend but bash , and the RESULT directory in bash. Both backends of a language give a deep pin the same form. A compiled transformer refuses a deep pin , as before. Failures Each of the following is a failure of the transformation, and failures are not cached: an in-memory backend with a Docker image, or with a conda environment that is not its process's; a conda environment together with a Docker image, and an invalid image spec, at dispatch; a required binary that is missing where the code runs; a Python CLI job with modules or globals, with a value that it cannot carry, or without a package that it needs; every failure class of a CLI job ( Environments , Failures ). Current limitations A third-party handler can ignore environment . The two functions make honouring it easy. Nothing enforces it. A Python CLI job with a deepcell pin or a checksum pin needs seamless-core , also where its code only passes members on. Code in a CLI job can resolve the members of a deepcell pin under remote: daskserver only. No Seamless configuration is exported to a job outside Dask. R and Julia code cannot resolve a checksum at all. A properly mixed value is written by the seamless-core of the process that runs the transformation, and read by the one in the job , and back. Nothing checks that two versions agree on the format. Every Python CLI run starts an interpreter , plus conda run (in the order of a second with conda ) or a container start. A failure under a CLI backend is titled Bash transformer exception , whatever the language. A job holds its process for as long as it runs , unless process_lock is false. In a container, nested Seamless work is not supported. Writing a job directory instead of running it is for bash transformations only. Non-goals A CLI backend for compiled transformers. A setting that lets a Python or compiled pin arrive as a file. Modules and globals under the Python CLI backend. Seamless installing an interpreter, a package or an environment on the executing host or in an image. A public format for what travels between a job and the process that runs the transformation. A handler returns a Python value to Seamless. Code locations Concern Module / symbol The two public functions seamless_transformer.languages ( check_in_memory_environment , execute_cli ) The CLI job launcher seamless_transformer.execute_bash ( execute_bash ) Dispatch to a backend seamless_transformer.run.run_transformation_dict metavars of Python builders seamless_transformer.transformer_class The check of the specification at dispatch seamless_transformer.transformation_cache

A Python build writes BACKEND into the Transformation's meta["metavars"] only when it was set. A Python transformation without it runs in memory. A handler language writes every metavar, defaults included ( Handler languages , Backends ). A handler that has both kinds declares BACKEND among its metavars and uses the same two values. The builder checks the value of a metavar with that name for every handler language. A compiled builder has no BACKEND . Its tf.metavars holds its output maxima ( Compiled transformers ), and assigning BACKEND raises.
docs.title: Selecting a backend

docs.text: BACKEND is not part of the transformation's identity. It is carried in __meta__ , under metavars , which is outside the checksum ( Identity and caching , Load-bearing vs orthogonal keys ). A result computed under one backend is served, from the cache, to a transformation that names the other. That is valid only because of parity ( Parity ). Two submissions of one transformation with different backends latch on to each other , unless strict_dunder is used. A transformation that arrives without its __meta__ runs under the default backend of its language. That is the in-memory backend for Python and the CLI backend for R and Julia. A fingertip recomputes under the default backend , in the process that wants the buffer.
docs.title: Backend and identity

docs.text: A rule about a backend is checked when the transformation runs, and at no other moment. Building a Transformation checks none of them, and neither does setting an environment. A result that is already recorded is returned without any of them, so a recorded result is served on a machine that has neither the environment nor the interpreter. This holds for the rules about conda, Docker, required binaries, properly mixed pins and seamless-core in this page and in Environments . The reason is that a result does not know which backend produced it. The environment and the backend are outside identity, so a cache hit runs nothing and needs nothing. The check of BACKEND itself is not such a rule. It does not depend on where the transformation runs, and it happens at assignment ( Selecting a backend ). A specification that could never work is refused at dispatch , not when it is set and not when the Transformation is built ( Environments , below).
docs.title: Every backend rule applies when the transformation runs

docs.text: A transformer's environment ( Environments ) is honoured, or the transformation fails. It is never ignored. What a backend can honour depends on its kind: The environment has CLI backend In-memory backend nothing runs runs a conda environment enters it, as a bash transformation does ( conda run ) runs only when its process is already in exactly that environment. Otherwise it fails a Docker image runs in a container, as a bash transformation does fails both refused at dispatch refused at dispatch
docs.title: Environments

docs.text: The rule is one rule for every in-memory backend: compiled transformers, Python in memory, and the in-memory backends of R, Julia and any other handler language. An in-memory backend cannot enter an environment. The code runs in the process that runs the transformation. That process is the calling process in process mode, and a worker process of the pool, the jobserver or the Dask worker otherwise. A Docker image always fails. The message names the language and, where the language has a CLI backend, says to use BACKEND="cli" . A conda environment is a requirement on the process. The process must already be running in exactly that environment: a specification that contains / is a path. The real path of the process's CONDA_PREFIX must equal the real path of the specification, so a symlink to the environment matches; any other specification is a name. The process's CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV must equal it. When they do not match, the transformation fails , and the message names both: what the transformer asks for and what the process has. The requirement is on every process that can run the transformation. In a worker pool that means the pool's own processes, which have the environment that the pool was started in. Which process that is follows from the execution backend ( Execution backends ). The check happens before the body , so no code has run when it fails.
docs.title: The in-memory rule

docs.text: A CLI backend wraps both specifications properly , for every language: conda as conda run , and a Docker image as a container run by docker, podman or apptainer, chosen by the executing host. The bash, R, Julia and Python CLI backends do the same thing, on the same machinery ( Environments ). What an environment needs from the executing host and from the image is in Environments , A conda environment , A Docker image and The runtime is chosen where the job runs . A CLI backend inherits the bash transformer's behaviour for everything else : the interpreter runs after the environment is entered, from the launcher transform.sh ; the executing host chooses the container runtime, and no image is pulled by default; in a container the job runs as the host user, in the job directory mounted at /seamless-job , which is also HOME ; read-buffer directories are bound read-only at their own paths; the failure classes, and the teardown of a cancelled job and its container; the nesting signal under conda, and none in a container. What the image or the conda environment must hold, besides bash in an image: CLI backend of Needs R Rscript ; the R packages RcppCNPy and jsonlite Julia julia ; the Julia packages NPZ and JSON Python python3 ; NumPy when an array crosses; seamless-core when a properly mixed value or a checksum crosses ( The Python CLI backend ) Seamless does not install any of these. Something that is missing is a failure of the transformation. In a container the host's environment variables are not inherited. The image supplies library and package depot paths. The Julia CLI backend uses the tracked Seamless Julia project staged in the job directory, regardless of JULIA_PROJECT ( Handler languages , Environments ).
docs.title: The CLI rule

docs.text: A conda environment together with a Docker image is refused, for every language and both kinds of backend. A script that needs a conda environment inside an image activates it itself.
docs.title: Docker together with conda

docs.text: Two things are checked at dispatch: a conda environment together with a Docker image, and the keys of the image spec ( Environments , The image spec ). Dispatch is the moment at which a transformation that has no recorded result is handed to an execution backend. Setting an environment, and building a Transformation, check nothing. A Transformer that has both a conda environment and an image builds, and so does one whose image spec has an unknown key. A recorded result is returned without the check. A submission that latches on to a running one dispatches nothing, and is not checked either. The executing host validates again before launch. A transformation that is run from its checksum alone, or that arrives by another road, has no other check. seamless-run is covered : --docker together with --conda fails when the command is dispatched, not while its arguments are parsed. Dispatch happens on the submitting side for process , spawn , remote: jobserver and remote: daskserver alike.
docs.title: The check happens at dispatch

docs.text: tf.environment.set_which([...]) lists binaries that must exist. They are looked up where the code runs. Backend Looked up CLI backend, every language in the script, after the conda environment is entered or inside the image. A binary that exists only in the environment satisfies the check, and one that exists only on the host does not in-memory backend on the PATH of the process that runs the code A record probe checks nothing. The look-up is not done on the submitting machine for any language.
docs.title: Required binaries

docs.text: A record probe is a Python in-memory transformation that carries the __env__ of the job whose surroundings it captures ( Execution records ). It runs on the host and is not checked against the environment that it carries: it does not fail for the conda environment or the image, and it does not check which .
docs.title: A record probe is exempt

docs.text: The two rules are carried by two functions of seamless_transformer.languages . They are public: a handler of any language honours its environment through one of them, or fails. from seamless_transformer.languages import ( check_in_memory_environment, execute_cli, ) check_in_memory_environment(environment, language) # raises, or returns None execute_cli(command, pins_, PINS, FILESYSTEM, OUTPUTPIN, environment) check_in_memory_environment(environment, language) applies The in-memory rule and looks the names of which up on the PATH of the process. environment is the transformer's environment as a dict, as the handler receives it ( Handler languages , The arguments ). It may be empty. language is the language name. It is used in the message. It returns None , or raises. The exception class is not specified. It is a function of its arguments and of the process's environment. It needs no running transformation, so it can be called outside one. execute_cli(command, pins_, PINS, FILESYSTEM, OUTPUTPIN, environment) runs a command as a CLI job and applies The CLI rule . Parameter Meaning command the command that starts the interpreter, run by bash in the job directory pins_ the names of the files and directories to write into the job directory PINS a dict from each of those names to its content: a Buffer , bytes, a dict of checksums, or the path of a file that exists on the executing host FILESYSTEM a dict from each name to its entry, as for a pin on file ( Handler languages , The arguments ) OUTPUTPIN the celltype in which the content of RESULT is read environment the transformer's environment, as a dict It returns the content of RESULT . For bytes , folder and deepfolder as OUTPUTPIN the bytes. For any other celltype the file is parsed as an .npy array, then as JSON, then as text, and a content that is none of these is returned as a uint8 array. A RESULT that is a directory gives a dict from each file's path in it to its content, in the same form. It takes the transformation's checksum and its abort test from the running transformation. Inside one, a cancel finds the job and tears it down, and a docker or podman container carries the label seamless.tf=<tf_checksum> . Outside one, the launch works without them. It wraps conda and Docker from environment . A handler cannot wrap one and forget the other. It looks which up in the script. A handler passes environment as it received it. A handler that calls neither function gets no environment handling and no which check from Seamless. Nothing enforces it.
docs.title: The two public functions

docs.text: BACKEND = "cli" makes a Python transformation run as a CLI job: the code runs in a python3 process of its own, in a job directory, on the machinery of bash transformations. Faces. The Python face ( Transformer("python") , direct , delayed ) and the workflow Context ( ctx.tf = function , a bound ctx.tf ). seamless-run has no such setting.
docs.title: The Python CLI backend

docs.text: The code is the same code. The in-memory backend and the CLI backend give it the same names with the same values: The code modes are the same : a block, a function, a lambda and an expression, recognized in the same way. The pins are the same values. The process that runs the transformation parses each pin as the in-memory backend does, and the job gets it back unchanged. Plain data, text, arrays and bytes cross without Seamless in the job. A bytes pin is bytes under both backends ( Pins , A transformer's code receives ). A deep pin has the form of How deep values reach a transformer ( Deep celltypes ) under both backends. The result is what the code returns , or the variable of the output name for block code, serialized under the result celltype as the in-memory backend does it. print and the standard streams are relayed while the code runs, as two streams ( Transformation logs , Streaming ). The code is self-contained, as it always is ( Modules and closures ).
docs.title: What stays the same

docs.text: The code runs in another process , with its own interpreter. Imports, global state and open files are not shared with the process that runs the transformation. Every run starts an interpreter, plus conda run or a container start. The interpreter is python3 on the PATH where the job runs: in the conda environment or the image when there is one, otherwise the PATH of the executing process. It is not the interpreter of the submitting process. The job needs what the code imports. The submitting process's packages do not exist there. A transformation with modules or globals fails when it runs. The message says to use BACKEND="mem" .
docs.title: What differs

docs.text: When The job needs always python3 an array is a pin or a result NumPy a properly mixed value is a pin or a result seamless-core, installed where the code runs a deepcell pin or a checksum pin seamless-core the code itself uses Seamless, for example for nested work Seamless A properly mixed value is a mixed value whose buffer is in the Seamless-mixed format, which is a value that does not reduce to plain data or to an array ( Celltypes and conversion ). A pin or a result of that kind is carried to and from the job through seamless-core. A checksum crossing into the job also needs seamless-core, whether the code only passes its members on or resolves them. A job with none of these runs in an environment that has no Seamless. Nothing checks for seamless-core beforehand ( Every backend rule applies when the transformation runs ). When it is missing, the import fails inside the job, and the failure is the Python error in the standard error trailer.
docs.title: Packages the job needs

docs.text: A returned value is carried as plain data, an array, bytes , a properly mixed value, or, as a member of a deep result, a checksum object. The process that runs the transformation then serializes it under the result celltype, with the calls that the in-memory backend uses. No serialization rule exists twice. There is no fallback encoding. A value that cannot be carried fails the transformation, and it never travels in a different representation. A folder or deepcell result is the dict that the code returns. Each member is a value or a checksum object ( Deep celltypes , The output side ). Nothing that a job wrote is loaded as a pickle. The process that runs the transformation reads a job's result as data only. The host rebuilds each CLI result and uses the in-memory serialization call. For a mixed result and for a value member of a deepcell result, the CLI accepts the same values as the in-memory backend: Returned value In-memory outcome Python CLI outcome None , booleans, integers, finite floats and strings Accepted as mixed values Accepted; carried as JSON, with the same result checksum Non-finite floats Accepted as mixed values using NumPy storage Accepted through .mixed , with the same result checksum Lists, tuples and dicts whose members are supported mixed values Accepted as mixed values Accepted as JSON where possible, otherwise .mixed , with the same result checksum bytes Accepted as a mixed value Accepted through .bytes ; the host serializes it as mixed and gets the same result checksum A NumPy scalar or array with a supported dtype, including an aligned structured array without padding Accepted as a mixed value Accepted through .mixed or .npy ; structured arrays use .mixed to preserve aligned-dtype metadata, with the same result checksum An aligned structured array with implicit padding and a supported structured dtype, directly or nested in a dict, list, or tuple result or deepcell value member Accepted as a mixed value Refused recursively because the NumPy mixed round trip can change padding bytes and the result checksum A structured subarray field whose base dtype has padding Fails; the in-memory mixed serializer does not support this dtype Refused by the recursive padding guard; both backends fail Another value accepted by Buffer(value, "mixed") Accepted as a mixed value Accepted through .mixed , using seamless-core in the job, with the same result checksum A Checksum object as an ordinary result Refused for mixed (and other non-checksum result celltypes) Refused with the same rule A Checksum object as a direct deepcell member A checksum, not a value A checksum entry in the index; the host rebuilds the same checksum object A Checksum nested inside a deepcell value member Part of the value; mixed serialization treats it as its checksum string Part of the .mixed value; host serialization gives the same member checksum A 64-character lowercase hexadecimal string as a deepcell member A value serialized under mixed A value, not a checksum; the same member checksum is produced A set or another value rejected by the in-memory serializer Fails Fails The same direct-member rule applies to a folder result: a Checksum object is a checksum, and any other member is a value. In particular, a checksum-looking string is never promoted to a checksum. A checksum nested inside a deepcell member follows the mixed-value serializer's recursive handling; only a direct Checksum member gets a checksum entry.
docs.title: Results

docs.text: Both Python backends give the same result, bit for bit, when both succeed. A backend may fail where the other succeeds. It may not succeed with a different result. This is what lets the backend stay outside identity. A result type is accepted by the CLI backend only when both backends give it the same result checksum. Every other type fails under the CLI backend. One-sided failures : Case CLI backend In-memory backend modules or globals fails accepted a properly mixed or checksum value, with no seamless-core in the job fails accepted a conda environment other than the process's, or a Docker image runs, in that environment fails a Decimal result with output celltype str fails because the runner cannot encode it accepted; the str celltype serializes str(value) an aligned structured array with implicit padding and a supported structured dtype, directly or nested in a dict, list, or tuple mixed result or deepcell value member refused recursively because the NumPy mixed round trip cannot preserve the padding bytes and checksum accepted as a mixed value Checksum.resolve() in the code, for a member of a deepcell pin works under remote: daskserver only works The guarantee is about the backend, not about the code. Code that depends on the interpreter's state, the working directory, an environment variable or a file outside its pins is not covered, as for any transformation. The text of a failure is not covered : the two backends report the same failure in different words.
docs.title: Parity

docs.text: The run takes the process lock like a bash body , and may run without it ( process_lock false, or a driver) ( Execution backends , The process lock ). A cancel tears the job down as it does for bash , and a container is removed ( Cancellation , A bash run that is cancelled ). A failure is the Bash transformer exception report ( Transformation logs , The failure text ). Its command is the interpreter's, and the Python traceback is in the standard error trailer. An in-memory Python body may run without the process lock , as it always has. The rule that an in-memory body must hold the lock is that of embedded interpreters ( Handler languages , The process lock ), and it does not extend to Python or compiled bodies.
docs.title: The process lock, cancellation and failures

docs.text: A Python CLI job is in the position of a bash job. A driver never takes the lock , under either backend. That is decided before the body starts. Code that is not a driver signals its parent at its first nested submission , as a bash body's seamless-run does, and the parent then gives the lock up ( Execution backends , Bash bodies ). The signal exists without an environment and under conda. It does not cross a container boundary. The job's process is configured from SEAMLESS_REMOTE_CLIENTS , before the code runs, when that variable is set in the job's environment and Seamless can be imported there. Nested work then goes to the same cluster and shares its caches, as a nested seamless-run does. Only the Dask worker exports the variable. Under remote: daskserver nested work therefore goes to the cluster. On the other execution backends nothing is exported, and a nested transformation runs inside the job's own process, with no cache and no dispatch. A nested seamless-run in a bash job fails there, for lack of a configuration, unless SEAMLESS_CACHE or SEAMLESS_REMOTE_CLIENTS is in the environment that the job inherits. Submissions from the job's process skip the permission routine of Dask , driver or not. The mark of a driver is not what decides it ( Execution backends , Drivers ). The code needs Seamless where it runs , and inside a container nested work is not supported.
docs.title: Drivers and nested work

docs.text: Deep celltypes follow the matrix of Deep celltypes , How deep values reach a transformer . Bash has a column of its own, and every other backend, CLI and in-memory alike, follows the other. A folder pin is a dict of contents under every backend but bash , and deepcell and deepfolder pins are dicts of checksum objects. Under a CLI backend a folder travels to the job as a directory that the runtime reads back into a dict. The code does not see that directory. A deepcell or deepfolder pin uses the checksum class of its language : seamless.Checksum in Python, and the checksum class of the language in R and Julia ( Handler languages , Checksum classes ). A deep result is a dict under every backend but bash , and the RESULT directory in bash. Both backends of a language give a deep pin the same form. A compiled transformer refuses a deep pin , as before.
docs.title: Deep pins and results

docs.text: Each of the following is a failure of the transformation, and failures are not cached: an in-memory backend with a Docker image, or with a conda environment that is not its process's; a conda environment together with a Docker image, and an invalid image spec, at dispatch; a required binary that is missing where the code runs; a Python CLI job with modules or globals, with a value that it cannot carry, or without a package that it needs; every failure class of a CLI job ( Environments , Failures ).
docs.title: Failures

docs.text: A third-party handler can ignore environment . The two functions make honouring it easy. Nothing enforces it. A Python CLI job with a deepcell pin or a checksum pin needs seamless-core , also where its code only passes members on. Code in a CLI job can resolve the members of a deepcell pin under remote: daskserver only. No Seamless configuration is exported to a job outside Dask. R and Julia code cannot resolve a checksum at all. A properly mixed value is written by the seamless-core of the process that runs the transformation, and read by the one in the job , and back. Nothing checks that two versions agree on the format. Every Python CLI run starts an interpreter , plus conda run (in the order of a second with conda ) or a container start. A failure under a CLI backend is titled Bash transformer exception , whatever the language. A job holds its process for as long as it runs , unless process_lock is false. In a container, nested Seamless work is not supported. Writing a job directory instead of running it is for bash transformations only.
docs.title: Current limitations

docs.text: A CLI backend for compiled transformers. A setting that lets a Python or compiled pin arrive as a file. Modules and globals under the Python CLI backend. Seamless installing an interpreter, a package or an environment on the executing host or in an image. A public format for what travels between a job and the process that runs the transformation. A handler returns a Python value to Seamless.
docs.title: Non-goals

docs.text: Concern Module / symbol The two public functions seamless_transformer.languages ( check_in_memory_environment , execute_cli ) The CLI job launcher seamless_transformer.execute_bash ( execute_bash ) Dispatch to a backend seamless_transformer.run.run_transformation_dict metavars of Python builders seamless_transformer.transformer_class The check of the specification at dispatch seamless_transformer.transformation_cache
docs.title: Code locations

docs.text: Modules and Closures (Contract) Seamless aims for “code is data”: what executes should be bound by content, not by location. Imported modules (project code) Goal: avoid “whatever version happens to be on that machine”. Preferred patterns: - Embed helper modules/packages into the transformation/module mechanism (content-bound). - Or install immutable artifacts (wheel/image) pinned by version+hash (also content-bound). Anti-pattern: - “Copy your repo/module onto the worker/server” (location-bound, non-auditable drift). System/compiled dependencies For dependencies like NumPy/BLAS/GPU stacks: - treat them as part of the environment envelope - record an environment signature for provenance - if determinism requirements are strict, pin versions/backends and relevant determinism knobs Closures Closures are implicit inputs. Rules: - Do not rely on captured outer-scope values unless you intentionally make them explicit. - Prefer passing configuration as explicit arguments, or injecting small constants via explicit, content-bound mechanisms. - If a closure value changes but is not part of the declared inputs, caching/identity can become incorrect. Dynamic imports and package data If embedding is used: - ensure the required submodules are actually included (dynamic imports can escape embedding-by-inspection) - ensure required non- .py package data is accounted for (if the embedding mechanism doesn’t capture it automatically)
docs.title: Modules and Closures

docs.text: File mounts (Contract) A mount is the attachment whose external resource is a file or a directory. The attachment contract of contracts/attachments.md applies in full — direction, scope, spec versus session, the sense and actuate disciplines, the three-way error model, the detector mechanism, the cut barrier and the lifecycle. This page specializes it for bytes on a filesystem. It does not restate a rule from that page; each section says where the file driver makes a generic rule concrete. Code locations: Concern Module / symbol Public handles seamless_workflow.attachments.api ( MountHandle , ContextMounts , load_graph ) Spec, normalization, celltype admission seamless_workflow.attachments.spec ( AttachmentSpec , validate_celltype ) Initial decision, classification, reassert, detector seamless_workflow.attachments.policy (pure functions) Transport: registry, broker, I/O pool seamless_workflow.attachments.fs.service ( FileSystemService , Registration , FileSystem , get_service , close_service ) Delivered directory leaves as local buffer sources registered by FileSystemService through seamless.caching.buffer_source ( BufferSource , replace_buffer_sources , unregister_buffer_sources ) — seamless-core Optional inotify hints seamless_workflow.attachments.fs.native.NativeNotifications Canonical bytes seamless.checksum.canonical ( canon_T , FILE_CELLTYPES , DIRECTORY_CELLTYPES ) — seamless-core, shared with the CLI file loader Graph entry and validation seamless_workflow.serialization.prepare_graph ; Context.get_graph / set_graph Errors seamless_workflow.attachments.session ( MountError , ConflictError ); seamless_workflow.errors ( AuthorityError , NodeError , PathError , ReentrantContextError , ClosedContextError ) The API ctx.a.mount(path, mode="rw", authority="file", *, persistent=True) # blocking; returns None del ctx.a.mount # unmount ctx.a.mount.spec # the AttachmentSpec, or None ctx.a.mount.status # the status dict, or None ctx.a.mount.error # delivery or conflict error, or None ctx.a.mount.clear_error() report = ctx.mounts.sync(timeout=None) report = await ctx.mounts.synchronization(timeout=None) ctx.mounts.errors # {(node_path, driver): error} ctx.set_graph(graph, mounts=True) mount is a class attribute of Cell — a property with a deleter — so del ctx.a.mount reaches the deleter and never sub-path deletion. It addresses the file slot only; a Jupyter widget attachment is detached through its hub. The cost is that a value key named mount is reachable only as ctx.a["mount"] , as for value or checksum ( contracts/cells.md , API-name arbitration ). mounts is reserved on the Context. ctx.mounts = x raises AttributeError("mounts is reserved for the Context mount API") , and a graph node at path ("mounts",) is refused with PathError("mounts is a reserved Context API name") . The plural is deliberate: it cannot be mistaken for mounting the Context itself. mount() blocks through the initial read and the first delivery attempt, and raises only for an invalid request — never for the state of the file ( contracts/attachments.md , Attach, detach, close ). A widget slot may coexist with this file slot; a second file mount on the same node is refused. path normalization. Anything os.fspath accepts — a str or an os.PathLike — is accepted; an empty path or one containing a NUL raises ValueError("mount path must be a nonempty text path") . The spec stores the path as given , and spec.path is that string. The registry resolves it against the current working directory at attach time (absolute, with symlinks in the parent chain resolved; see The path-overlap registry ). Whether the mount is a file or a directory follows from the celltype , not from a flag or from the path. status ctx.a.mount.status is None when the file slot is unoccupied; otherwise it is a dict whose keys are contract. Widget-slot status is available from its hub: Key Value state "active" , "tripped" (the detector has fired) or "closing" node_checksum the node's checksum hex if the node is complete , else None disk_checksum the believed file checksum: a 64-hex string, or one of the two sentinel strings "ABSENT" and "INVALID" ( attachments.policy.ABSENT / .INVALID ) in_sync node_checksum is not None , and either equals disk_checksum or the two match the latest acknowledged source/canonical-file checksum pair (a null node value with an absent file also counts), and there is no sense error pending a delivery is queued but not dispatched in_flight a delivery has been dispatched and not yet acknowledged sense_error the MountError currently failing the cell, or None error the MountError / ConflictError on the mount, or None sense_error and error are Exception objects , while Cell.exception is a string — the same MountError , rendered with its "<path>: <reason>" prefix ( contracts/attachments.md , Error typing ). Errors The three messages quoted in full below are contract and pinned by tests: "Only whole Context cell nodes can be mounted" , "Cell is already mounted; unmount first" and "Mounted celltype cannot change; unmount first" . NodeError 's "Mounts require an existing whole cell node" is contract as well. Error Raised when ValueError a bad path , mode or authority ; an illegal file-strict combination; a path that overlaps another registration in this process; a cell that is already mounted — ValueError("Cell is already mounted; unmount first") ; retyping a mounted cell, or replacing it with a builder of a different celltype — ValueError("Mounted celltype cannot change; unmount first") TypeError persistent is not a bool ; the celltype is not mountable; deepfolder with a mode other than "r" AttributeError a standalone Cell — AttributeError("mount is only available for bound workflow cells") ; a sub-path projection ( ctx.a.b ) or a read-only handle, including a transformer's result ctx.tf.result — AttributeError("Only whole Context cell nodes can be mounted") ; ctx.mounts = x . Whether a bound as_celltype handle is refused, and with which error, is unspecified (deferred) NodeError the node does not exist, or is not a cell — NodeError("Mounts require an existing whole cell node") . AuthorityError a sensing mount on a node with an incoming edge; an incoming edge into a sensing-mounted node; clearing a mounted cell — AuthorityError("Cannot clear a mounted cell; unmount first") . ctx.a = Cell(celltype=<same>) is not refused : it unmounts and clears ( Unmount, persistence and close ) PathError any invalid mount spec in a graph — unknown fields, a bad mode or authority, an illegal file-strict combination, a non-mountable or sense-only celltype — plus a mount on a non-cell node, an unreadable graph version and a graph connection into a sensing-mounted node. A fault the spec itself would have raised is wrapped as "Invalid mount spec: <original message>" ReentrantContextError mount() , clear_error() , unmounting or the barrier called from the controller thread ClosedContextError any of the same calls after close() ( contracts/attachments.md , Scope ) TimeoutError sync() / synchronization() expiry; the predicate is withdrawn and nothing is cancelled KeyError clear_error() when the file slot is unoccupied. It addresses only the file slot and does not clear a widget session's error. Whether this is contract is deferred : the rest of the unoccupied file-slot surface answers None or is a no-op, so the KeyError reads as an inconsistency rather than a designed refusal. Do not depend on the exception type MountError never raised; it is reported , on the cell as a string or on the mount as an object The general split: an invalid request raises TypeError / ValueError ; the same fault inside a graph raises PathError . Spec validation and normalization mode , authority and persistent live on the generic AttachmentSpec class, but their semantics are file semantics , and they belong here. Field Values Meaning mode "r" , "w" , "rw" which directions are active: sense, actuate, or both authority "file" , "cell" , "file-strict" resolves the initial conflict only. It is not a continuous ownership rule: after the initial decision, every later file change is an authoritative input in a sensing mode, and every later node change is delivered in an actuating one persistent bool whether the file survives unmounting ( Unmount, persistence and close ) Validation, in the order the spec applies it: mode must be one of the three: ValueError("mode must be r, w or rw") . authority must be one of the three: ValueError("invalid mount authority") . persistent must be exactly a bool — a truthy value is not accepted: TypeError("persistent must be bool") . "file-strict" requires a sensing mode and persistent=True : ValueError("file-strict requires sensing and persistent=True") . file-strict means the file is required : a missing path is a sense error rather than a silently absent value, and deleting the file at unmount would contradict the declaration. mode="w" with authority="file" is silently normalized to authority="cell" . A write-only mount never reads, so there is no initial file value for the file to win with. The normalization is visible: spec.authority reads "cell" , and that is what get_graph() serializes. An unmountable celltype raises at attach time and at graph load. The reason is what the two celltypes declare. A write mount materializes every leaf onto disk , which is exactly what deepfolder — "an index; the contents stay by reference" — says it does not do, while folder means "the contents of a directory" ( contracts/deep-celltypes.md ). The restriction costs one retype and nothing else: the two index buffers are byte-identical , and the conversion between them is free in both directions. And a transformer cannot produce a deepfolder at all , so folder is the only celltype a computed directory can arrive in. The two enforcement points follow the request/graph split of Errors : An invalid request to mount() raises TypeError . Because the default mode is rw , the bare ctx.a.mount(path) on a deepfolder cell raises too — deliberately, with a message naming both remedies: text TypeError: Celltype 'deepfolder' can only be sensed: mount with mode='r', or use celltype 'folder' to write An invalid mount spec in a graph raises PathError , wrapping the same text, also with mounts=False ( Graph serialization ): text PathError: Invalid mount spec: Celltype 'deepfolder' can only be sensed: mount with mode='r', or use celltype 'folder' to write validate_celltype(celltype, mode) is the single enforcement point, called from _mount_validate , from load_graph and from prepare_graph . Its mode parameter is required , deliberately, so that no caller can skip the rule. The initial decision table At attach time the controller evaluates one decision against the node's value in that turn and the initial observation. The inputs are the effective mode and authority, the file state, and whether the node has a complete value . F and N are compared as canonical checksums . "No value" means the node has no checksum , which is distinct from a null value. On the file side, an absent path, a zero-byte file and an initially empty directory all additionally report "no value" , which is what makes them unable to override an existing cell value; an explicit null\n file does not, and can. In both tables the rows are ordered, and the first matching row wins — that is how the policy function is written. The node has no complete value: # mode authority file action 1 w any any nothing now; write when the node completes 2 r , rw any rejected sense error 3 r , rw file-strict absent node ← null, and a sense error (the null is stored but masked) 4 r , rw file , cell absent node ← null 5 r , rw any zero-byte / empty directory node ← null 6 r , rw any F node ← F For a file mount in rw , adopting F also schedules a conditional write when the observed bytes are non-canonical. This applies even when an existing node already has the same canonical checksum: checksum equality does not suppress the normalization write. In r , adoption leaves the file bytes alone. The node has a complete value N : # mode authority file action 1 r , rw file-strict absent sense error; N is kept 2 any any absent / zero-byte / empty directory, and N is null nothing 3 w , rw any absent / zero-byte / empty directory write N 4 r any absent / zero-byte / empty directory nothing 5 w ( cell ) F = N nothing 6 w ( cell ) F ≠ N , or rejected write N 7 rw cell F ≠ N , or rejected write N ; logged once 8 r , rw cell otherwise nothing; F becomes the baseline, and later file changes flow in 9 r , rw file , file-strict rejected sense error 10 r , rw file , file-strict F = N nothing 11 r , rw file , file-strict F ≠ N node ← F ; logged once Rejected files. A file may be unreadable, or impossible to canonicalize as the celltype. Where the table would install F into the node, the cell gets a sense error instead: it is failed , its .exception is the MountError 's string, and monitoring stays active. Everywhere else a rejected file counts as a present file that differs from N . Either way the session starts with the belief INVALID . Nothing in this table is a continuous rule. It runs exactly once per session, at attach; every later observation goes through the classification below. Observation classification, and the one belief about the file The session keeps one belief about the file : a checksum (or the sentinel ABSENT / INVALID ) plus a fingerprint. It is comparison-only — never resolved, holding no claim on anything. Echo detection, write skipping and write preconditions all derive from it. Every observation carries a watch sequence ( ws ), owned by the transport and advanced under the registration's lock on every detected change and on every completed write . Class Condition Effect stale ws <= processed_ws discard unchanged the checksum equals the belief (for ABSENT / INVALID , the fingerprint too) update the fingerprint only. Identical-content rewrites and touch end here rejected unreadable, or not canonicalizable as the celltype belief := INVALID ; modes with r : sense error; w : reassert absent the file is missing the node is left unchanged; file-strict : sense error, otherwise any sense error is cleared; w : reassert echo the checksum equals the in-flight delivery's canonical file checksum our own write, seen before its acknowledgement: adopt it as the belief foreign anything else modes with r : sense it; w : reassert A foreign observation in a sensing mode installs the checksum and sets both the belief and the actuation baseline in the same turn — so canonical content is not written straight back; for rw , non-canonical file bytes instead request a conditional canonical write — and clears the sense error. A zero-byte file maps to null; an emptied directory maps to {} . Four rules make this converge: One belief, not a list of what we last wrote. Suppose we deliver C1 ; a foreign writer replaces it with C2 , which is sensed; the writer then reverts to C1 . A last-written list would discard that final C1 as our own echo and leave the node at C2 while the file holds C1 . Against the belief — which is C2 by then — it is correctly classified foreign . Discarding a stale observation loses nothing. It is either a duplicate, or content read before one of our own writes landed, even if it reached ingress after that write's acknowledgement. If the discarded read happened to see a newer foreign change, the broker detects that change again, because its baseline moves only with its own polls and with completed writes — a read never moves it. A write advances the watch sequence. An acknowledgement carries the sequence the write itself produced, so any observation whose content predates the write carries a smaller sequence and is discarded as stale, however late it arrives. Without this, a read taken just before our write could be accepted just after its acknowledgement and revert the node. An unchanged observation can still clear a sense error. If a sense error is set and the observation carries a real checksum — not ABSENT or INVALID — the value is re-installed and the error cleared. This defensive case lets a forced re-poll recover a cell whose file has not changed since. Canonical bytes For each mountable celltype T the mount uses exactly two functions, both defined by the existing serializer and deserializer : write: resolve the node's buffer and canonicalize it with canon_T before writing (compressed, if the path carries a compression suffix). The node checksum is preserved; the delivered file checksum is the checksum of the canonical bytes. Without a hashserver, a node buffer that was missing from the buffer cache was fingertipped before the node took the checksum ( contracts/workflow-context.md , A Context without a hashserver ); read: canon_T(bytes) = serialize(deserialize(bytes, T), T) , and the observed checksum is the checksum of canon_T(bytes) . If deserialization raises, the observation is rejected . For the code celltypes ( text , python , ipython , yaml ), deserialize here is the strict UTF-8 decode only: canon_T does not run the syntax check of the reference parser, exactly as the serializer an assignment uses does not ( contracts/celltypes-and-conversion.md , the serializer table). Four consequences: a file written by the mount reads back as an exact echo of the canonical delivery , without changing the node checksum. The acknowledgement records the source checksum and canonical file checksum as a synchronized pair. node_checksum and disk_checksum may therefore differ while in_sync=True . The filesystem transport sends this acknowledgement under its I/O lock before any readback observation can be sent, so that readback compares against the canonical file belief. A later foreign observation is compared against the current file belief, not a history of deliveries; a user-formatted file maps to the checksum of its value , so reformatting JSON by hand is not a change; there is no mount-local parsing. A mount parses neither more leniently nor more strictly than a user assignment of the same value: it checks exactly what an assignment checks. For the code celltypes that excludes syntax. ctx.a.set("def (:\n") is accepted as complete , and so is a mounted file with that content; neither is a sense error. The syntax error surfaces downstream: a transformer that runs the code fails with the SyntaxError as its own failure, and a .value read raises HashTypeValidationError on every read without failing the cell ( contracts/cells.md , .buffer and .value ). Fixing the file is an ordinary change, sensed like any other. rw canonicalizes non-canonical file bytes after sensing , including initial adoption by an empty cell and formatting-only edits. The canonical checksum installed in the cell then equals the checksum of the decompressed file bytes. This write uses the ordinary fingerprint conflict guard; r mounts leave the file untouched. canon_T is idempotent, and that is property-tested. T is always the cell's output celltype , including for a connected cell; the producer's input type is stored separately ( contracts/cells.md ). Retyping while mounted is refused ( Errors ). For example, an empty Cell("plain") mounted with mode="rw" on a file containing {"a":1} adopts {"a": 1} and rewrites the file using canonical plain serialization. After a successful ctx.mounts.sync() , the cell checksum equals seamless-checksum mounted-file.json ; canonicalizing only the cell buffer while leaving the original JSON bytes on disk does not satisfy this rule. Later formatting-only edits are rewritten canonically as well, without changing the cell checksum. With mode="r" , the original file bytes remain. For compressed files, the equality is over the decompressed bytes. Null files A missing path is absent , never null. At mount time it cannot override an existing value; under file-strict it is a sense error. A zero-byte file and b"null\n" both read as null , before celltype-specific parsing. They differ at mount time only: the zero-byte file reports "no value" and cannot override, the explicit null\n can. A newline-only file is not special and undergoes normal parsing. A null delivery truncates an existing file to zero bytes — also for compressed paths, where it writes zero bytes and not a compressed empty stream — and never creates a missing file : a null delivery whose belief is ABSENT is suppressed at dispatch. A null value with an absent file therefore counts as in sync . bytes null reads as b"" . bytes is the one celltype where empty is null, in both directions ( contracts/cells.md ). Directories do not converge on null; see Null on a directory mount is terminal . Compression A .gz or .zst suffix means: decompress before canon_T on read, and compress the canonical bytes on write — deterministically (gzip with mtime=0 at level 6; zstd at level 3). The canonical checksum is always taken over the decompressed bytes , as everywhere else in Seamless ( contracts/compression.md ). Compressed bytes are not stable across compressor versions and settings, so a foreign recompression of identical content classifies as unchanged ( Limits : the checksum is the correctness guard). Fingerprints, polling and the racy window Fingerprint: existence plus (st_dev, st_ino, st_size, st_mtime_ns, st_ctime_ns) . The inode makes atomic replacement visible even when size and mtime match. The ctime makes permission and ownership changes visible, so a file that was unreadable is read again once it is fixed. A directory's fingerprint is the root stat plus the sorted (relative path, stat) list of every non-temporary leaf. One broker thread polls every registration's stat at the poll interval. Racy files. A file whose mtime is within the racy window of the present moment — for a directory, any leaf's mtime — is re-read at the next poll even when its fingerprint is unchanged , until it ages out. Otherwise a same-size rewrite within one mtime tick would be invisible. This is the fix git applies to "racily clean" index entries. Stable read: stat, read, stat; retried with bounded backoff if the two fingerprints differ, and rejected as OSError("File changed throughout stable read") after five attempts. An editor that saves by atomic rename never exposes a half-written file; one that truncates and rewrites in place may, briefly, and that shows as a short-lived sense error. Shared reads. Equal r -only registrations of the same path and celltype share one poll and one read; each session gets its own claim on the resulting buffer. Native hints are optional and advisory.
