docs.text: Making a Seamless web server (Guide) This page is a guide , not a contract. It tells you how to build a web application whose server side is a workflow Context: how to think about it, how to develop it with hot reloading on both sides, and how to deploy it. The normative behaviour lives in contracts/shares.md , contracts/mounts.md and contracts/workflow-context.md ; this page links to them instead of restating them. A few parts describe tools that do not exist yet: the pack tool and Cloudless in the deployment tactics. They are marked (not yet implemented) where they occur and collected under Implementation status . The idea: shared cells are the REST API A Seamless web server is a workflow Context plus shares . There is no route table, no request handler and no serializer to write. A shared cell is the whole REST API you need, and the reactive workflow does the work behind it. You need You write The browser sees Show a value ctx.x.share() GET /<ns>/x , pushed again on every change over the websocket Take input ctx.x.share(readonly=False) PUT /<ns>/x , optionally conditional with ?marker=n Serve a computed result ctx.out = ctx.tf.result; ctx.out.share() GET /<ns>/out ; the workflow recomputes it when its inputs change Serve a page or an asset a text or bytes cell, share(path="index.html") GET with the right content type Describe the API nothing /openapi.json , /<ns>/state-graph Receive live updates nothing the websocket at /<ns> , wrapped by /seamless-client.js What happens on a request: A PUT is a write to the cell. Its dependents recompute under the reactive Context, and a result that reaches a share is announced to every websocket client. A GET resolves stored bytes and never computes. The request handlers run on the server's own thread and run no user code. All logic lives in the graph : transformers between cells. The serving script builds the graph and shares some of its cells; it does not respond to requests. Design rules One cell per quantity the page shows or edits. The share key defaults to the node path ( ctx.sub.a is served at /<ns>/sub/a ). Inputs are writable shares, outputs are read-only shares of connected cells. A writable share is the node's producer, so it cannot have an incoming edge. To serve a computed value, connect it into a cell and share that cell read-only. A user action is a write. For request and response, use a writable input cell and a read-only result cell, connected by a transformer. Pick the celltype by what the page reads. plain serves JSON, text serves raw text, bytes serves a file as it is. A str cell serves a quoted JSON string. Shareable celltypes are listed in contracts/shares.md . Everything in a namespace is shared by every visitor. There is no authentication and no sessions. For isolation between users, give each user their own Context and namespace. A minimal server Adapted from seamless-workflow/examples/share-sliders/serve.py (install seamless-workflow[share] ): import os from pathlib import Path import seamless from seamless import Cell from seamless_workflow import Context, shareserver def build(ctx, page_path=None): """Populate ctx with the application's cells, transformers and shares.""" def add(a, b): return a + b ctx.a = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.a.set(10) ctx.b = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.b.set(20) ctx.add = add ctx.add.pins.a = ctx.a ctx.add.pins.b = ctx.b ctx.c = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.c = ctx.add.result ctx.a.share(readonly=False) # inputs: PUT allowed ctx.b.share(readonly=False) ctx.c.share() # output: read-only if page_path is not None: # a hand-written page; a built front end is packed instead ctx.page = Cell(celltype="text") ctx.page.mount(page_path, mode="r") ctx.page.share(path="index.html", toplevel=True) def start(page_path=Path(__file__).with_name("index.html")): """Configure the server once per process, then build a fresh live Context.""" if shareserver.url is None: # configure() after the server started raises host = os.environ.get("SEAMLESS_SHARE_HOST", "127.0.0.1") port = int(os.environ.get("SEAMLESS_SHARE_PORT", shareserver.port)) shareserver.configure(host=host, port=port) ctx = Context() ctx.shares.namespace = "app" # runtime state; set before the first share try: build(ctx, page_path) except Exception: ctx.close() raise return ctx build(ctx) is the part that is independent of how the server is run; the pack tool of Deployment calls the same function. The page is a plain file. seamless-client.js is served by the share server itself: <script src="/seamless-client.js"></script> <script> const app = connect_seamless(null, null, "app"); // same origin, namespace "app" const slider = document.getElementById("a"), sum = document.getElementById("c"); app.self.onsharelist = keys => { // keys of the shares that exist now app.c.onchange = () => { sum.value = app.c.value; }; slider.oninput = () => app.a.set(slider.value); // PUT }; </script> value is text (a Blob for binary shares). JSON is not parsed for you. Handlers are attached in onsharelist , because entries appear and disappear with the shares of the namespace. The server is one per process : REST and websocket on one port, started by the first share, stopped by seamless.close() . It defaults to 0.0.0.0:5813 , with no authentication and no TLS. Bind to 127.0.0.1 for development ( SEAMLESS_SHARE_HOST , SEAMLESS_SHARE_PORT , shareserver.configure ). Returning to a previous input Suppose an input goes X → Y → X. When the shared result moves on to Y, the cell and the share release their claims on X's result. Without a hashserver, that buffer is then kept only by a tempref, and it is evicted once the tempref expires. Back at X, the transformer hits its cache: the result checksum for X is known, but its bytes are gone. Without a hashserver, the Context fixes this for you. A cell with a share, a w file mount or a widget, or a cell that an archive download lists, does not take a checksum whose buffer is not in memory. The cell stays waiting while the Context fingertips the buffer: it reads it back from a local buffer source, or else recomputes it in this process. Meanwhile, the share keeps serving the Y result under its marker, the websocket sends nothing, the mounted file is not written, and ctx.c.checksum is None . Then the X result is served and announced as one ordinary update. For a folder cell, a missing leaf counts too: the Context runs the folder's producer again to regenerate it, even when the folder's index is still in memory. Every transformer the Context runs also fingertips missing inputs, so the cells downstream of a cell that has no share recover too. A Context without a hashserver What this means for an application: Returning to X may recompute the evicted part when no local buffer source holds it. The producers must therefore be reproducible. The page may see a delay , not an error. The cell's waiting state is in /<ns>/state-graph , so a page can show progress while it waits. A GET still never computes. It answers 503 only if the fingertip failed, for example because the producer is not reproducible. A download requested while a listed cell is waiting answers 409 . Only a change of the cell's checksum is covered. Sharing a cell that is already complete, but whose buffer has expired, triggers no fingertip, so that share answers 503 . Share the cell before its value matters, as build(ctx) does, or call ctx.c.fingertip() from the session. With a hashserver, non-scratch results are published , stay resolvable, and nothing needs fingertipping. A read-only hashserver publishes nothing; use a writable one for an application that computes. Buffer storage Direct shares accept a fixed set of celltypes that excludes folder , deepfolder and deepcell . To serve directory contents, share derived plain or bytes cells, or include a folder cell in a separate archive download. Archive downloads also resolve existing buffers, and never compute. Without a hashserver, nothing keeps a downloaded folder's leaf files: they are regenerated when the folder's value changes, but once they are evicted, the download answers 503 . To keep a folder downloadable, mount it with ctx.f.mount(path, mode="w") ; the written files then supply its leaves. Seamless does not add that mount for you. Shareable celltypes · Downloads Development Two processes Put the front end's dev server (Vite or similar) in front, and the Seamless process behind it. The dev server compiles and hot-reloads the front end. It proxies the share namespace and the client script to the Seamless process. The Seamless process holds the Context and the share server. A share server only serves stored bytes and cannot proxy or hot-reload a front end. Same origin in development and production. The proxy means the front end code is identical in both. CORS is open, so connect_seamless(5813) would also work, but it builds the port into the code. Start the two in separate terminals. The backend runs interactively, so the Context stays inspectable and editable: # terminal 1: backend conda activate <env> python -i backend.py # terminal 2: front end conda activate <env> npm run dev vite.config.ts export default defineConfig({ base: './', plugins: [/* the framework plugin */], server: { proxy: { '/app': { target: 'http://127.0.0.1:5813', ws: true }, // REST and websocket '/seamless-client.js': 'http://127.0.0.1:5813', '/openapi.json': 'http://127.0.0.1:5813', }}, }) ws: true is needed on the namespace entry , because the websocket is GET /<ns> with an upgrade. Choose a namespace name that no front end route starts with. Vite matches proxy keys by prefix. Load the client with a plain <script src="/seamless-client.js"> tag and call connect_seamless(null, null, "<ns>") once, from its own small module that turns shared cells into the framework's reactive state. Hot-swapping a component re-evaluates its module; keeping the connection in its own module prevents a second websocket. State kept in writable shared cells survives full page reloads and is visible to Python. Keep the front end's durable state there. A no-build page can instead be a text cell mounted with mode="r" (as in the example). An edit is served within the mount's polling interval, but the browser is not told and must be reloaded by hand. Do not compile inside the Context. A build step run as a transformer puts the sources and node_modules into the cache key and pays a full build per save. Compile offline; let the graph record only the result. Three ways to change the Seamless side The front end hot-reloads by itself. The Seamless side has three mechanisms, which differ in what they cost and what state they keep. 1. Live edit 2. %run -i reload 3. Restart What you do change cells and the graph in the live session re-run the script in IPython stop and start the process Context the same object closed, a new one built a new process Share server untouched untouched restarted State written from a browser kept reset to the script's defaults, unless mounted reset, unless mounted Front end shares message on the websocket no disconnect; only changed values are announced disconnect, then reconnect Requires the script kept in step a script that is safe to re-run mounted state; a hardened client 1. Live edit in the interactive session Zero restart. Assign cells, transformers and connections in the running session, by hand or by a coding agent attached to it; the workflow recomputes and the browser follows. The script is the source of truth; the live session is a preview. Every live change must also be made in backend.py , or the next reload or restart reverts it. Adding or removing a share is announced to the front end as a new shares message on the websocket, which calls onsharelist . Attach handlers for new keys there. /openapi.json is generated per request and is always current. There is no push for it. A front end that keeps a copy (generated types, a key list) re-fetches it after the cell list changes; the websocket shares message is the trigger. 2. %run -i : reload the script, keep the server The script is re-run in IPython's interactive namespace. This is the equivalent of a hot reload. The workflow Context is replaced (the ctx variable is re-defined); the share server is not , because it exists independently of Contexts. Write the script so that it is safe to re-run: # backend.py: run with `python -i backend.py`, reload with `%run -i backend.py` try: ctx.close() # the previous run's Context; frees its namespace except NameError: pass # first run ctx = start() Close the old Context first. A second live Context claiming a taken namespace raises ValueError("Share namespace '<name>' is in use") . Guard shareserver.configure with if shareserver.url is None , as start() above does. configure() after the server started raises RuntimeError . Do not call seamless.close() in a reloadable script. It stops the share server. Keep it for a non-interactive main() that runs once and exits. A reload resets state that browsers wrote. The new Context starts from the script's defaults. Mount the cells that must survive (mechanism 3). Markers keep increasing across the reload. A re-shared URL continues its marker sequence for the lifetime of the server. The hold on close keeps the reload invisible in the browser for values that did not change ( contracts/shares.md , The hold on close ): ctx.close() does not remove the shares at once. The server keeps serving them, with their checksums and markers, for a hold window (10 s by default), and keeps the websockets open. The Context's teardown is not visible, and /openapi.json does not drop to an empty document. The new Context's first share takes the namespace over, and each share at a held URL re-attaches . A cell whose value is unchanged produces no marker bump and therefore no websocket update. A cell whose value differs produces one ordinary update. A PUT sent during the reload waits for its share to be re-attached, and is then processed by the new Context. A held share that the new script no longer makes is removed when the window ends, as on any close. The hold serves; it never carries a value into the new Context. State that a browser wrote into an unmounted cell still returns to the script's default. 3. Mounts with authority="file" : persistent state A mounted cell keeps its value in a file. That makes state survive a %run -i reload and a full restart of the Seamless process , a "tepid reload". ctx.params = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.params.set({"threshold": 0.5}) # the default; set it before mounting ctx.params.mount("state/params.json", mode="rw", authority="file") ctx.params.share(readonly=False) First run : the file is absent, so the default is written to it. Every later run : the file wins over the script's default ( contracts/mounts.md , The initial decision table , row 11, logged once). Every accepted PUT is written to the file , and an edit of the file is served and announced. authority resolves only the initial conflict. After attach, every file change and every cell change flows as usual. Mount only state worth keeping. Do not mount derived cells; they are recomputed. Keep the state directory out of version control. persistent=True is the default ; the file survives unmount and Context close. Hardening the front end for restarts A restarted process restarts its markers. The front end must cope with a server that vanishes and comes back. Reconnect automatically. seamless-client.js retries a lost websocket with backoff (1 s, doubling, up to 30 s). Every connection starts with a shares message that carries the checksum and marker of every share in the namespace. The client's restart rule ( contracts/shares.md , seamless-client.js ): if, after reconnecting, the markers are lower than the ones the front end already holds, the server process restarted. One key that is exactly one lower, because the server has not yet processed the client's own PUT to it, does not count. Mounted cells were restored from their files, so the front end's own state is current: the client adopts the new markers and does not re-read the values. If that was wrong (unmounted state was reset), the user reloads the page by hand. A write sent after a restart, before the client has adopted the new markers, carries the old marker. It is normally refused with 409 , and the client drops the local change. Until the reconnect lets the client conclude that the server restarted, it ignores the server's lower marker, so the page keeps showing the dropped change until the reconnect; the client then reads that value. Show a disconnected state instead of letting the user edit as if connected. Deployment Development needs Node, a dev server and a live interactive Context. Deployment needs none of them: a built, static front end, and a Context that serves it. There are two levels. Level 1: the serving script For a front end that is one hand-written file, the development script is already the deployment , as in examples/share-sliders : a text cell mounted with mode="r" and shared at the top level, plus the data cells. Run python serve.py , bind explicitly, and put a reverse proxy in front. A built application (many hashed files) runs into five limits of this level: One cell per file. Folder cells cannot be shared. Top-level share keys have one segment. /assets/x.js cannot be a top-level share; inside a namespace a key may have several segments. Hashed names change on every build , so the set of mounted shares changes. The browser client never reports changes of file-like shares. Keys with a . are not auto-read. The redirect from / and /<ns>/ to index.html drops the query string. Level 2 absorbs the first limit in the pack tool, and removes the other four: files are shared under a namespace at their relative paths, every build is a new graph so changing names cost nothing, a running graph's files never change, and the proxy can redirect / with the query string kept. Level 2: pack the build into a graph Compile offline, pack dist/ into a Context with one bytes cell per file, each shared at its path, and save the graph. The graph holds only checksums; the bytes live on a hashserver. A generic server loads the graph and serves it. The server needs no Node and no application code. src/ --npm run build--> dist/ --pack--> Context (one bytes cell per file + backend nodes) | get_graph() | publish v v graph.json (checksums) hashserver --rsync--> deploy hashserver | | +-----> generic server: set_graph(mounts=False, shares=True) --resolves--+ 1. Build with a relative base Set base: './' in the Vite config and run the production build: npm ci # reproducible install; pin the Node version npm run build # vite build -> dist/ base: './' makes the page load its assets relative to wherever index.html is served, so the same build works under any namespace. Keep Vite's content hashes in deployment builds. Each build produces a new graph, so changing names cost nothing, and the proxy can mark assets immutable. Files loaded at run time (workers, .wasm , fonts) must be in dist/ too, with pinned content types. 2. Pack The pack tool is generic: it walks dist/ , makes a cell per file, shares it at its relative path and writes the graph. If the application has a backend, call its build(ctx) first (without a page_path ), so static files and backend nodes end up in one graph. import json, mimetypes from pathlib import Path import seamless, seamless.config from seamless import Cell from seamless_workflow import Context, shareserver NULL_CONTENTS = (b"", b"null\n", b"null") # these are null: the share would answer 204 def node_name(rel): # "assets/index-DD5wxIS0.js" -> "web__assets__index_DD5wxIS0_js" return "web__" + "".join(c if c.isalnum() else "_" for c in rel.replace("/", "__")) def pack(dist, graph_out, backend=None): seamless.config.init() # build stage: a writable hashserver shareserver.configure(host="127.0.0.1", port=0) # share() records specs; nothing is exposed ctx = Context() try: if backend is not None: backend(ctx) # the application's own nodes names = set() for f in sorted(Path(dist).rglob("*")): if not f.is_file(): continue rel = f.relative_to(dist).as_posix() data = f.read_bytes() if data in NULL_CONTENTS: raise ValueError(f"{rel}: content would be served as null (204)") name = node_name(rel) if name in names: raise ValueError(f"{rel}: node name collision") names.add(name) mimetype = mimetypes.guess_type(rel)[0] or "application/octet-stream" setattr(ctx, name, Cell(celltype="bytes")) cell = getattr(ctx, name) cell.set(data) cell.share(path=rel, mimetype=mimetype) # pinned into the graph's share entry graph = ctx.get_graph() finally: ctx.close() seamless.close() # flushes pending hashserver writes Path(graph_out).write_text(json.dumps(graph, indent=1, sort_keys=True)) What the pack tool must get right: Run it as its own process. seamless.close() ends Seamless for the whole process: no Context can be built afterwards, and neither can a second pack or a serve . The same holds for the serving process below. Celltype bytes for every file. It is the one celltype whose buffer is the file as it is, so the served body is the built file byte for byte. Pin the content type at pack time. Without a mimetype , the server guesses from the extension on the serving host, and a browser refuses a module script that is not served with a JavaScript type. The pinned value is stored in the graph's share entry. Refuse null contents. An empty file, or one that is exactly null , is the null value, and a share answers 204 with no body. Generated node names. The share path carries the real file name; the node name is only an identifier. Publishing is automatic : a non-scratch cell publishes its literal to the hashserver when the Context claims it. seamless.close() reports buffers it could not write; treat that as a failed build. Verify before shipping. Batch-check every checksum in the graph against the hashserver's GET /has-now , which, unlike /has , does not count buffers that are only promised. 3. Hashserver Build side Deploy side Mode writable read-only when the graph has no writable shares and no transformers; writable once PUT values or computed results must survive Contents every buffer the Context published a copy: the buffer directory is plain files named by checksum, so rsync transfers only what is new Reachability build machine or CI only the serving process only; never public Unchanged files are never uploaded or transferred again. 4. Serve The shipped command loads one saved graph and serves its declared shares. Install seamless-suite for the seamless-serve-graph entry point and its HTTP dependency. The implementation is seamless_workflow.serve_graph:main ; python -m seamless_workflow.serve_graph is equivalent. seamless-serve-graph graph.json The share contract defines the command's behavior. Give it a local UTF-8 JSON file containing a current workflow graph. A graph with shares uses __seamless_workflow__: "0.6" or later, and a graph with downloads "0.7" ; older current workflow versions cannot declare them. Original legacy exports need migration before this command can load them. The runner creates one Context in the default ctx namespace and calls ctx.set_graph(graph, mounts=False, shares=True) . Graph-declared file mounts are disabled; shares are restored. A graph can also contain transformers, which begin deriving when loaded. Open /ctx/index.html for a page shared there. A share declared toplevel=True can be served from /index.html . The share server uses its normal bind configuration, currently 0.0.0.0:5813 by default. Configure the listener in Python with seamless_workflow.shareserver.configure() if you need a different address or port in a custom serving script. The command has no listener flags. Its HTTP and websocket endpoints use the current share protocol and built-in /seamless-client.js . Put the desired cluster and execution mode in the usual seamless-config files for the directory from which you launch the command. The runner initializes that configuration before creating the Context, so a configured hashserver, database, jobserver or daskserver is used through the normal modern stack. See Setting up a local cluster and Remote execution . The command has no remote-service flags. The runner does not query /has-now for every referenced buffer. Check availability as a separate deployment step if a later browser 503 is unacceptable. SIGINT or SIGTERM closes the Context and Seamless. There is no dedicated health endpoint; GET /openapi.json shows the HTTP server is responding, while GET /ctx/state-graph reports node states. 5. Reverse proxy The share server has no compression, no TLS and no long-lived caching. A reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) supplies them: Compression and TLS termination. Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable on /<ns>/assets/* . This is safe only because the deployment build keeps content hashes. Every share response otherwise carries Cache-Control: no-cache with the checksum as ETag , so every page load revalidates every file. Redirect / straight to /<ns>/index.html , keeping the query string, instead of relying on the server's own 302 , which drops it. Access control , and the exposure rules below. Exposure, state and releases Every share is readable by anyone who reaches the port , and every writable share is writable by them. Bind to loopback and let the proxy do access control. /<ns>/state-graph and /openapi.json are always served. The state graph carries every node's path, celltype, state, checksum and error text, also for nodes that are not shared. Block the state-graph path at the proxy if it must not be public. Loading a graph opens endpoints and can run transformer code. Deploy a graph file you built and verified. If an application must inspect a graph of unknown origin, load it through the Python API with shares=False and mounts=False . One Context means one shared state. For a tool where each user has their own state, load the static graph once at a fixed namespace, and give each session its own backend Context at its own namespace, built from a template graph. The page reads the session id from its URL and calls connect_seamless(null, null, "s-" + id) . Sessions share the static buffers, because the checksums are the same. The share server has no custom routes, so creating sessions needs a small control listener, with idle expiry (not yet implemented) . Keep a versioned graph file for each release. The serving command reads a local JSON file; deploy that file and its referenced buffers together. Rolling back means launching a previous graph file whose buffers are still available. The compile step is outside Seamless identity. The graph records what was built, not how. Record the "how" in a cell (git commit, lockfile checksum, exact Node version) and share it read-only, so the page can show it. Taking it further: serve a workflow as data The destination of level 2 is that the static front end and the Python backend ship as one kind of artifact : a saved workflow graph, with backend nodes recomputed or cache-hit on the server's execution backend. The generic seamless-serve-graph command serves a local graph file now; Cloudless for per-session instances remains unimplemented. Build the application so that its server side is a build(ctx) function: that is the part that moves into the graph unchanged. Checklist Model each shown or edited quantity as a cell; inputs are writable shares, outputs are read-only shares of connected cells. Keep all logic in the graph. Add no request code. Develop with the dev server in front, python -i backend.py behind, a namespace of its own, and /seamless-client.js and /openapi.json proxied. Keep the script in step with every live edit; keep it safe to re-run with %run -i (close the old Context, guard configure , no seamless.close() ). Mount, with authority="file" , the state that must survive reloads. Harden the client: reconnect, tolerate a restarted server, never assume a write succeeded. Deploy with relative base, pinned content types, hashed names, a hashserver copy, a startup check and a reverse proxy. Implementation status Exercised against the code: bytes cells shared at multi-segment paths with a pinned mimetype ; the share entry in get_graph() and the absence of a mount entry for unmounted cells; set_graph(graph, mounts=False, shares=True) into a fresh Context under the same namespace, with markers continuing; the ValueError for a namespace that a live Context holds; the share server staying up after ctx.close() ; authority="file" persistence of a PUT across two Contexts; the build / start example and its %run -i header (a PUT to a recomputes c ; the old Context is closed, the namespace is re-claimed and the defaults return); and the pack and serve sketches, run in a single process over the local buffer cache. That run showed the graph holding only value.checksum per cell node, pinned content types, no mount entries, bodies equal to the files, and GET /<ns>/ answering the index.html share. The graph-serving command is implemented. Its focused tests cover the required graph-file argument, JSON loading into a Context, a real Context's serialized-graph path, configuration initialization, cleanup after loading fails, and signal handler restoration. The command uses current workflow serialization and the modern share protocol. Not implemented, and described above as the intended behaviour: The pack tool as a shipped command (the code above is a sketch) and Cloudless . Not verified: The hold on close and the client's restart rule ( contracts/shares.md ) in the reload and restart workflows above. The hashserver round trip: pack and serve as separate processes, with the buffers transferred through a hashserver, and the startup check against /has-now . Whether a Context with a read-only hashserver tries to publish the literals it fetches. Declare the hashserver read-only in the deployment configuration and look for write attempts in its log. Behaviour of Cell.set() for a single value of several MB. The contract states a 1 GiB request limit for PUT.

A few parts describe tools that do not exist yet: the pack tool and Cloudless in the deployment tactics. They are marked (not yet implemented) where they occur and collected under Implementation status .

To serve a computed value, connect it into a cell and share that cell read-only. A user action is a write. For request and response, use a writable input cell and a read-only result cell, connected by a transformer. Pick the celltype by what the page reads. plain serves JSON, text serves raw text, bytes serves a file as it is. A str cell serves a quoted JSON string. Shareable celltypes are listed in contracts/shares.md . Everything in a namespace is shared by every visitor. There is no authentication and no sessions. For isolation between users, give each user their own Context and namespace.
docs.title: Design rules

docs.text: Adapted from seamless-workflow/examples/share-sliders/serve.py (install seamless-workflow[share] ): import os from pathlib import Path import seamless from seamless import Cell from seamless_workflow import Context, shareserver def build(ctx, page_path=None): """Populate ctx with the application's cells, transformers and shares.""" def add(a, b): return a + b ctx.a = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.a.set(10) ctx.b = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.b.set(20) ctx.add = add ctx.add.pins.a = ctx.a ctx.add.pins.b = ctx.b ctx.c = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.c = ctx.add.result ctx.a.share(readonly=False) # inputs: PUT allowed ctx.b.share(readonly=False) ctx.c.share() # output: read-only if page_path is not None: # a hand-written page; a built front end is packed instead ctx.page = Cell(celltype="text") ctx.page.mount(page_path, mode="r") ctx.page.share(path="index.html", toplevel=True) def start(page_path=Path(__file__).with_name("index.html")): """Configure the server once per process, then build a fresh live Context.""" if shareserver.url is None: # configure() after the server started raises host = os.environ.get("SEAMLESS_SHARE_HOST", "127.0.0.1") port = int(os.environ.get("SEAMLESS_SHARE_PORT", shareserver.port)) shareserver.configure(host=host, port=port) ctx = Context() ctx.shares.namespace = "app" # runtime state; set before the first share try: build(ctx, page_path) except Exception: ctx.close() raise return ctx build(ctx) is the part that is independent of how the server is run; the pack tool of Deployment calls the same function. The page is a plain file. seamless-client.js is served by the share server itself: <script src="/seamless-client.js"></script> <script> const app = connect_seamless(null, null, "app"); // same origin, namespace "app" const slider = document.getElementById("a"), sum = document.getElementById("c"); app.self.onsharelist = keys => { // keys of the shares that exist now app.c.onchange = () => { sum.value = app.c.value; }; slider.oninput = () => app.a.set(slider.value); // PUT }; </script> value is text (a Blob for binary shares). JSON is not parsed for you. Handlers are attached in onsharelist , because entries appear and disappear with the shares of the namespace. The server is one per process : REST and websocket on one port, started by the first share, stopped by seamless.close() . It defaults to 0.0.0.0:5813 , with no authentication and no TLS. Bind to 127.0.0.1 for development ( SEAMLESS_SHARE_HOST , SEAMLESS_SHARE_PORT , shareserver.configure ).
docs.title: A minimal server

docs.text: Suppose an input goes X → Y → X. When the shared result moves on to Y, the cell and the share release their claims on X's result. Without a hashserver, that buffer is then kept only by a tempref, and it is evicted once the tempref expires. Back at X, the transformer hits its cache: the result checksum for X is known, but its bytes are gone. Without a hashserver, the Context fixes this for you. A cell with a share, a w file mount or a widget, or a cell that an archive download lists, does not take a checksum whose buffer is not in memory. The cell stays waiting while the Context fingertips the buffer: it reads it back from a local buffer source, or else recomputes it in this process. Meanwhile, the share keeps serving the Y result under its marker, the websocket sends nothing, the mounted file is not written, and ctx.c.checksum is None . Then the X result is served and announced as one ordinary update. For a folder cell, a missing leaf counts too: the Context runs the folder's producer again to regenerate it, even when the folder's index is still in memory. Every transformer the Context runs also fingertips missing inputs, so the cells downstream of a cell that has no share recover too. A Context without a hashserver What this means for an application: Returning to X may recompute the evicted part when no local buffer source holds it. The producers must therefore be reproducible. The page may see a delay , not an error. The cell's waiting state is in /<ns>/state-graph , so a page can show progress while it waits. A GET still never computes. It answers 503 only if the fingertip failed, for example because the producer is not reproducible. A download requested while a listed cell is waiting answers 409 . Only a change of the cell's checksum is covered. Sharing a cell that is already complete, but whose buffer has expired, triggers no fingertip, so that share answers 503 . Share the cell before its value matters, as build(ctx) does, or call ctx.c.fingertip() from the session. With a hashserver, non-scratch results are published , stay resolvable, and nothing needs fingertipping. A read-only hashserver publishes nothing; use a writable one for an application that computes. Buffer storage Direct shares accept a fixed set of celltypes that excludes folder , deepfolder and deepcell . To serve directory contents, share derived plain or bytes cells, or include a folder cell in a separate archive download. Archive downloads also resolve existing buffers, and never compute. Without a hashserver, nothing keeps a downloaded folder's leaf files: they are regenerated when the folder's value changes, but once they are evicted, the download answers 503 . To keep a folder downloadable, mount it with ctx.f.mount(path, mode="w") ; the written files then supply its leaves. Seamless does not add that mount for you. Shareable celltypes · Downloads
docs.title: Returning to a previous input

docs.text: Put the front end's dev server (Vite or similar) in front, and the Seamless process behind it. The dev server compiles and hot-reloads the front end. It proxies the share namespace and the client script to the Seamless process. The Seamless process holds the Context and the share server. A share server only serves stored bytes and cannot proxy or hot-reload a front end. Same origin in development and production. The proxy means the front end code is identical in both. CORS is open, so connect_seamless(5813) would also work, but it builds the port into the code. Start the two in separate terminals. The backend runs interactively, so the Context stays inspectable and editable: # terminal 1: backend conda activate <env> python -i backend.py # terminal 2: front end conda activate <env> npm run dev vite.config.ts export default defineConfig({ base: './', plugins: [/* the framework plugin */], server: { proxy: { '/app': { target: 'http://127.0.0.1:5813', ws: true }, // REST and websocket '/seamless-client.js': 'http://127.0.0.1:5813', '/openapi.json': 'http://127.0.0.1:5813', }}, }) ws: true is needed on the namespace entry , because the websocket is GET /<ns> with an upgrade. Choose a namespace name that no front end route starts with. Vite matches proxy keys by prefix. Load the client with a plain <script src="/seamless-client.js"> tag and call connect_seamless(null, null, "<ns>") once, from its own small module that turns shared cells into the framework's reactive state. Hot-swapping a component re-evaluates its module; keeping the connection in its own module prevents a second websocket. State kept in writable shared cells survives full page reloads and is visible to Python. Keep the front end's durable state there. A no-build page can instead be a text cell mounted with mode="r" (as in the example). An edit is served within the mount's polling interval, but the browser is not told and must be reloaded by hand. Do not compile inside the Context. A build step run as a transformer puts the sources and node_modules into the cache key and pays a full build per save. Compile offline; let the graph record only the result.
docs.title: Two processes

docs.text: The front end hot-reloads by itself. The Seamless side has three mechanisms, which differ in what they cost and what state they keep. 1. Live edit 2. %run -i reload 3. Restart What you do change cells and the graph in the live session re-run the script in IPython stop and start the process Context the same object closed, a new one built a new process Share server untouched untouched restarted State written from a browser kept reset to the script's defaults, unless mounted reset, unless mounted Front end shares message on the websocket no disconnect; only changed values are announced disconnect, then reconnect Requires the script kept in step a script that is safe to re-run mounted state; a hardened client
docs.title: Three ways to change the Seamless side

docs.text: Zero restart. Assign cells, transformers and connections in the running session, by hand or by a coding agent attached to it; the workflow recomputes and the browser follows. The script is the source of truth; the live session is a preview. Every live change must also be made in backend.py , or the next reload or restart reverts it. Adding or removing a share is announced to the front end as a new shares message on the websocket, which calls onsharelist . Attach handlers for new keys there. /openapi.json is generated per request and is always current. There is no push for it. A front end that keeps a copy (generated types, a key list) re-fetches it after the cell list changes; the websocket shares message is the trigger.
docs.title: 1. Live edit in the interactive session

docs.text: The script is re-run in IPython's interactive namespace. This is the equivalent of a hot reload. The workflow Context is replaced (the ctx variable is re-defined); the share server is not , because it exists independently of Contexts. Write the script so that it is safe to re-run: # backend.py: run with `python -i backend.py`, reload with `%run -i backend.py` try: ctx.close() # the previous run's Context; frees its namespace except NameError: pass # first run ctx = start() Close the old Context first. A second live Context claiming a taken namespace raises ValueError("Share namespace '<name>' is in use") . Guard shareserver.configure with if shareserver.url is None , as start() above does. configure() after the server started raises RuntimeError . Do not call seamless.close() in a reloadable script. It stops the share server. Keep it for a non-interactive main() that runs once and exits. A reload resets state that browsers wrote. The new Context starts from the script's defaults. Mount the cells that must survive (mechanism 3). Markers keep increasing across the reload. A re-shared URL continues its marker sequence for the lifetime of the server. The hold on close keeps the reload invisible in the browser for values that did not change ( contracts/shares.md , The hold on close ): ctx.close() does not remove the shares at once. The server keeps serving them, with their checksums and markers, for a hold window (10 s by default), and keeps the websockets open. The Context's teardown is not visible, and /openapi.json does not drop to an empty document. The new Context's first share takes the namespace over, and each share at a held URL re-attaches . A cell whose value is unchanged produces no marker bump and therefore no websocket update. A cell whose value differs produces one ordinary update. A PUT sent during the reload waits for its share to be re-attached, and is then processed by the new Context. A held share that the new script no longer makes is removed when the window ends, as on any close. The hold serves; it never carries a value into the new Context. State that a browser wrote into an unmounted cell still returns to the script's default.
docs.title: 2. %run -i: reload the script, keep the server

docs.text: A mounted cell keeps its value in a file. That makes state survive a %run -i reload and a full restart of the Seamless process , a "tepid reload". ctx.params = Cell(celltype="plain") ctx.params.set({"threshold": 0.5}) # the default; set it before mounting ctx.params.mount("state/params.json", mode="rw", authority="file") ctx.params.share(readonly=False) First run : the file is absent, so the default is written to it. Every later run : the file wins over the script's default ( contracts/mounts.md , The initial decision table , row 11, logged once). Every accepted PUT is written to the file , and an edit of the file is served and announced. authority resolves only the initial conflict. After attach, every file change and every cell change flows as usual. Mount only state worth keeping. Do not mount derived cells; they are recomputed. Keep the state directory out of version control. persistent=True is the default ; the file survives unmount and Context close.
docs.title: 3. Mounts with authority="file": persistent state

docs.text: A restarted process restarts its markers. The front end must cope with a server that vanishes and comes back. Reconnect automatically. seamless-client.js retries a lost websocket with backoff (1 s, doubling, up to 30 s). Every connection starts with a shares message that carries the checksum and marker of every share in the namespace. The client's restart rule ( contracts/shares.md , seamless-client.js ): if, after reconnecting, the markers are lower than the ones the front end already holds, the server process restarted. One key that is exactly one lower, because the server has not yet processed the client's own PUT to it, does not count. Mounted cells were restored from their files, so the front end's own state is current: the client adopts the new markers and does not re-read the values. If that was wrong (unmounted state was reset), the user reloads the page by hand. A write sent after a restart, before the client has adopted the new markers, carries the old marker. It is normally refused with 409 , and the client drops the local change. Until the reconnect lets the client conclude that the server restarted, it ignores the server's lower marker, so the page keeps showing the dropped change until the reconnect; the client then reads that value. Show a disconnected state instead of letting the user edit as if connected.
docs.title: Hardening the front end for restarts

docs.text: Development needs Node, a dev server and a live interactive Context. Deployment needs none of them: a built, static front end, and a Context that serves it. There are two levels.
docs.title: Deployment

docs.text: For a front end that is one hand-written file, the development script is already the deployment , as in examples/share-sliders : a text cell mounted with mode="r" and shared at the top level, plus the data cells. Run python serve.py , bind explicitly, and put a reverse proxy in front. A built application (many hashed files) runs into five limits of this level: One cell per file. Folder cells cannot be shared. Top-level share keys have one segment. /assets/x.js cannot be a top-level share; inside a namespace a key may have several segments. Hashed names change on every build , so the set of mounted shares changes. The browser client never reports changes of file-like shares. Keys with a . are not auto-read. The redirect from / and /<ns>/ to index.html drops the query string. Level 2 absorbs the first limit in the pack tool, and removes the other four: files are shared under a namespace at their relative paths, every build is a new graph so changing names cost nothing, a running graph's files never change, and the proxy can redirect / with the query string kept.
docs.title: Level 1: the serving script

docs.text: Compile offline, pack dist/ into a Context with one bytes cell per file, each shared at its path, and save the graph. The graph holds only checksums; the bytes live on a hashserver. A generic server loads the graph and serves it. The server needs no Node and no application code. src/ --npm run build--> dist/ --pack--> Context (one bytes cell per file + backend nodes) | get_graph() | publish v v graph.json (checksums) hashserver --rsync--> deploy hashserver | | +-----> generic server: set_graph(mounts=False, shares=True) --resolves--+
docs.title: Level 2: pack the build into a graph

docs.text: Set base: './' in the Vite config and run the production build: npm ci # reproducible install; pin the Node version npm run build # vite build -> dist/ base: './' makes the page load its assets relative to wherever index.html is served, so the same build works under any namespace. Keep Vite's content hashes in deployment builds. Each build produces a new graph, so changing names cost nothing, and the proxy can mark assets immutable. Files loaded at run time (workers, .wasm , fonts) must be in dist/ too, with pinned content types.
docs.title: 1. Build with a relative base

docs.text: The pack tool is generic: it walks dist/ , makes a cell per file, shares it at its relative path and writes the graph. If the application has a backend, call its build(ctx) first (without a page_path ), so static files and backend nodes end up in one graph. import json, mimetypes from pathlib import Path import seamless, seamless.config from seamless import Cell from seamless_workflow import Context, shareserver NULL_CONTENTS = (b"", b"null\n", b"null") # these are null: the share would answer 204 def node_name(rel): # "assets/index-DD5wxIS0.js" -> "web__assets__index_DD5wxIS0_js" return "web__" + "".join(c if c.isalnum() else "_" for c in rel.replace("/", "__")) def pack(dist, graph_out, backend=None): seamless.config.init() # build stage: a writable hashserver shareserver.configure(host="127.0.0.1", port=0) # share() records specs; nothing is exposed ctx = Context() try: if backend is not None: backend(ctx) # the application's own nodes names = set() for f in sorted(Path(dist).rglob("*")): if not f.is_file(): continue rel = f.relative_to(dist).as_posix() data = f.read_bytes() if data in NULL_CONTENTS: raise ValueError(f"{rel}: content would be served as null (204)") name = node_name(rel) if name in names: raise ValueError(f"{rel}: node name collision") names.add(name) mimetype = mimetypes.guess_type(rel)[0] or "application/octet-stream" setattr(ctx, name, Cell(celltype="bytes")) cell = getattr(ctx, name) cell.set(data) cell.share(path=rel, mimetype=mimetype) # pinned into the graph's share entry graph = ctx.get_graph() finally: ctx.close() seamless.close() # flushes pending hashserver writes Path(graph_out).write_text(json.dumps(graph, indent=1, sort_keys=True)) What the pack tool must get right: Run it as its own process. seamless.close() ends Seamless for the whole process: no Context can be built afterwards, and neither can a second pack or a serve . The same holds for the serving process below. Celltype bytes for every file. It is the one celltype whose buffer is the file as it is, so the served body is the built file byte for byte. Pin the content type at pack time. Without a mimetype , the server guesses from the extension on the serving host, and a browser refuses a module script that is not served with a JavaScript type. The pinned value is stored in the graph's share entry. Refuse null contents. An empty file, or one that is exactly null , is the null value, and a share answers 204 with no body. Generated node names. The share path carries the real file name; the node name is only an identifier. Publishing is automatic : a non-scratch cell publishes its literal to the hashserver when the Context claims it. seamless.close() reports buffers it could not write; treat that as a failed build. Verify before shipping. Batch-check every checksum in the graph against the hashserver's GET /has-now , which, unlike /has , does not count buffers that are only promised.
docs.title: 2. Pack

docs.text: Build side Deploy side Mode writable read-only when the graph has no writable shares and no transformers; writable once PUT values or computed results must survive Contents every buffer the Context published a copy: the buffer directory is plain files named by checksum, so rsync transfers only what is new Reachability build machine or CI only the serving process only; never public Unchanged files are never uploaded or transferred again.
docs.title: 3. Hashserver

docs.text: The shipped command loads one saved graph and serves its declared shares. Install seamless-suite for the seamless-serve-graph entry point and its HTTP dependency. The implementation is seamless_workflow.serve_graph:main ; python -m seamless_workflow.serve_graph is equivalent. seamless-serve-graph graph.json The share contract defines the command's behavior. Give it a local UTF-8 JSON file containing a current workflow graph. A graph with shares uses __seamless_workflow__: "0.6" or later, and a graph with downloads "0.7" ; older current workflow versions cannot declare them. Original legacy exports need migration before this command can load them. The runner creates one Context in the default ctx namespace and calls ctx.set_graph(graph, mounts=False, shares=True) . Graph-declared file mounts are disabled; shares are restored. A graph can also contain transformers, which begin deriving when loaded. Open /ctx/index.html for a page shared there. A share declared toplevel=True can be served from /index.html . The share server uses its normal bind configuration, currently 0.0.0.0:5813 by default. Configure the listener in Python with seamless_workflow.shareserver.configure() if you need a different address or port in a custom serving script. The command has no listener flags. Its HTTP and websocket endpoints use the current share protocol and built-in /seamless-client.js . Put the desired cluster and execution mode in the usual seamless-config files for the directory from which you launch the command. The runner initializes that configuration before creating the Context, so a configured hashserver, database, jobserver or daskserver is used through the normal modern stack. See Setting up a local cluster and Remote execution . The command has no remote-service flags. The runner does not query /has-now for every referenced buffer. Check availability as a separate deployment step if a later browser 503 is unacceptable. SIGINT or SIGTERM closes the Context and Seamless. There is no dedicated health endpoint; GET /openapi.json shows the HTTP server is responding, while GET /ctx/state-graph reports node states.
docs.title: 4. Serve

docs.text: The share server has no compression, no TLS and no long-lived caching. A reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) supplies them: Compression and TLS termination. Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable on /<ns>/assets/* . This is safe only because the deployment build keeps content hashes. Every share response otherwise carries Cache-Control: no-cache with the checksum as ETag , so every page load revalidates every file. Redirect / straight to /<ns>/index.html , keeping the query string, instead of relying on the server's own 302 , which drops it. Access control , and the exposure rules below.
docs.title: 5. Reverse proxy

docs.text: Every share is readable by anyone who reaches the port , and every writable share is writable by them. Bind to loopback and let the proxy do access control. /<ns>/state-graph and /openapi.json are always served. The state graph carries every node's path, celltype, state, checksum and error text, also for nodes that are not shared. Block the state-graph path at the proxy if it must not be public. Loading a graph opens endpoints and can run transformer code. Deploy a graph file you built and verified. If an application must inspect a graph of unknown origin, load it through the Python API with shares=False and mounts=False . One Context means one shared state. For a tool where each user has their own state, load the static graph once at a fixed namespace, and give each session its own backend Context at its own namespace, built from a template graph. The page reads the session id from its URL and calls connect_seamless(null, null, "s-" + id) . Sessions share the static buffers, because the checksums are the same. The share server has no custom routes, so creating sessions needs a small control listener, with idle expiry (not yet implemented) . Keep a versioned graph file for each release. The serving command reads a local JSON file; deploy that file and its referenced buffers together. Rolling back means launching a previous graph file whose buffers are still available. The compile step is outside Seamless identity. The graph records what was built, not how. Record the "how" in a cell (git commit, lockfile checksum, exact Node version) and share it read-only, so the page can show it.
docs.title: Exposure, state and releases

docs.text: The destination of level 2 is that the static front end and the Python backend ship as one kind of artifact : a saved workflow graph, with backend nodes recomputed or cache-hit on the server's execution backend. The generic seamless-serve-graph command serves a local graph file now; Cloudless for per-session instances remains unimplemented. Build the application so that its server side is a build(ctx) function: that is the part that moves into the graph unchanged.
docs.title: Taking it further: serve a workflow as data

docs.text: Model each shown or edited quantity as a cell; inputs are writable shares, outputs are read-only shares of connected cells. Keep all logic in the graph. Add no request code. Develop with the dev server in front, python -i backend.py behind, a namespace of its own, and /seamless-client.js and /openapi.json proxied. Keep the script in step with every live edit; keep it safe to re-run with %run -i (close the old Context, guard configure , no seamless.close() ). Mount, with authority="file" , the state that must survive reloads. Harden the client: reconnect, tolerate a restarted server, never assume a write succeeded. Deploy with relative base, pinned content types, hashed names, a hashserver copy, a startup check and a reverse proxy.
docs.title: Checklist

docs.text: Exercised against the code: bytes cells shared at multi-segment paths with a pinned mimetype ; the share entry in get_graph() and the absence of a mount entry for unmounted cells; set_graph(graph, mounts=False, shares=True) into a fresh Context under the same namespace, with markers continuing; the ValueError for a namespace that a live Context holds; the share server staying up after ctx.close() ; authority="file" persistence of a PUT across two Contexts; the build / start example and its %run -i header (a PUT to a recomputes c ; the old Context is closed, the namespace is re-claimed and the defaults return); and the pack and serve sketches, run in a single process over the local buffer cache. That run showed the graph holding only value.checksum per cell node, pinned content types, no mount entries, bodies equal to the files, and GET /<ns>/ answering the index.html share. The graph-serving command is implemented. Its focused tests cover the required graph-file argument, JSON loading into a Context, a real Context's serialized-graph path, configuration initialization, cleanup after loading fails, and signal handler restoration. The command uses current workflow serialization and the modern share protocol. Not implemented, and described above as the intended behaviour: The pack tool as a shipped command (the code above is a sketch) and Cloudless . Not verified: The hold on close and the client's restart rule ( contracts/shares.md ) in the reload and restart workflows above. The hashserver round trip: pack and serve as separate processes, with the buffers transferred through a hashserver, and the startup check against /has-now . Whether a Context with a read-only hashserver tries to publish the literals it fetches. Declare the hashserver read-only in the deployment configuration and look for write attempts in its log. Behaviour of Cell.set() for a single value of several MB. The contract states a 1 GiB request limit for PUT.

docs.text: Seamless Command Language seamless_config discovers configuration through two optional files in the work directory and its parents: File Recommended policy Purpose seamless.yaml Commit to version control Project-wide, deterministic defaults seamless.profile.yaml Add to .gitignore Local, developer-specific overrides (e.g. cluster hostnames or experimental settings) Both files use the same command language described below. load_config_files() reads the file pair in the current workdir. If either file contains inherit_from_parent , the loader also inspects the parent directory and prepends its commands so they run before the child’s entries. This repeats until a directory without inherit_from_parent is reached (or the filesystem root), which means parent defaults are always applied before the local overrides. Syntax Each document must be a YAML list. Every list item is either a bare command name ( inherit_from_parent ) or a single-key mapping ( cluster: newton ). If the file parses as valid YAML but not a list, the loader raises an error and shows an example ( - project: myproject ). Available commands Command Arguments Description cluster string Calls seamless_config.select_cluster(value) execution string ( process / spawn / remote ) Calls seamless_config.select_execution(value) queue string Calls seamless_config.select_queue(value) remote null or string ( daskserver / jobserver ) Calls seamless_config.select_remote(value) persistent boolean Calls seamless_config.select_persistent(value) record boolean Calls seamless_config.select_record(value) . When true , successful executions persist a full execution record (environment fingerprints, compilation context, freshness, etc.) instead of the default minimal record. Invalidates the cached record-mode flag in the transformer runtime. node string or null Calls seamless_config.select_node(value) . Selects a named node within the active cluster (advanced: cluster-internal scheduling). project string Calls seamless_config.select_project(value) subproject string Calls seamless_config.select_subproject(value) inherit_from_parent – Also read commands from the parent directory and prepend them clusters mapping Updates the local _clusters dict and runs before other commands stage <name> list of commands Executes the nested list only when the current stage equals <name> The queue command requires the current cluster to expose queues in its definition and fails with a ValueError when the named queue is missing. The remote command accepts only null , daskserver or jobserver . The persistent command forces persistent storage on or off; when omitted it defaults to true if a cluster is selected and false otherwise. Internally, commands are split into two passes: those with priority (currently only clusters ) and the rest. Between the passes the loader calls seamless_config.cluster.define_clusters(_clusters) so the later commands use the freshest cluster data. If no execution command is encountered, init() defaults to remote when a cluster is selected and otherwise falls back to process . Clusters only need to be defined when execution is set to remote ; for other modes, an undefined cluster triggers a warning that also notes that persistence is unavailable, while execution: remote without a cluster raises an error. Stage blocks Stage-specific configuration uses YAML keys that begin with stage and a literal stage name. For example: - stage build: - execution: remote When seamless_config.select_stage("build") has been called, the commands inside the block are executed as if they appeared in the outer list; otherwise they are skipped. Example # seamless.yaml (checked in) - project: my-shared-project - inherit_from_parent # seamless.profile.yaml (ignored in Git) - clusters: local: tunnel: false frontends: [...] mycluster: tunnel: true frontends: [...] - cluster: local - stage prod: - cluster: mycluster The seamless.profile.yaml snippet defines the local and mycluster clusters, selects the local entry as the active cluster, and only switches to the mycluster cluster when the current stage equals prod .

docs.text: Here is the final version of the plan proposed in shutdown.md point 5, taking Codex's comments at the end of the document into account. There will be only one central shutdown routine, part of seamless-core , and called seamless.close() , analogous to file.close() . All current shutdown logic is moved into this routine.For now, the user is asked to call seamless.close() when the interpreter shuts down to get the guarantee of no-buffer-writes-lost and no-interpreter-hang-at-shutdown. The routine will also register itself with atexit . At the beginning it sets a flag so that it won't run twice. Also, it won't run from inside a spawned worker. At the beginning, after the run-twice flag check, it will check if it was called from atexit . If so, a warning is printed that it should have been called earlier. As soon as shutdown starts, worker restarts are disabled (manager/handles restart flags are cleared) so no workers are respawned during shutdown. Then, it will inspect sys.modules to detect which Seamless packages were actually imported. Parts a.-d. need only a shutdown if seamless-remote has been imported. Parts e.-h. need only a shutdown if seamless-transformer has been imported, and worker.has_spawned() is True. The shutdown routine itself may not make any imports, since it may be executed at interpreter shutdown. Then, a global seamless._closed flag is set. Main thread coroutines involving Buffer, Checksum and Transformation instances are asked to check for this flag at the beginning and after every await, and exit (preferably silently) when this flag is set. The same is true for request coroutines from the workers to the main process. Worker monitor/health asyncio also stops running because of this flag. Coroutines that do not observe the flag in time are cancelled after a gentle timeout, to prevent hanging shutdown. Spawned workers now receive a shutdown request. Coroutines created by the process manager corresponding to requests and responses are now cancelled and/or their threads are joined, with a gentle timeout. The process manager’s event loop thread and default executor are then stopped/shutdown so no daemon threads remain. Spawned worker processes now receive an interrupt signal, and a join is attempted with a short shutdown. It is recorded which processes did not die. The parent-side RPC pipe plumbing is now shut down, apart from the shared memory blocks. The buffers still inside the buffer writer queue are now extracted into a list, and the queue itself is being shut down. The remote-client keepalive worker and the aiohttp sessions are also shut down, gently. This routine assumes buffer write clients/servers were configured and activated earlier; it will not import or configure them at shutdown. A first attempt is made to write the buffers using sync HTTP requests, using 1 sec timeout per megabyte of the buffer, for a minimum of 3 seconds. Exceptions are silently caught. Successfully written buffers are removed from the list. Ordering of transformation DB entries vs. buffer uploads is not enforced here: if a DB entry survives but a result buffer is missing, recomputation remains possible provided the input buffers (the transformation JSON dict and its referenced buffers) were written remotely; “scratch” paths intentionally skip result storage. Ensuring input buffers are persisted remains the prerequisite for the cache guarantee. The spawned workers are now more aggressively killed (SIGTERM). Regardless of whether they exit, the parent sweeps its shared memory: for each worker PID, reset_pid is called on the SharedMemoryRegistry and then the registry is closed; any remaining pointers tracked by _WorkerManager._pointers are released/unlinked. The aiohttp sessions are now aggressively killed, printing exceptions on failure. A final attempt is made to write the buffers using sync HTTP requests, with double the timeout. Exceptions are printed. Any buffers still unwritten after the second attempt are reported/aggregated (per checksum and target); no silent drop remains. The maximum effort to kill a spawn worker is made (SIGKILL). If that still doesn't work, a warning is printed out that the interpreter may hang upon exit. All joins/flushes use bounded timeouts where possible. An aggregated summary of outstanding failures (buffer writes that never completed, workers requiring SIGKILL, shm sweep status) is emitted before any unbounded or high-risk step; only then are desperate measures attempted.
